band-e-kaisar-260.summary: After defeating Valerian in 260, Sasanian king Shapur I settles Roman prisoners in Khuzestan, where tradition and Arabic geographers credit them with building 'Caesar's dam' at Shushtar: a 500-metre masonry weir carrying a road on arches, raising Karun river water to feed canals, with water channelled through mill races cut in rock. This complex, with Gargar canal and later mills, forms Shushtar Historical Hydraulic System, inscribed by UNESCO in 2009. Hartung and Kuros's engineering study describes dam, bridge and sluices as one design. Claims that Sasanian Persia also had windmills rest on a story about Umar's assassin in 644; first reliable descriptions of Sistan's vertical-axis windmills come from al-Masudi and al-Istakhri in the tenth century.

sources.title: Hartung, Fritz and Kuros, Gh. R., 'Historische Talsperren im Iran', in Garbrecht (ed.), 'Historische Talsperren', vol. 1, Wittwer (1987), pp. 221-274
sources.author: Hartung, Fritz; Kuros, Gh. R.
sources.confirms: Engineering survey of Sasanian dams including Band-e Kaisar at Shushtar, its weir, arched bridge and canal functions.

sources.title: Lucas, Adam, 'Wind, Water, Work: Ancient and Medieval Milling Technology', Brill (2006)
sources.author: Lucas, Adam
sources.confirms: Reviews Sasanian water mills and dam-bridges.
sources.qualifies: Finds no reliable evidence for Persian windmills before the ninth to tenth centuries; the seventh-century anecdote is late and unverifiable.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Shushtar Historical Hydraulic System'
sources.confirms: Describes the Band-e Kaisar, Gargar canal and mills as a Sasanian-era hydraulic system of the third century CE.

band-e-kaisar-260.verification_note: Attribution to Roman prisoners after 260 derives from medieval Arabic sources; archaeological dating is Sasanian but not year-specific.
band-e-kaisar-260.detail: Construction is dated by tradition of Roman captives after 260 and by Sasanian masonry; no inscription survives, so 260 is approximate. A Roman-engineer story comes from Tabari and later writers and most historians accept it as plausible, since Shapur's inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam boasts of deporting Roman populations to Persia. Surviving mills at Shushtar are medieval and later rebuilds on Sasanian channels. Adam Lucas's survey finds no Sasanian windmill evidence; vertical-axis mills of Sistan are first described in ninth- and tenth-century Arabic geography, and horizontal-axis European windmills appear only after 1180.

picture.alt: Band-e Kaisar bridge-dam at Shushtar, Iran
picture.credit: Jb-mhr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

band-e-kaisar-260.dating_note: Attribution to Roman prisoners after 260 derives from medieval Arabic sources; archaeological dating is Sasanian but not year-specific.

liu-hui-pi-263.summary: In his 263 commentary on Jiuzhang suanshu, Liu Hui supplies justifications for its procedures, among them an argument for Pythagorean rule by dissection, a limit argument for a circle's area, and 'cutting the circle' (geyuan shu): starting from a hexagon he doubles sides to 96 and bounds pi near 3.14, noting that continuing gives 3.1416 at 3,072 sides. He also treats a pyramid's volume by infinite decomposition and appends Haidao suanjing, nine survey problems using double differences. Karine Chemla's work shows his commentary makes algorithms' correctness explicit. Dated by his own preface to Jingyuan's fourth year, it is China's earliest extant mathematical proof text.

sources.title: Chemla, Karine, 'Geometrical Figures and Generality in Ancient China and Beyond: Liu Hui and Zhao Shuang, Plato and Thabit ibn Qurra', Science in Context 18 (2005)
sources.author: Chemla, Karine
sources.confirms: Analyses Liu Hui's 263 commentary as a body of proofs and his use of figures in the Nine Chapters.

sources.title: 'Jiuzhang suanshu' with Liu Hui's commentary and preface, digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Liu Hui
sources.confirms: Liu Hui's preface and commentary, including the circle-cutting method under problem 1.31 (今有圓田) and references to 徽術.

sources.title: Lam Lay Yong and Shen Kangshen, 'The Chinese concept of Cavalieri's principle and its applications', Historia Mathematica 12 (1985)
sources.author: Lam Lay Yong; Shen Kangshen
sources.confirms: Explains Liu Hui's volume arguments and the later Zu Geng principle.

liu-hui-pi-263.detail: Year 263 comes from Liu Hui's preface. Whether his 3.1416 value at 3,072 sides is his or a later interpolation is debated; some manuscripts attribute it to him explicitly. Haidao suanjing uses pairs of gnomons to measure an island's height and distance, a surveying algorithm later copied in Tang state examinations. Liu Hui's principle that 'the finer we cut, the less is lost' anticipates limit reasoning, and his treatment of a yangma pyramid argues by repeated halving that remainders vanish. He also noted that a sphere-volume formula in Nine Chapters was wrong, a problem Zu Geng solved two centuries later.

picture.alt: Diagram of Liu Hui's sea island survey problem using two gnomons
picture.credit: Diagram after Liu Hui, later edition, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

aksum-coinage-270.summary: Around 270 CE Endubis, king of Aksum in northern Ethiopia, issues coins in three metals bearing his portrait, name and title in Greek, with an ear of barley or wheat and a disc-and-crescent symbol. Later kings add Ge'ez legends for bronze and, from Ezana's reign in the 340s, replace pagan symbols with a cross, making Aksum among the first states to put Christian imagery on money. David Phillipson's synthesis treats coinage as evidence for Aksum's Red Sea trade with Rome, South Arabia and India; gold issues follow Roman weight standards. Aksumite coins turn up at Arikamedu and in Yemen. Minting continues until about 620, when Persian and Arab expansion cuts Red Sea routes. Earlier states south of Egypt, including Meroe, never struck coin.

sources.title: Phillipson, David W., 'Foundations of an African Civilisation: Aksum and the Northern Horn, 1000 BC - AD 1300', James Currey (2012)
sources.author: Phillipson, David W.
sources.confirms: Dates Aksumite coinage from Endubis c. 270 CE, describes metals, legends and Christian symbols and discusses trade.

sources.title: Munro-Hay, Stuart, 'Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity', Edinburgh University Press (1991)
sources.author: Munro-Hay, Stuart
sources.confirms: Chapter 9 catalogues Aksumite coinage from Endubis, with Greek legends and trimetallic issues.

sources.title: British Museum, 'Gold coin of Endubis, king of Aksum', collection record
sources.confirms: Museum record of Endubis gold coinage dated c. 270 to 290 CE.

aksum-coinage-270.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
aksum-coinage-270.detail: Coinage dating rests on stylistic sequence and Roman weight standards, so 270 is approximate within c. 270 to 290. No Aksumite coin carries a date. Hoard evidence and die studies by Munro-Hay underpin a king list; absolute years for early kings depend on few external references, including Mani's Kephalaia naming Aksum among four great kingdoms of his day. Gold coins weigh about 2.7 grams, half a Roman aureus. Legends read 'Endubis king of Aksum, man of Dakhu' in Greek, and some issues add 'Bisi Dakhu', a clan or regimental title repeated by later kings. Gilding of silver and bronze coins is a feature unique to Aksum.

picture.alt: Gold coin of Aphilas, king of Aksum, early fourth century
picture.credit: Roma Numismatics (coin of Aphilas), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

tikal-stela-29-292.summary: Stela 29 at Tikal, Guatemala, carries a Long Count date of 8.12.14.8.15, equivalent to 6 July 292 CE, and a portrait of a ruler holding a double-headed serpent bar; it is Maya lowlands' earliest dated monument. Long Count notation counts days from a base in 3114 BCE in a modified vigesimal system of baktuns, katuns, tuns, winals and kins, a positional scheme requiring a zero placeholder. Simon Martin's synthesis of Maya political history follows dated stelae from Tikal, Calakmul, Copan and dozens of other kingdoms through 909 CE, documenting dynasties, wars and alliances. Calakmul's eroded early monuments show a rival state in Campeche that contested Tikal through the Classic period; its earliest dated monument, Stela 114, is from 435 CE.

sources.title: Martin, Simon, 'Ancient Maya Politics: A Political Anthropology of the Classic Period 150-900 CE', Cambridge University Press (2020)
sources.author: Martin, Simon
sources.confirms: Uses dated monuments from Tikal Stela 29 (292 CE) onward to reconstruct Classic Maya dynastic politics including the Tikal-Calakmul rivalry.

sources.title: Houston, Stephen et al., 'A Maya royal palace, residential compound and city: the Tikal-Calakmul rivalry reconsidered', Antiquity 95 (2021)
sources.author: Houston, Stephen; Garrison, Thomas; Roman, Edwin
sources.confirms: Discusses Tikal's early monuments and its relations with Calakmul.

sources.title: Kennett, Douglas J. et al., 'Correlating the Ancient Maya and Modern European Calendars with High-Precision AMS 14C Dating', Scientific Reports 3 (2013)
sources.author: Kennett, Douglas J.
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon dating of a Tikal lintel supports the GMT correlation used to convert Long Count dates to 292 CE.

tikal-stela-29-292.detail: Date depends on GMT correlation, confirmed by Kennett's 2013 AMS dating of Tikal Temple I lintel wood. Stela 29 was found broken in a dump in 1959, so original context is lost; its ruler is unnamed or named on a missing fragment, though Martin links him to Tikal's dynasty founder Yax Ehb Xook's successors. Earlier Long Count dates exist on Gulf coast monuments and at Takalik Abaj and El Baul in Guatemala's Pacific piedmont. Calakmul's Stela 114 of 435 CE is its earliest dated monument. Over 5,000 Maya inscriptions survive, most carved between 250 and 900.

picture.alt: Temples at Tikal, Guatemala
picture.credit: Laslovarga, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

codex-replaces-scroll-300.summary: Roberts and Skeat's survey of dated Egyptian book fragments showed codices rising from near zero in first century to parity with rolls around 300 CE and dominance by 400. Christian scriptures appear in codex form from their earliest second-century witnesses, while pagan literature stays on rolls far longer. Bagnall's 2009 reassessment argues Christian preference reflects cost and small-community book production rather than theology, and dates early Christian codices more cautiously. Codices allow random access, two-sided writing and larger texts in one volume, enabling collections like Codex Sinaiticus (mid fourth century) which binds a complete Bible. By 500 CE parchment codices are Europe's and Mediterranean's normal book form.

sources.title: Roberts, Colin H. and Skeat, T. C., 'The Birth of the Codex', Oxford University Press for the British Academy (1983); reviewed by Gamble, Journal of Biblical Literature 104 (1985)
sources.author: Roberts, Colin H.; Skeat, T. C.
sources.confirms: Tabulates surviving Greek books by century, showing the codex reaching parity with the roll around 300 CE and near-universal Christian use of the codex.

sources.title: Bagnall, Roger S., 'Early Christian Books in Egypt', Princeton University Press (2009)
sources.author: Bagnall, Roger S.
sources.confirms: Re-examines dating of early Christian codices and the economics of book production.
sources.qualifies: Argues palaeographic dates for second-century Christian codices are often too early and that cost, not theology, drove Christian codex use.

codex-replaces-scroll-300.verification_note: Parity of codex and roll around 300 CE is a statistical inference from dated fragments; adoption spans the second to fifth centuries.
codex-replaces-scroll-300.detail: Year 300 marks statistical parity rather than a single event and is approximate. Martial around 85 CE advertises parchment codices of his poems as travel editions, earliest literary reference. Wax tablet notebooks (pugillares) are a likely ancestor. Parchment replaces papyrus in codices over fourth century, partly because folded sheets of skin tolerate sewing better. Leuven Database of Ancient Books now lets scholars re-run Roberts and Skeat's counts with thousands more fragments; proportions hold, though dating of individual papyri by handwriting alone carries wide margins. Codex Sinaiticus, with about 730 surviving leaves, was written by at least three scribes around 350.

picture.alt: Page of Codex Sinaiticus, fourth century, opening of Matthew
picture.credit: Codex Sinaiticus Project, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

codex-replaces-scroll-300.dating_note: Parity of codex and roll around 300 CE is a statistical inference from dated fragments; adoption spans the second to fifth centuries.

kofun-300.summary: From mid third century, communities in Nara basin build zenpo-koen-fun, keyhole-shaped mounds up to 486 metres long surrounded by moats and ringed with haniwa clay cylinders and figures. Hashihaka at Sakurai is among earliest; Daisen kofun at Sakai, attributed to Nintoku and dated to fifth century, is largest. Grave goods shift from bronze mirrors and jasper bracelets to iron armour, swords, and horse trappings including stirrups by fifth century, tracing imported technology from Korea. Mozu-Furuichi group was inscribed by UNESCO in 2019. Gina Barnes's work on state formation reads kofun scale and distribution as a record of political hierarchy forming under Yamato leadership.

sources.title: Barnes, Gina L., 'State Formation in Japan: Emergence of a 4th-Century Ruling Elite', Routledge (2007)
sources.author: Barnes, Gina L.
sources.confirms: Analyses early kofun (third to fourth centuries), mound typology, grave goods and the emergence of a Yamato elite.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group: Mounded Tombs of Ancient Japan'
sources.confirms: Describes 49 kofun of the third to sixth centuries including Daisen kofun, keyhole form, moats, haniwa and grave goods.

sources.title: Mizoguchi, Koji, 'The Archaeology of Japan: From the Earliest Rice Farming Villages to the Rise of the State', Cambridge University Press (2013)
sources.author: Mizoguchi, Koji
sources.confirms: Covers kofun chronology and the shift to iron armour and horse gear in the fifth century.

kofun-300.verification_note: Early kofun chronology relies on pottery seriation and contested radiocarbon dates; period boundaries are conventional.
kofun-300.detail: Kofun period conventionally runs c. 250 to 600; 300 is a representative year and approximate. Hashihaka's dating to 240s to 260s by radiocarbon on pottery residues is debated, bearing on identification with Himiko of Wei zhi. Imperial Household Agency restrictions limit excavation of largest mounds. Daisen kofun's mound is 486 metres long with three moats covering 46 hectares, and Edo-period estimates of labour run to 2,000 workers for sixteen years. Haniwa figures of warriors, horses, houses and boats, placed on mound terraces, record armour types and saddle gear otherwise known only from Korean and Chinese parallels.

picture.alt: Daisen kofun keyhole mound and moat, Sakai
picture.credit: Sakai Yayoi, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

kofun-300.dating_note: Early kofun chronology relies on pottery seriation and contested radiocarbon dates; period boundaries are conventional.

moche-gilding-300.summary: Heather Lechtman's analysis of Moche objects from Loma Negra in Peru's Piura valley revealed gold and silver surface layers on copper only 0.5 to 2 microns thick, far thinner than leaf or fusion gilding. Replication experiments showed that dissolving gold in a hot solution of corrosive minerals (salts and nitre, as found in Peruvian deserts) and dipping copper causes gold to plate out by replacement; heating then bonds this film. Dated by style and radiocarbon to about 100 to 400 CE, this is a chemical plating process achieved without electricity, 1,500 years before Volta. Moche smiths also alloy tumbaga and use depletion gilding. Lechtman argues Andean metallurgy valued colour and surface over hardness, a cultural rather than purely technical logic.

sources.title: Lechtman, Heather, 'Pre-Columbian Surface Metallurgy', Scientific American 250 (1984)
sources.author: Lechtman, Heather
sources.confirms: Describes electrochemical replacement gilding on Moche copper from Loma Negra and replication experiments.

sources.title: Lechtman, Heather, 'Andean Value Systems and the Development of Prehistoric Metallurgy', Technology and Culture 25 (1984)
sources.author: Lechtman, Heather
sources.confirms: Interprets Moche surface metallurgy within Andean cultural values.

sources.title: Lechtman, Heather; Erlij, Antonieta; Barry, Edward J., 'New Perspectives on Moche Metallurgy: Techniques of Gilding Copper at Loma Negra, Northern Peru', American Antiquity 47 (1982)
sources.author: Lechtman, Heather; Erlij, Antonieta; Barry, Edward J.
sources.confirms: Technical report of microanalysis and dating of Loma Negra gilded objects to the early Moche period.

moche-gilding-300.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
moche-gilding-300.detail: Loma Negra objects are unprovenanced from looting, so dating is stylistic (Moche I to III) with a range of about 100 to 400 CE; 300 is approximate. Whether Moche smiths understood plating as a chemical process is unknowable, but repeatability across many objects shows controlled practice. Later Sican and Chimu smiths continued these methods. Sipan's royal tombs, excavated by Walter Alva from 1987, add gilded copper, gold and silver regalia of about 250 to 300 CE in secure context. Lechtman's experiments used solutions of common salt, potassium nitrate and potassium aluminium sulphate, all available in coastal Peru.

picture.alt: Moche gilded copper animal ornament from Loma Negra, Metropolitan Museum of Art
picture.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

nazca-puquios-300.summary: In Peru's Nazca and Ica valleys, some 36 puquios tap groundwater through sloping filtration galleries and open trenches, with spiral-walled access shafts (ojos) spaced along their course for cleaning and air flow. Katharina Schreiber and Josue Lancho Rojas argue they were built by Nazca people between about 300 and 600 CE in response to drought, based on settlement shifts, associated pottery and construction with Nazca-style rounded cobbles. Some scholars prefer a colonial Spanish date, since no puquio is directly dated and chronicles are silent; Schreiber's settlement evidence persuades most Andeanists. Puquios let farming continue when rivers ran dry and remain in use at Cantalloc. Comparable filtration galleries in Iran and Garamantian Libya were devised independently.

sources.title: Schreiber, Katharina J. and Lancho Rojas, Josue, 'The Puquios of Nasca', Latin American Antiquity 6 (1995)
sources.author: Schreiber, Katharina J.; Lancho Rojas, Josue
sources.confirms: Describes puquio construction and argues for Nazca-period origin (Middle Nasca, c. 300 to 600 CE) from settlement patterns and drought.
sources.qualifies: Acknowledges a minority view that puquios are colonial constructions.

sources.title: Schreiber, Katharina and Lancho Rojas, Josue, 'Irrigation and Society in the Peruvian Desert: The Puquios of Nasca', Lexington Books (2003)
sources.author: Schreiber, Katharina; Lancho Rojas, Josue
sources.confirms: Monograph treatment of puquio distribution, engineering and dating.

nazca-puquios-300.verification_note: Nazca-period origin (c. 300 to 600) rests on settlement patterns; a colonial date is argued by a minority.
nazca-puquios-300.detail: Year 300 is approximate and contested; dating is indirect since channels are cleaned yearly. Proponents of a pre-Hispanic date point to Middle Nasca settlements appearing beside puquio outlets during a drought around 400 to 500 CE. Nazca geoglyphs, drawn in these centuries, have no demonstrated hydraulic function despite popular claims. A 2016 satellite study by Rosa Lasaponara suggested spiral ojos funnel wind into galleries to push water, a hypothesis not yet tested on site. Cantalloc's puquios still irrigate cotton, maize and beans, and local comunidades clean them each year in a communal faena.

picture.alt: Spiral access shafts of the Cantalloc puquios at Nazca
picture.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

nazca-puquios-300.dating_note: Nazca-period origin (c. 300 to 600) rests on settlement patterns; a colonial date is argued by a minority.

peutinger-map-300.summary: Peutinger's map is a medieval copy, about 6.75 metres long and 34 cm high, of a Roman original showing roads, way-stations with distances, rivers, and cities from Britain to Sri Lanka and India. Richard Talbert dates its archetype to around 300 CE, under Tetrarchy, and reads its design as a display of imperial reach rather than a traveller's tool. Symbols for baths, granaries and lodgings match stations (mansiones and mutationes) of cursus publicus, a state relay system founded by Augustus that moved officials, dispatches and supplies on requisitioned animals and lodging. Together map and relay show how Rome administered distance: standardised stages, posted distances and road-side infrastructure across roughly 100,000 km of road.

sources.title: Talbert, Richard J. A., 'Rome's World: The Peutinger Map Reconsidered', Cambridge University Press (2010)
sources.author: Talbert, Richard J. A.
sources.confirms: Dates the map's archetype to c. 300 CE and interprets its design and route network; describes its coverage from Britain to India.

sources.title: Kolb, Anne, 'Transport and Communication in the Roman State: the cursus publicus', in Adams and Laurence (eds), 'Travel and Geography in the Roman Empire', Routledge (2001)
sources.author: Kolb, Anne
sources.confirms: Describes the cursus publicus as a state relay of stations, animals and lodging for officials and dispatches, founded under Augustus and regulated in the Theodosian Code.

peutinger-map-300.verification_note: Archetype dated c. 300 CE by Talbert; alternatives from the third to fifth century have been argued; the surviving copy is c. 1200.
peutinger-map-300.detail: Dating of its archetype ranges from Severan period to fifth century; Talbert's c. 300 is widely followed but some scholars prefer a fourth-century date based on Constantinople's prominence. Its surviving copy (Vienna, ONB Cod. 324) was made around 1200 and lacks a first sheet covering Britain and Spain. Book 8 of Theodosian Code regulates cursus publicus, limiting loads per vehicle and warrants (evectiones). Anne Kolb's study of cursus publicus shows relay stations spaced a day's travel apart with mutationes for horse changes between. Suetonius credits Augustus with founding this relay so couriers could be questioned on arrival.

picture.alt: Segment of the Tabula Peutingeriana, medieval copy of a Roman route map, Austrian National Library
picture.credit: Konrad Peutinger copy, Austrian National Library, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

peutinger-map-300.dating_note: Archetype dated c. 300 CE by Talbert; alternatives from the third to fifth century have been argued; the surviving copy is c. 1200.

diocletian-price-edict-301.summary: Issued in late 301 and carved on stone across eastern provinces, this edict lists maximum prices in denarii for grains, wine, oil, meat, textiles, slaves, transport by sea route, and daily wages for farm labourers, carpenters, teachers and scribes, with death as penalty for overcharging. Its preamble blames greed for prices rising 'eightfold'. Lactantius reports that goods disappeared from sale and that Diocletian abandoned his law after much bloodshed. Simon Corcoran's study of Tetrarchic legislation places it beside a currency reform of that year. Over 40 fragments from Aphrodisias, Stratonicea and elsewhere make it antiquity's richest price list and a documented failure of command pricing.

sources.title: Corcoran, Simon, 'The Empire of the Tetrarchs: Imperial Pronouncements and Government AD 284-324', Oxford University Press (1996; rev. 2000)
sources.author: Corcoran, Simon
sources.confirms: Analyses the Prices Edict of 301, its text, distribution in the eastern provinces and relation to the currency edict.

sources.title: Lactantius, 'De mortibus persecutorum 7' (c. 315), trans. William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7, New Advent
sources.author: Lactantius
sources.confirms: Chapter 7 reports that Diocletian set prices by law, that goods were withheld from market, prices rose and the law was repealed after much blood.

sources.title: Crawford, M. H. and Reynolds, J. M., 'The Aezani Copy of the Prices Edict', Zeitschrift fur Papyrologie und Epigraphik 34 (1979)
sources.author: Crawford, M. H.; Reynolds, J. M.
sources.confirms: Publishes a major copy of the edict with price lists for goods and wages.

diocletian-price-edict-301.detail: Date is fixed by consular dating in its preamble to between 20 November and 9 December 301. Economic historians debate whether it aimed at provisioning armies rather than general markets and whether 'failure' applied everywhere; copies are almost all from Greek-speaking provinces. Listed prices give historians their best quantitative view of late Roman relative costs: a modius of wheat at 100 denarii, a farm labourer's day at 25 with keep, a teacher of rhetoric at 250 per pupil per month, and purple silk at 150,000 per pound. Aphrodisias fragments, studied by Reynolds and Crawford, preserve a near-complete Latin text.

picture.alt: Marble fragment of Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices, Lemnos
picture.credit: Tomisti, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stirrup-china-322.summary: A pottery horse from a Western Jin tomb at Changsha (c. 302) shows a single mounting stirrup; a tomb at Xiangshan near Nanjing dated 322 contains a figurine with paired stirrups, and iron and gilt-bronze stirrups come from fourth-century Xianbei graves such as Feng Sufu's (415) at Beipiao. Stirrups had a role in heavy cavalry of northern dynasties. They reach Korea and Japan by fifth century, Avars bring them to Europe by about 600, and Byzantine and Frankish riders adopt them in seventh and eighth centuries. Lynn White's thesis that stirrups produced feudalism is widely rejected; their effect on mounted combat and travel is accepted.

sources.title: Dien, Albert E., 'The Stirrup and its Effect on Chinese Military History', Ars Orientalis 16 (1986); reprinted in Rogers (ed.), 'Warfare in China to 1600', Routledge (2005)
sources.author: Dien, Albert E.
sources.confirms: Reviews tomb figurines of 302 and 322 and excavated stirrups, places paired stirrups in early fourth-century China and discusses the Lynn White hypothesis.

sources.title: Curta, Florin, 'The Earliest Avar-Age Stirrups, or the Stirrup Controversy Revisited', in Curta (ed.), 'The Other Europe in the Middle Ages', Brill (2008)
sources.author: Curta, Florin
sources.confirms: Dates the arrival of stirrups in Europe with the Avars to the late sixth and seventh centuries and reviews the stirrup controversy.

stirrup-china-322.verification_note: Lynn White's link between stirrups and European feudalism is widely rejected; the Chinese chronology is accepted.
stirrup-china-322.detail: Its 322 date is from a tomb epitaph and is secure for this figurine; Changsha's single stirrup of c. 302 is read as a mounting aid. Claims for earlier stirrups in India (Sanchi reliefs, loops for a big toe) and in Scythian contexts are not accepted as true stirrups. White set out his thesis in 'Medieval Technology and Social Change' in 1962; Sawyer, Hilton and Dien later criticised it. Early Chinese stirrups were wood cores wrapped in gilt bronze or lacquered leather, like Feng Sufu's pair; iron stirrups follow in fifth century. Mounted archers of Northern Wei and Koguryo tomb murals at Ji'an show paired stirrups by about 400.

picture.alt: Iron stirrups of the Jin period
picture.credit: Gary Todd, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stirrup-china-322.dating_note: Lynn White's link between stirrups and European feudalism is widely rejected; the Chinese chronology is accepted.

aksum-stelae-330.summary: In Aksum's northern stelae field, kings of about 300 to 350 CE erect single-block granite stelae quarried four kilometres away at Gobedra, carved to resemble buildings of up to thirteen storeys with beam ends, windows and doors, and set over subterranean tombs. Stele 1, at 33 metres and about 520 tonnes, is among the largest monoliths ever attempted and fell during or soon after erection. Stele 2 (24.6 metres), taken to Rome in 1937, was returned and re-erected in 2008. Phillipson's excavations date these giant stelae to early fourth century and link their end to Ezana's conversion, after which royal tombs change form. Quarrying, transport by ramp and lever, and raising show workforce and planning comparable to Roman monumental building.

sources.title: Phillipson, David W., 'Foundations of an African Civilisation: Aksum and the Northern Horn, 1000 BC - AD 1300', James Currey (2012)
sources.author: Phillipson, David W.
sources.confirms: Dates the carved giant stelae to the early fourth century, describes their dimensions, quarry and tombs, and connects their end to Christianisation.

sources.title: Harrower, Michael J. et al., 'Beta Samati: discovery and excavation of an Aksumite town', Antiquity 93 (2019)
sources.author: Harrower, Michael J.
sources.confirms: Provides radiocarbon chronology for Aksumite settlement and early Christian architecture in the fourth century.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Aksum'
sources.confirms: Describes the stelae field, giant obelisks and royal tombs of the first to thirteenth centuries.

aksum-stelae-330.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
aksum-stelae-330.detail: Dating to c. 300 to 350 comes from excavation of associated tombs and pottery; 330 is approximate. Whether Stele 1 ever stood is debated; Phillipson argues it collapsed during erection, crushing a tomb roof. Six decorated stelae survive; over 120 plain ones stand in Aksum's fields. Roman-era accounts (Periplus, Procopius) describe Aksum as a trading power with Adulis as its port. Quarry faces at Gobedra show rows of wedge slots for splitting granite, and a depiction of a lioness is carved nearby. Base plates with carved offering bowls stood before each stele, and Tomb of the Brick Arches beneath yielded ivory, glass and metalwork of fourth-century date.

picture.alt: Stelae in the northern stelae field at Aksum
picture.credit: Allamiro, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ezana-geez-340.summary: Ezana's inscriptions at Aksum, cut in vocalised Ge'ez (an Ethiopic script with vowel marks added in his reign), Sabaean letters and Greek, record campaigns against Beja and Noba peoples and a Nile expedition reaching Meroe's region, with early texts dedicated to Mahrem and Ares and later ones to 'the Lord of Heaven'. Coins switch from disc-and-crescent to cross. Rufinus's church history tells how Frumentius, a Syrian boy shipwrecked and raised at court, converted Aksum and was consecrated bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria around 330 to 340. Constantius II's letter of 356 to Ezana and Saizana, preserved in Athanasius, confirms his reign. Vocalised Ge'ez remains Ethiopia's liturgical script; Aksum stands with Armenia and Rome among earliest Christian states.

sources.title: Phillipson, David W., 'Foundations of an African Civilisation: Aksum and the Northern Horn, 1000 BC - AD 1300', James Currey (2012)
sources.author: Phillipson, David W.
sources.confirms: Discusses Ezana's trilingual inscriptions, vocalisation of Ge'ez, conversion and coinage change c. 340.

sources.title: Athanasius, 'Apologia ad Constantium 31' (c. 357), letter of Constantius II to Aizanas and Sazanas, trans. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, New Advent
sources.author: Athanasius of Alexandria
sources.confirms: Preserves Constantius II's letter to 'Aizanas and Sazanas' concerning bishop Frumentius, fixing Ezana's reign in the mid fourth century.

sources.title: Rufinus of Aquileia, 'Historia Ecclesiastica 10.9-10' (c. 402), on Frumentius and Aedesius
sources.author: Rufinus of Aquileia
sources.confirms: Narrates Frumentius's upbringing at Aksum and consecration by Athanasius.

ezana-geez-340.verification_note: Conversion placed c. 330 to 350 from numismatic sequence and Constantius II's letter of 356; no inscription carries an absolute date.
ezana-geez-340.detail: Ezana's conversion is dated between about 330 and 350 by coin and inscription sequence and by Constantius's letter; 340 is approximate. Vocalisation of Ge'ez appears first within his inscriptions, some unvocalised and some vocalised, which suggests reform during his reign. Whether his Nile campaign destroyed Meroe is debated; most scholars see Meroe already in decline. His Greek inscription calls him 'king of Aksumites, Himyarites, Raeidan, Ethiopians, Sabaeans, Silee, Tiyamo, Beja and Kasu', claiming lands on both sides of Red Sea. Ezana Stone, found in 1981 outside Aksum, is trilingual in Greek, Sabaean and Ge'ez.

picture.alt: Ezana Stone trilingual inscription at Aksum
picture.credit: Rod Waddington from Kergunyah, Australia, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ezana-geez-340.dating_note: Conversion placed c. 330 to 350 from numismatic sequence and Constantius II's letter of 356; no inscription carries an absolute date.

ge-hong-zhouhou-340.summary: Ge Hong (283 to 343), alchemist and official, compiles a handbook of cheap remedies 'to keep up one's sleeve'. Among them: 'a handful of qinghao, soaked in two sheng of water, wrung out, take the juice whole' for intermittent fevers. In 1971 Tu Youyou's team, reading this low-temperature instruction, switched to ether extraction of Artemisia annua and isolated artemisinin, now a first-line antimalarial; Hsu's 2006 article traces this link. His text also gives an early description of an epidemic with pustules that leave scars, read by historians as smallpox, and of rabies treatment. Ge Hong's Baopuzi records alchemical experiments with mercury and sulphur. His handbook shows a practical, empirical strand in fourth-century Chinese medicine.

sources.title: Hsu, Elisabeth, 'Reflections on the discovery of the antimalarial qinghao', British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology 61 (2006)
sources.author: Hsu, Elisabeth
sources.confirms: Traces artemisinin's discovery to Ge Hong's Zhouhou beiji fang (fourth century) and its instruction to wring out qinghao in cold water.

sources.title: Tu, Youyou, 'The discovery of artemisinin (qinghaosu) and gifts from Chinese medicine', Nature Medicine 17 (2011)
sources.author: Tu, Youyou
sources.confirms: Tu's own account of reading Ge Hong's recipe and adopting low-temperature extraction in 1971.

sources.title: Sivin, Nathan, 'Chinese Alchemy: Preliminary Studies', Harvard University Press (1968)
sources.author: Sivin, Nathan
sources.confirms: Studies Ge Hong's Baopuzi and dates his life and works to the early fourth century.

ge-hong-zhouhou-340.verification_note: Received text includes later additions; attribution of specific recipes to Ge Hong is probable, not certain.
ge-hong-zhouhou-340.detail: Composition is placed in 330s to 340s; 340 is approximate. Received Zhouhou beiji fang includes additions by Tao Hongjing (c. 500) and Yang Yongdao (1144), so attribution of individual recipes to Ge Hong is not certain. Hsu notes qinghao in Ge Hong's text may refer to Artemisia apiacea rather than A. annua. His rabies treatment applied brain of a rabid dog to its bite wound, which Needham compared to later immunisation logic. Tu Youyou's 2011 Nature Medicine account credits this one sentence with prompting a switch from hot extraction, which destroyed artemisinin, to ether at low temperature; she received a Nobel Prize in 2015.

picture.alt: Woodcut portrait of Ge Hong, Wellcome Collection (later woodcut)
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, after Gan Bozong, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ge-hong-zhouhou-340.dating_note: Received text includes later additions; attribution of specific recipes to Ge Hong is probable, not certain.

sichuan-brine-wells-347.summary: Chang Qu's gazetteer of Sichuan, completed around 347 CE, describes salt wells at Linqiong and elsewhere and 'fire wells' (huojing) whose flames were used to evaporate brine, history's earliest record of natural gas burned for industrial heat. Han tomb bricks from Sichuan show brine hoisted from a derrick-topped well and piped by bamboo to evaporating pans over furnaces. Li Bing is credited by that text with opening salt wells near Chengdu in third century BCE. Hans Ulrich Vogel's study of Chinese salt technology traces this industry to percussion-drilled deep wells of Song and to Shenhai well of 1835, which passed 1,000 metres. Salt was a state monopoly, so these wells were also fiscal infrastructure.

sources.title: Vogel, Hans Ulrich, 'Salt Production Techniques in Ancient China: The Aobo Tu', Brill (1993)
sources.author: Vogel, Hans Ulrich
sources.confirms: Surveys Chinese salt production including Sichuan brine wells, Han tomb brick depictions and natural-gas 'fire wells' recorded in Huayang guozhi.

sources.title: Chang Qu, 'Huayang guozhi, Shu zhi' (c. 347), Chinese Text Project
sources.author: Chang Qu
sources.confirms: Records 火井 fire wells and salt wells in Linqiong and the Shu region.

sources.title: Needham, Joseph et al., 'Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 2: Mechanical Engineering', Cambridge University Press (1965), on Sichuan brine wells
sources.author: Needham, Joseph
sources.confirms: Discusses Han brine-well reliefs and bamboo piping of brine and gas.

sichuan-brine-wells-347.verification_note: Text date is secure; dating of bamboo gas pipelines to the Han is inferred from reliefs and later texts.
sichuan-brine-wells-347.detail: Huayang guozhi's completion between 348 and 354 gives its year; brine wells are older, documented by Han reliefs from first and second centuries. Whether gas was piped in bamboo by Han or only later is debated; clearest descriptions of bamboo gas pipelines are Song and later. Chang Qu writes that people lit fire wells with household flame and that brine boiled over them yielded salt of good colour, while ordinary fire gave poor salt. Han wells were dug by hand to a few tens of metres; Song percussion drilling with iron bits and bamboo casing reached several hundred metres, as Su Shi described in 1070s.

picture.alt: Shenhai well derrick at Zigong, Sichuan, a nineteenth-century brine well in the tradition Chang Qu records (later well)
picture.credit: Zhangzhugang, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sichuan-brine-wells-347.dating_note: Text date is secure; dating of bamboo gas pipelines to the Han is inferred from reliefs and later texts.

maya-zero-astronomy-350.summary: Classic Maya scribes write numbers with bars, dots and a shell or flower sign for zero in positional Long Count notation, among antiquity's earliest zero placeholders; a zero appears in monumental dates by 300 CE. Astronomical knowledge survives mainly in Dresden Codex, a bark-paper book painted around 1200 to 1250 whose Venus table tracks that planet's 584-day cycle with corrections over 104 years, and whose eclipse table predicts eclipse seasons across 33 years. Harvey and Victoria Bricker show these tables rest on observations and base dates reaching back into Classic period, with Venus table's historical base in tenth century and earlier entries implied. Aveni's survey sets Maya astronomy alongside architectural alignments at Classic cities.

sources.title: Bricker, Harvey M. and Bricker, Victoria R., 'Astronomy in the Maya Codices', American Philosophical Society (2011)
sources.author: Bricker, Harvey M.; Bricker, Victoria R.
sources.confirms: Analyses the Dresden Codex Venus and eclipse tables, their base dates and derivation from earlier Classic-period observations.

sources.title: Aveni, Anthony F., 'Skywatchers: A Revised and Updated Version of Skywatchers of Ancient Mexico', University of Texas Press (2001); reviewed by Milbrath, Latin American Antiquity 14 (2003)
sources.author: Aveni, Anthony F.
sources.confirms: Surveys Maya positional numeration with zero, Venus and eclipse tables and Classic-period astronomical alignments.

sources.title: SLUB Dresden, 'Codex Dresdensis', Mscr.Dresd.R.310, digitised facsimile
sources.confirms: Digitised manuscript showing Venus and eclipse tables used for imagery.

maya-zero-astronomy-350.verification_note: Dresden Codex is thirteenth century; its tables encode earlier Classic observations whose start dates are inferred, not fixed.
maya-zero-astronomy-350.detail: Year 350 is approximate and stands for Classic-period origin of methods recorded in a much later codex; it is not a date for any surviving table. Saturno's 2012 discovery of astronomical notations on walls at Xultun, dated about 814 CE, provides Classic-period tables matching Dresden structures. Zero placeholders in Long Count dates appear on Gulf coast monuments before 100 CE. Dresden Codex, 39 leaves painted on both sides, reached Dresden's royal library in 1739 and was damaged by water in 1945. Ernst Forstemann deciphered its Venus table in 1880s, establishing Maya numeration for modern scholarship.

picture.alt: Venus table pages of the Dresden Codex (thirteenth-century codex)
picture.credit: Lacambalam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

maya-zero-astronomy-350.dating_note: Dresden Codex is thirteenth century; its tables encode earlier Classic observations whose start dates are inferred, not fixed.

meroe-decline-350.summary: Meroe on middle Nile, capital of Kush from about 300 BCE, left slag heaps once estimated at tens of thousands of tonnes from bloomery furnaces, and pyramid fields for over forty rulers. Excavation by Jane Humphris dates intensive iron production from sixth century BCE to fourth century CE, with charcoal demand shaping surrounding landscape. Royal pyramid burials stop around 350 CE; Ezana's inscription records an Aksumite expedition reaching Meroe's region, and Noba and Blemmye groups appear in Nubia. David Edwards reads this as drawn-out transformation into post-Meroitic polities rather than a single sack. Meroitic script, written since second century BCE, falls out of use and remains only partly understood.

sources.title: Humphris, Jane et al., 'A New Radiocarbon Chronology for Ancient Iron Production in the Meroe Region of Sudan', African Archaeological Review 34 (2017)
sources.author: Humphris, Jane; Scheibner, Thomas
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon dates for iron smelting at Meroe spanning the first millennium BCE to the fourth century CE.

sources.title: Edwards, David N., 'The Nubian Past: An Archaeology of the Sudan', Routledge (2004)
sources.author: Edwards, David N.
sources.confirms: Discusses Meroe's late phase, cessation of royal burials in the fourth century, Aksumite intervention and post-Meroitic transition.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe'
sources.confirms: Describes Meroe as Kushite capital from the third century BCE to the fourth century CE with pyramids and iron production.

meroe-decline-350.verification_note: End of royal pyramids placed c. 350 CE from burial sequence; Ezana's inscription is undated and its role is debated.
meroe-decline-350.detail: Year 350 marks approximate end of royal burials; dating combines radiocarbon, pottery and Ezana's undated inscription. Old estimates of Meroe as an 'African Birmingham' overstated output; Humphris's work gives smaller but sustained production from about 25 furnaces excavated so far. Attribution of Meroe's fall to Aksum is not supported by destruction layers, and post-Meroitic tumuli at el-Hobagi show elites continuing royal symbolism into fifth century. Meroitic script, with 23 signs in hieroglyphic and cursive forms, is read phonetically since Griffith's 1909 work but its language is only partly interpreted, with Claude Rilly's Nilo-Saharan identification gaining support.

picture.alt: Pyramids of Meroe drawn by Frederic Cailliaud in 1821 (1821 drawing)
picture.credit: Frederic Cailliaud, 1826, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

meroe-decline-350.dating_note: End of royal pyramids placed c. 350 CE from burial sequence; Ezana's inscription is undated and its role is debated.

ulfilas-gothic-alphabet-350.summary: Ulfilas (Wulfila), born among Goths around 311 and consecrated bishop in 341, creates an alphabet of 27 letters from Greek with Latin and runic additions and translates most of Christian scripture into Gothic in 350s and 360s, working among Gothic Christians settled in Moesia. Philostorgius and Socrates record alphabet and translation; Codex Argenteus, written in Ostrogothic Italy around 520 in silver and gold ink on purple parchment, preserves Gospels. Heather and Matthews treat this translation as earliest literary monument of any Germanic language and a model for later missionary scripts. It shows how a writing system could be engineered for a spoken language in one generation.

sources.title: Heather, Peter and Matthews, John, 'The Goths in the Fourth Century', Translated Texts for Historians 11, Liverpool University Press (1991)
sources.author: Heather, Peter; Matthews, John
sources.confirms: Translates and discusses the sources on Ulfilas (Philostorgius, Auxentius, Socrates), his alphabet, Bible translation and settlement in Moesia around 348.

sources.title: Falluomini, Carla, 'The Gothic Version of the Gospels and Pauline Epistles', de Gruyter (2015)
sources.author: Falluomini, Carla
sources.confirms: Studies the Gothic Bible's text and the Codex Argenteus as a sixth-century Italian manuscript of Ulfilas's translation.

ulfilas-gothic-alphabet-350.verification_note: Composition falls between c. 348 and 383; no year is fixed in the sources.
ulfilas-gothic-alphabet-350.detail: Translation work is placed between Ulfilas's move to Moesia (c. 348) and his death in 383; 350 is approximate. Tradition holds he omitted Kings as too warlike for Goths, a detail from Philostorgius. Codex Argenteus, now in Uppsala, contains about 188 of an original 336 leaves; one more leaf turned up at Speyer in 1970. Gothic letters follow Greek order and numerical values, with runic-derived signs for u and o and Latin-derived forms for several others. Surviving Gothic also includes Codex Carolinus fragments of Romans and Skeireins, a commentary on John, found as palimpsests in Wolfenbuttel and Milan.

picture.alt: Folio of Codex Argenteus, Gothic Gospels in silver ink on purple parchment, c. 520 (c. 520 manuscript)
picture.credit: Codex Argenteus, Uppsala University Library, scan by uploader, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

ulfilas-gothic-alphabet-350.dating_note: Composition falls between c. 348 and 383; no year is fixed in the sources.

teotihuacan-tikal-378.summary: Tikal Stela 31 and Marcador, with monuments at El Peru and Uaxactun, record that on 11 Eb 15 Mak (16 January 378) a lord named Sihyaj K'ahk' 'arrived' at Tikal and that ruler Chak Tok Ich'aak I 'entered the water' (died) that day. A year later Yax Nuun Ahiin I, son of a figure called Spearthrower Owl linked to Teotihuacan, is installed as king. David Stuart's 2000 reading of these texts argues for Teotihuacan intervention, supported by Central Mexican weaponry, talud-tablero architecture and green obsidian at Tikal, and by Maya-style murals and burials at Teotihuacan. Debate continues over whether this was conquest, alliance or elite emulation, but dated texts make it pre-Columbian America's best documented inter-regional political event.

sources.title: Stuart, David, 'The Arrival of Strangers: Teotihuacan and Tollan in Classic Maya History', in Carrasco, Jones and Sessions (eds), 'Mesoamerica's Classic Heritage: From Teotihuacan to the Aztecs', University Press of Colorado (2000), pp. 465-513
sources.author: Stuart, David
sources.confirms: Reads Tikal Stela 31 and related texts as recording Sihyaj K'ahk's arrival on 16 January 378 and a Teotihuacan-linked dynastic change.

sources.title: Martin, Simon, 'Ancient Maya Politics: A Political Anthropology of the Classic Period 150-900 CE', Cambridge University Press (2020)
sources.author: Martin, Simon
sources.confirms: Synthesises the 378 'entrada' and its political consequences at Tikal and neighbouring cities.

sources.title: Sugiyama, Nawa et al., 'Early Maya presence at Teotihuacan: new data from the Plaza of the Columns Complex', Antiquity 94 (2020)
sources.author: Sugiyama, Nawa
sources.confirms: Reports Maya-style murals and material at Teotihuacan dated to the fourth century, showing two-way contact.

teotihuacan-tikal-378.verification_note: Date is secure; interpretation as conquest versus alliance remains debated.
teotihuacan-tikal-378.detail: Date is fixed by Long Count under GMT correlation. Spearthrower Owl's identity as a Teotihuacan ruler rests on Stuart's reading of a glyph; Braswell's 2003 edited volume collects dissenting views. Strontium isotope studies of Tikal burials have not yet identified Central Mexican individuals from this date, though Burial 10, assigned to Yax Nuun Ahiin, contains Teotihuacan-style ceramics. At Teotihuacan, Nawa Sugiyama's team found a Maya-style mural fragment and a deposit of smashed Maya elite burials in Plaza of the Columns around 350 to 400, suggesting diplomatic ties later broken. El Peru's Stela 15 records Sihyaj K'ahk' passing through eight days earlier.

picture.alt: Tikal Stela 31 recording the arrival of Sihyaj K'ahk'
picture.credit: HJPD, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

teotihuacan-tikal-378.dating_note: Date is secure; interpretation as conquest versus alliance remains debated.

ammianus-incendiary-390.summary: Writing his history in Rome around 390, the former officer Ammianus describes malleoli, fire-darts: a reed shaft with an iron cage holding 'fire and some inflammable matter', shot slowly from a loosened bow, which 'burns persistently, and water poured upon it rouses the fire to still greater heat; and there is no way of extinguishing it except by sprinkling it with dust'. In his Persian excursus he names naphtha, 'a glutinous substance which looks like pitch', and 'Medic oil' smeared on missiles. These passages, with earlier accounts of petroleum at Hit, document knowledge of petroleum incendiaries in late Roman warfare three centuries before Kallinikos's Greek fire of 672, which Roland's analysis treats as a projected, pressurised development of such mixtures.

sources.title: Ammianus Marcellinus, 'Res Gestae 23.4.14-15 and 23.6.16, 37-38' (c. 390), trans. J. C. Rolfe, LacusCurtius
sources.author: Ammianus Marcellinus
sources.confirms: Verbatim: fire-darts burn persistently, water increases the heat, only dust extinguishes; naphtha described as glutinous like pitch; Medic oil smeared on missiles.

sources.title: Roland, Alex, 'Secrecy, Technology, and War: Greek Fire and the Defense of Byzantium, 678-1204', Technology and Culture 33 (1992)
sources.author: Roland, Alex
sources.confirms: Treats Greek fire as a petroleum-based incendiary projected by siphon, introduced c. 672 to 678, with antecedents in earlier naphtha weapons; discusses secrecy and loss of the recipe.

sources.title: Kelly, Gavin, 'Ammianus Marcellinus: The Allusive Historian', Cambridge University Press (2008); reviewed by Woods, Classical Review 60 (2010)
sources.author: Kelly, Gavin
sources.confirms: Dates composition of the surviving books to the late 380s and early 390s in Rome.

ammianus-incendiary-390.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
ammianus-incendiary-390.detail: Year 390 is approximate for composition of books 23 onward. Ammianus's own expedition with Julian in 363 passed Persian bitumen springs. Greek fire proper (Byzantine 'liquid fire') combined distilled petroleum with a pump and siphon; its recipe was a state secret and is lost, so its relation to these Roman incendiaries is inferred, not documented. Procopius in sixth century describes 'Medes' oil' which Greeks call naphtha, and Theophanes credits Kallinikos of Heliopolis with fire that saved Constantinople in 670s. Pliny (NH 2.235) had already described naphtha near Babylon as a substance that leaps to flame. Earlier Hellenistic texts (Aeneas Tacticus) describe pitch and sulphur incendiaries without petroleum.

picture.alt: Page of Ammianus Marcellinus's history in Vatican manuscript lat. 1873, ninth century (ninth-century manuscript)
picture.credit: Vatican Library, Vat. lat. 1873, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

delhi-iron-pillar-400.summary: A Sanskrit inscription in Gupta Brahmi on this pillar, now in Delhi's Qutb complex, records dedication as a standard of Vishnu by a king Chandra, identified with Chandragupta II (r. c. 375 to 415). It stands 7.2 metres with about one metre underground, weighs over six tonnes and was forge-welded from many lumps of wrought iron. Balasubramaniam's corrosion studies show a thin protective layer of iron hydrogen phosphate formed from high phosphorus content and Delhi's climate, explaining its survival. It is antiquity's largest forged iron object and evidence of Gupta smithing capacity; Pliny's praise of Indian iron and wootz trade belong to one metallurgical tradition.

sources.title: Balasubramaniam, R., 'On the corrosion resistance of the Delhi iron pillar', Corrosion Science 42 (2000)
sources.author: Balasubramaniam, R.
sources.confirms: Analyses the pillar's composition, the protective iron hydrogen phosphate layer and dates the pillar to the Gupta period c. 400 CE.

sources.title: Fleet, John F., 'Inscriptions of the Early Gupta Kings and Their Successors', Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum III (1888), no. 32, Meharauli iron pillar inscription
sources.author: Fleet, John F.
sources.confirms: Edition and translation of the pillar inscription naming king Chandra and the dedication to Vishnu.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi'
sources.confirms: Describes the iron pillar within the Qutb complex and its fourth-century date.

delhi-iron-pillar-400.verification_note: Palaeography and the name Chandra point to Chandragupta II (c. 375 to 415); alternative attributions exist.
delhi-iron-pillar-400.detail: Identifying Chandra with Chandragupta II is majority opinion; some assign it to Samudragupta or an earlier Chandra, so 400 is approximate. Original location is debated, with Udayagiri favoured, and it was moved to Delhi probably in the eleventh century. Corrosion resistance depends on Delhi's dry climate; a fragment kept at a seaside site rusted. Composition averages 0.25 percent phosphorus and very low sulphur and manganese, consistent with charcoal smelting of phosphoric ore. Forge-welding marks show hammering of hot iron lumps around a central core, a method also seen in Dhar and Mandu pillars of later centuries.

picture.alt: Iron pillar of Delhi in the Qutb complex
picture.credit: Mark A. Wilson, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

delhi-iron-pillar-400.dating_note: Palaeography and the name Chandra point to Chandragupta II (c. 375 to 415); alternative attributions exist.

jenne-jeno-400.summary: Excavations by Roderick and Susan McIntosh from 1977 at Jenne-jeno in Mali show settlement from about 250 BCE, growth to a 33-hectare mound ringed by a mud-brick wall two kilometres long by about 400 CE, and a cluster of some 70 satellite mounds within four kilometres. Residents smelted iron from ore brought over 50 kilometres, grew African rice, fished, herded and made terracotta statuettes and fine pottery; copper and gold arrive later through Saharan links. No palace, temple or elite quarter is found. Roderick McIntosh describes a heterarchical city in which specialised communities cluster yet keep separate identities. Jenne-jeno predates Arab accounts of West African towns by centuries and counters assumptions that Sahelian urbanism began with trans-Saharan trade.

sources.title: McIntosh, Susan Keech and McIntosh, Roderick J., 'The Inland Niger Delta before the Empire of Mali: Evidence from Jenne-Jeno', Journal of African History 22 (1981)
sources.author: McIntosh, Susan Keech; McIntosh, Roderick J.
sources.confirms: Presents radiocarbon chronology from c. 250 BCE, growth to a walled town by c. 400 CE, iron working and regional trade.

sources.title: McIntosh, Roderick J. and McIntosh, Susan Keech, 'Cities without Citadels: Understanding Urban Origins along the Middle Niger', in Shaw et al. (eds), 'The Archaeology of Africa', Routledge (1993); see also 'Early Urban Clusters in China and Africa: The Arbitration of Social Ambiguity', Journal of Field Archaeology 18 (1991)
sources.author: McIntosh, Roderick J.
sources.confirms: Develops the clustered, heterarchical urban model for Jenne-jeno.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Old Towns of Djenne'
sources.confirms: Notes Djenne-Djeno as inhabited from 250 BCE and a centre of trans-Saharan gold trade.

jenne-jeno-400.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
jenne-jeno-400.detail: Phase III (c. 400 to 900 CE) marks peak size; 400 is approximate for wall construction. Chronology is radiocarbon with over 30 dates. Looting of terracottas since 1980s destroyed context for much statuary, and Mali's 1990s export ban followed. Satellite surveys by McIntosh and later by Anne Mayor refine settlement counts. Its wall, 3.7 metres wide at base, is built of cylindrical mud bricks and may have served against flood as much as attack. Djenne, three kilometres away, inherits trade after Jenne-jeno's abandonment around 1400 and becomes a centre of Islamic learning with its great mosque.

picture.alt: Terracotta head from the Jenne region, Mali
picture.credit: National Museum in Szczecin, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

kutai-inscriptions-400.summary: Seven stone sacrificial posts (yupa) found near Muara Kaman on Mahakam river in East Kalimantan record in Sanskrit verse that king Mulavarman, grandson of Kundungga and son of Asvavarman, gave gifts of cattle, land and gold to brahmins at a sacred place called Vaprakesvara. Letters are an early form of Pallava-derived script, dated palaeographically by J. Ph. Vogel in 1918 to about 400 CE. These are Indonesia's oldest known inscriptions, slightly before Purnavarman's at Tarumanagara in West Java. They show Indian ritual, script and kingship adopted in a Borneo river polity trading forest products, with local names (Kundungga) beside Sanskrit ones, and mark Southeast Asia's entry into written history through Indian Ocean exchange.

sources.title: Vogel, J. Ph., 'The Yupa Inscriptions of King Mulavarman, from Koetei (East Borneo)', Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 74 (1918)
sources.author: Vogel, J. Ph.
sources.venue: Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde
sources.confirms: Edits and translates the yupa inscriptions, names Mulavarman, Asvavarman and Kundungga and dates the script to c. 400 CE.

sources.title: Coedes, George, 'The Indianized States of Southeast Asia', trans. Cowing, University of Hawaii Press (1968)
sources.author: Coedes, George
sources.confirms: Discusses the Kutai inscriptions as earliest Sanskrit epigraphy in Indonesia, c. 400 CE.

kutai-inscriptions-400.verification_note: Palaeographic dating to c. 400 CE; no absolute date in the texts.
kutai-inscriptions-400.detail: Dating is palaeographic only, so 400 is approximate; estimates range from late fourth to mid fifth century. Four stones were found in 1879 and three in 1940, and all seven are in Museum Nasional, Jakarta. Earlier Indic contact with Southeast Asia (Oc Eo in Vietnam's Mekong delta, Khuan Luk Pat in Thailand) shows in Roman and Indian beads, intaglios and seals without local texts. One yupa records a gift of 20,000 cattle; another says Asvavarman founded a dynasty, implying Kundungga was a local chief before Indianisation. Region is oceania under this brief's definition, which includes Southeast Asian islands.

picture.alt: Yupa inscription of Mulavarman from Kutai, Museum Nasional Jakarta
picture.credit: Ms Sarah Welch, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

kutai-inscriptions-400.dating_note: Palaeographic dating to c. 400 CE; no absolute date in the texts.

moche-huaca-del-sol-400.summary: At Cerro Blanco in Peru's Moche valley, Huaca del Sol, a stepped platform once about 340 by 160 metres and over 40 metres high, is built in stages from sun-dried adobe bricks laid in tall columns; Hastings and Moseley estimate more than 143 million bricks. Over 100 distinct maker's marks pressed into bricks occur in discrete columns, which they interpret as labour tax paid by communities each responsible for a segment, a system resembling later Inca mit'a. Across its plain, Huaca de la Luna carries polychrome friezes of a fanged deity and hosted sacrifices of captives. Construction spans roughly 100 to 600 CE; 400 marks a major phase. Spanish treasure hunters diverted Moche river against it in 1600s and washed away two thirds.

sources.title: Hastings, C. Mansfield and Moseley, M. Edward, 'The Adobes of Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna', American Antiquity 40 (1975)
sources.author: Hastings, C. Mansfield; Moseley, M. Edward
sources.confirms: Estimates brick counts, documents maker's marks in segmented columns and interprets them as labour tax.

sources.title: Uceda, Santiago and Mujica, Elias (eds), 'Moche: Hacia el final del milenio', Pontificia Universidad Catolica del Peru (2003)
sources.author: Uceda, Santiago; Mujica, Elias
sources.confirms: Reports excavations at Huaca de la Luna including construction phases and friezes.

sources.title: Quilter, Jeffrey, 'The Moche of Ancient Peru: Media and Messages', Peabody Museum Press (2010)
sources.author: Quilter, Jeffrey
sources.confirms: Synthesises Moche chronology (c. 100 to 800 CE), architecture and iconography.

moche-huaca-del-sol-400.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
moche-huaca-del-sol-400.detail: Year 400 is approximate for a principal construction phase dated by ceramics and radiocarbon. Brick counts are estimates from surviving volume. Whether marks denote communities, work gangs or individuals is debated; Moseley's labour-tax model is widely cited. Current Moche chronology sees several regional polities rather than one state, with northern and southern spheres divided at Paijan desert. Huaca de la Luna excavations led by Santiago Uceda since 1991 uncovered Plaza 3A with remains of over 70 sacrificed men, some killed during El Nino rains. Both huacas were built over several centuries by adding new outer shells.

picture.alt: Excavations at Huaca de la Luna with Huaca del Sol beyond
picture.credit: Burkhard Mücke, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tiwanaku-raised-fields-400.summary: On Bolivia's altiplano, planting platforms a metre high and up to 200 metres long separated by water-filled canals cover tens of square kilometres around Tiwanaku and Katari basin. Kolata's experiments with rebuilt fields showed canal water absorbing solar heat by day and releasing it at night, raising crop-level temperatures and protecting potatoes and quinoa from frost, while canal muck supplies fertiliser. Kolata dated expansion of field systems to Tiwanaku IV and V (c. 400 to 1000 CE) and linked them to state management, a claim Clark Erickson contests, attributing fields to community labour over a longer span. Janusek and Kolata's 2004 study of Katari valley refines this chronology. Tiwanaku's monumental core of andesite gateways and sunken courts grows in these centuries.

sources.title: Kolata, Alan L., 'The Agricultural Foundations of the Tiwanaku State: A View from the Heartland', American Antiquity 51 (1986)
sources.author: Kolata, Alan L.
sources.confirms: Describes raised field systems in the Pampa Koani and dates their expansion to Tiwanaku IV-V, arguing for state organisation.
sources.qualifies: Erickson (1993, 2006) argues for community-based construction and a longer chronology.

sources.title: Janusek, John Wayne and Kolata, Alan L., 'Top-down or bottom-up: rural settlement and raised field agriculture in the Lake Titicaca Basin, Bolivia', Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 23 (2004)
sources.author: Janusek, John Wayne; Kolata, Alan L.
sources.confirms: Reviews settlement survey and dating of raised fields in the Katari basin and weighs state versus community models.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Tiwanaku: Spiritual and Political Centre of the Tiwanaku Culture'
sources.confirms: Describes Tiwanaku's growth from about 400 CE and its monumental architecture.

tiwanaku-raised-fields-400.verification_note: Kolata's state-directed Tiwanaku IV-V chronology (c. 400 to 1000) is contested by Erickson's longer, community-based model.
tiwanaku-raised-fields-400.detail: Year 400 is approximate for field expansion; raised fields near Titicaca appear in Late Formative contexts before Tiwanaku's rise. Dating is radiocarbon from field fill and settlements. Rehabilitation projects in 1980s and 1990s reported potato yields of 20 tonnes per hectare against regional averages near 2 to 5, though farmer adoption lapsed once project funding ended. Erickson's work at Huatta on Peru's shore of Titicaca found raised fields dating from about 1000 BCE. Tiwanaku's Akapana platform and Kalasasaya enclosure with its Gateway of the Sun date to Tiwanaku IV, around 500 to 800.

picture.alt: Kalasasaya temple platform at Tiwanaku, Bolivia
picture.credit: Pelegrin-RAM, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tiwanaku-raised-fields-400.dating_note: Kolata's state-directed Tiwanaku IV-V chronology (c. 400 to 1000) is contested by Erickson's longer, community-based model.

kumarajiva-401.summary: Captured at Kucha in 384 and held in Liangzhou for seventeen years, monk Kumarajiva reaches Chang'an in 401 at invitation of Yao Xing of Later Qin, who installs him with hundreds of assistants in Xiaoyao Garden. Over twelve years his team translates Lotus Sutra, Diamond Sutra, Vimalakirti, Amitabha Sutra and Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka treatises, replacing word-for-word renderings with idiomatic Chinese, reading drafts aloud for correction. Jan Nattier's studies of early Chinese Buddhist translation show how his versions became standard across East Asia; a Diamond Sutra of 868 printed at Dunhuang carries his text. His bureau is a model of organised, collaborative translation between Indic and Chinese literary cultures.

sources.title: Nattier, Jan, 'A Guide to the Earliest Chinese Buddhist Translations', International Research Institute for Advanced Buddhology, Soka University (2008)
sources.author: Nattier, Jan
sources.confirms: Surveys Chinese Buddhist translation practice up to the fourth century and the shift exemplified by Kumarajiva's team.

sources.title: Lu, Yang, 'Narrative and Historicity in the Buddhist Biographies of Early Medieval China: The Case of Kumarajiva', Asia Major 17 (2004)
sources.author: Lu, Yang
sources.confirms: Analyses the Gaoseng zhuan biography, dating Kumarajiva's arrival in Chang'an to 401 and his translation activity under Yao Xing.

sources.title: Huijiao, 'Gaoseng zhuan 2, Biography of Kumarajiva' (c. 530), Taisho 2059, CBETA
sources.author: Huijiao
sources.confirms: Primary biography recording arrival in Chang'an in the third year of Hongshi (401) and translation work with state support.

kumarajiva-401.detail: Arrival year 401 is given in biographies and is secure; his death is dated 409 or 413. Scholars debate how much translation was Kumarajiva's and how much came from assistants such as Sengrui and Sengzhao. About 35 translations are credited to him in modern catalogues against 300 in medieval lists. Gaoseng zhuan reports he compared translating to chewing rice for another to eat, losing flavour. Yao Xing's patronage included a lecture hall where Kumarajiva explained Sanskrit sense while scribes drafted Chinese and hundreds of monks debated wording. His Lotus Sutra translation remains that used in Japanese Tendai and Nichiren liturgy.

picture.alt: Modern statue of Kumarajiva at Kizil Caves, Kuqa
picture.credit: Yoshi Canopus, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hypatia-415.summary: Hypatia, daughter of mathematician Theon, teaches philosophy and mathematics in Alexandria to pagans and Christians, including future bishop Synesius, who writes asking her for a hydrometer and an astrolabe. Suda credits her with commentaries on Diophantus's Arithmetica, Apollonius's Conics and Ptolemy's astronomical tables, and Theon's edition of Almagest book 3 is said to be revised by her. In March 415, during conflict between prefect Orestes and bishop Cyril, a crowd led by lector Peter drags her from her carriage, kills her in a church and burns her body, as Socrates Scholasticus records. Her death marks public danger to scholarship in late antique cities, though Alexandrian schools continued.

sources.title: Deakin, Michael A. B., 'Hypatia and Her Mathematics', American Mathematical Monthly 101 (1994)
sources.author: Deakin, Michael A. B.
sources.confirms: Reviews the evidence for Hypatia's commentaries on Diophantus, Apollonius and Ptolemy and the circumstances of her death in 415.

sources.title: Socrates Scholasticus, 'Ecclesiastical History 7.15' (c. 440), trans. A. C. Zenos, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, New Advent
sources.author: Socrates Scholasticus
sources.confirms: Book 7 chapter 15 describes Hypatia's learning, her murder by a mob under Peter the reader in Lent during Cyril's episcopate, and dates it to the fourth consulate of Honorius and Theodosius (415).

sources.title: Dzielska, Maria, 'Hypatia of Alexandria', Harvard University Press (1995)
sources.author: Dzielska, Maria
sources.confirms: Reconstructs her circle, teaching and death from Synesius, Socrates and Damascius.

hypatia-415.detail: Year 415 is given by Socrates' consular date and is secure. Her birth falls between 350 and 370. Suda lists commentaries under her name; Deakin and Cameron argue she edited her father's work rather than writing original treatises. Later legends, from Gibbon to Agora, released in 2009, overstate links between her death and destruction of Alexandria's Library, which had declined centuries earlier. Synesius's letters show her teaching Neoplatonist philosophy privately and advising city officials. Damascius, writing a century later, adds that she lectured publicly in a philosopher's cloak and was admired for chastity and eloquence.

picture.alt: Hypatia, painting by Charles William Mitchell, 1885 (1885 painting)
picture.credit: Charles William Mitchell, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

augustine-city-of-god-426.summary: In Book 22, chapter 24, completed around 426 at Hippo, Augustine asks: 'What wonderful, one might say stupefying, advances has human industry made in the arts of weaving and building, of agriculture and navigation!' He lists 'poisons, weapons, engines of destruction' beside health remedies and discovery of 'the movements and connections of the stars', concluding that 'the genius of man' has 'invented and applied countless astonishing arts'. In Confessions 10.35 (c. 400) he condemned 'a certain vain and curious longing, cloaked under the name of knowledge and learning', calling it 'this malady of curiosity' behind theatre spectacles and idle investigation of nature. Both texts shaped medieval attitudes: craft and invention as gifts of human nature, speculative curiosity as a vice.

sources.title: Augustine, 'The City of God 22.24' (426), trans. Marcus Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, New Advent
sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.confirms: Verbatim passages on advances in weaving, building, agriculture and navigation, on poisons, weapons and engines of destruction, and on 'the genius of man' inventing 'countless astonishing arts'.

sources.title: Augustine, 'Confessions 10.35' (c. 400), trans. J. G. Pilkington, New Advent
sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.confirms: Verbatim: 'a certain vain and curious longing, cloaked under the name of knowledge and learning' and 'this malady of curiosity'.

sources.title: Walsh, P. G., 'The Rights and Wrongs of Curiosity (Plutarch to Augustine)', Greece and Rome 35 (1988)
sources.author: Walsh, P. G.
sources.confirms: Analyses Augustine's treatment of curiositas in Confessions 10.35 within the classical and Christian tradition.

sources.title: O'Daly, Gerard, 'Augustine's City of God: A Reader's Guide', Oxford University Press (1999)
sources.author: O'Daly, Gerard
sources.confirms: Dates composition of the City of God from 413 to 426/427 and discusses Book 22.

augustine-city-of-god-426.detail: Book 22 was finished in 426 or 427. Augustine's Retractationes list City of God among works completed before 427. His double stance admires human artifice as evidence of a blessed nature while fearing curiositas, though Book 22 affirms invention. His examples of curiositas include watching a lizard catch flies, stopping to see a mangled corpse, and consulting astrologers. Medieval writers from Bernard of Clairvaux to Aquinas cite his Confessions passage when ranking curiosity among vices, while Hugh of St Victor cites Book 22 to defend mechanical arts.

picture.alt: Page of Augustine's De civitate Dei in a BnF manuscript (medieval manuscript)
picture.credit: Bibliotheque nationale de France, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

nalanda-427.summary: Xuanzang, resident in the 630s, says Nalanda was founded by Shakraditya, identified with Kumaragupta I (r. c. 415 to 455), and enlarged by successors. Excavations at Bargaon in Bihar from 1915 reveal eleven monasteries and six brick temples in a planned row, with cells, lecture halls, wells and a great stupa at Temple 3. Chinese pilgrims report thousands of students studying Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar, medicine and astronomy after a selective entrance debate, supported by village revenues and royal grants. Earlier learning centres such as Taxila, described in Jatakas and by Greek visitors, had no comparable campus. Nalanda ran until about 1200, sending teachers to Tibet and receiving students from China, Korea and Sumatra.

sources.title: Stewart, Mary L., 'Nalanda Mahavihara: A Critical Analysis of the Archaeology of an Indian Buddhist Site', BAR International Series 529 (1989); Brill reissue
sources.author: Stewart, Mary L.
sources.confirms: Reviews the excavations and Chinese pilgrim accounts and dates foundation to the fifth-century Gupta kings.

sources.title: Scharfe, Hartmut, 'Education in Ancient India', Handbook of Oriental Studies, Brill (2002)
sources.author: Scharfe, Hartmut
sources.confirms: Discusses Taxila and Nalanda as educational institutions, curricula and admission practices reported by Xuanzang and Yijing.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara at Nalanda, Bihar'
sources.confirms: Describes the site's remains from the third century BCE to the thirteenth century CE and its role as a monastic and scholastic institution.

nalanda-427.verification_note: Xuanzang's attribution to Shakraditya (Kumaragupta I) gives a fifth-century foundation; archaeological phases confirm Gupta origins without a fixed year.
nalanda-427.detail: Foundation year 427 is conventional, derived from Kumaragupta's reign, and approximate. Taxila, active from the sixth century BCE, is often called a university but was a city with individual teachers' households, as Scharfe notes. Seals excavated at Nalanda read 'Sri-Nalanda-Mahavihariya-Arya-Bhikshu-Sanghasya'. Yijing, resident around 675 to 685, describes daily routine, water clocks for timekeeping, and a library; Tibetan tradition names three library buildings. UNESCO inscribed Nalanda in 2016. Recent excavation at Juafardih nearby suggests earlier Kushan-period monastic occupation, and copper plates record land grants from Pala kings and a Sumatran ruler, Balaputradeva, in the ninth century.

picture.alt: Temple 3 stupa at Nalanda Mahavihara
picture.credit: Sumitsurai, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

nalanda-427.dating_note: Xuanzang's attribution to Shakraditya (Kumaragupta I) gives a fifth-century foundation; archaeological phases confirm Gupta origins without a fixed year.

codex-theodosianus-438.summary: Compiled from 429 and published in 438 at Constantinople and Rome, Codex Theodosianus collects imperial constitutions since Constantine in sixteen books. Book 14 regulates Rome's corporati: bakers (pistores), river shippers, pork suppliers and lime burners. A law of 365 orders that no one 'once assigned to the corpus of bakers' be allowed 'by any means the opportunity and power of leaving', even with consent of all other bakers, nor to move from one bakery to another. Book 8 regulates cursus publicus. Jill Harries reads such laws as evidence of state efforts to fix labour for Rome's food supply, and of their limited efficacy. It is late antiquity's main legal record of how a state managed essential crafts.

sources.title: Codex Theodosianus 14.3.8 (365 CE), ed. Mommsen, digitized by A. Koptev at Droit Romain, Universite Grenoble Alpes
sources.confirms: Latin text of CTh 14.3.8 dated 15 January 365 forbidding anyone assigned to the bakers' corpus from leaving or changing workshop; titles 14.1 to 14.4 on decuries, corporati, bakers and suppliers.

sources.title: Harries, Jill, 'Law and Empire in Late Antiquity', Cambridge University Press (1999)
sources.author: Harries, Jill
sources.confirms: Analyses the compilation and publication of the Codex in 438 and the nature and efficacy of late Roman public law.

sources.title: Matthews, John F., 'Laying Down the Law: A Study of the Theodosian Code', Yale University Press (2000)
sources.author: Matthews, John F.
sources.confirms: Reconstructs the commission of 429 to 437 and promulgation at Rome in 438.

codex-theodosianus-438.detail: Hereditary binding of corporati, coloni and curiales is attested from Constantine's reign onward; 438 is a compilation date, not origin of this policy. Modern scholars (Sirks, Harries) debate whether these laws describe a caste system or repeated, often ineffective, attempts to secure supply. Book 14 also covers Rome's grain, pork and wine distributions. Laws on bakers (CTh 14.3) number 22 constitutions from 319 to 417, including one making a baker's son-in-law liable to serve and another forbidding bakers to take holy orders as escape. Pharr's 1952 Princeton translation makes all 2,500 constitutions available in English.

picture.alt: Munich manuscript of the Breviary of Alaric, an abridgement of Codex Theodosianus (later manuscript)
picture.credit: Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Clm 22501, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

hohokam-canals-450.summary: In Arizona's Phoenix basin, Hohokam communities dig gravity canals from Salt River, with main channels up to 20 kilometres long and several metres wide, feeding laterals and fields of maize, beans, cotton and agave. Emil Haury's excavations at Snaketown dated early canals to Pioneer period, and later work places first canals around 300 to 500 CE, growing by 1100 to over 500 kilometres of main channels serving tens of thousands of hectares. Canals descend at carefully managed gradients to avoid scouring or silting. Hohokam also fire red-on-buff pottery, make shell jewellery with etched designs and build ballcourts. Modern Phoenix canals follow Hohokam alignments in several places, as recorded by Omar Turney's 1929 map.

sources.title: Haury, Emil W., 'The Hohokam: Desert Farmers and Craftsmen: Excavations at Snaketown, 1964-1965', University of Arizona Press (1976)
