sources.author: Haury, Emil W.
sources.confirms: Reports canals at Snaketown from the Pioneer period and describes Hohokam irrigation engineering.

sources.title: Doolittle, William E., 'Canal Irrigation in Prehistoric Mexico: The Sequence of Technological Change', University of Texas Press (1990); and Howard, Jerry B., 'Paleohydraulics: Techniques for Modeling the Operation and Growth of Prehistoric Canal Systems', in 'The Operation and Evolution of an Irrigation System', Soil Systems Publications in Archaeology 18 (1993)
sources.author: Doolittle, William E.
sources.confirms: Surveys canal irrigation in the Southwest and Mexico including Hohokam systems and their chronology.

sources.title: National Park Service, 'Hohokam Culture'
sources.confirms: Describes Hohokam irrigation along the Salt and Gila rivers as the largest canal systems north of Peru, with the culture spanning the first years CE to about 1450.

hohokam-canals-450.verification_note: First canals dated c. 300 to 500 CE after revision of Haury's earlier Pioneer-period chronology.
hohokam-canals-450.detail: Year 450 is approximate; Haury's Pioneer-period dates (from 300 BCE) were revised later to c. 300 to 500 CE for first canals. Dating relies on radiocarbon, ceramics and archaeomagnetism. Hohokam systems reached peak extent in Classic period (1150 to 1450) and were abandoned after floods and salinisation; O'odham descendants kept smaller systems. Canal cross-sections at Park of Four Waters show channels 5 metres deep and 20 metres wide at top. Jerry Howard's paleohydraulic modelling estimates System 2 on Salt's north bank could irrigate 7,000 hectares. Shell etching used fermented cactus juice as acid, a technique unique to Hohokam.

picture.alt: Preserved Hohokam canal segment in Arizona
picture.credit: MWyattB, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hohokam-canals-450.dating_note: First canals dated c. 300 to 500 CE after revision of Haury's earlier Pioneer-period chronology.

ajanta-470.summary: Twenty-nine rock-cut halls in a basalt gorge in Maharashtra include two phases: early Satavahana caves of the second to first centuries BCE and a main phase under Vakataka king Harisena, dated by Walter Spink to a short burst of about 462 to 480. Painters work on mud-and-lime plaster with earth pigments, lapis lazuli and lamp black, depicting Jataka tales with detailed looms, carts, ships, armour and musical instruments, making these murals a visual archive of Gupta-era material culture. Spink argues work stopped abruptly at Harisena's death. With Bagh, Ajanta holds most surviving ancient Indian painting; UNESCO inscribed it in 1983.

sources.title: Spink, Walter M., 'Ajanta: History and Development, vol. 1: The End of the Golden Age', Brill (2005)
sources.author: Spink, Walter M.
sources.confirms: Argues for a compressed Vakataka chronology of c. 462 to 480 and analyses the caves' abandonment after Harisena's death.
sources.qualifies: Spink's short chronology is contested by scholars who spread the work over a longer period.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Ajanta Caves'
sources.confirms: Describes the two phases of excavation and the murals' technique and subjects.

ajanta-470.verification_note: Spink's short chronology (462 to 480) is debated; alternatives spread the main phase from the late fifth to early sixth century.
ajanta-470.detail: Year 470 sits within Spink's 462 to 480 range and is approximate; other scholars spread work from late fifth into early sixth century. Pigment analysis identifies lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan, its earliest known use in Indian painting, alongside red and yellow ochre, green glauconite and kaolin. Painters laid a rough plaster of mud, rice husk and vegetable fibre, then lime wash, then outlines in red before colour. Conservation since 1920 has caused losses; copies made by Robert Gill in the 1840s and 1850s burned at Crystal Palace in 1866. Inscriptions name donors including Harisena's minister Varahadeva for Cave 16.

picture.alt: Padmapani bodhisattva mural in Cave 1 at Ajanta
picture.credit: Photo Dharma from Sadao, Thailand, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

ajanta-470.dating_note: Spink's short chronology (462 to 480) is debated; alternatives spread the main phase from the late fifth to early sixth century.

zu-chongzhi-pi-480.summary: Suishu's arithmetic treatise records that Zu Chongzhi (429 to 500) found a circle's circumference, for a diameter of one zhang, to lie between 3 zhang 1 chi 4 cun 1 fen 5 li 9 hao 2 miao 7 hu and ... 6 hu, that is between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, giving a 'close ratio' (milu) of 355/113 and a 'rough ratio' of 22/7. His method is lost with his book Zhui shu, dropped from Tang curriculum as too hard. Chen and Qu's 2026 reconstruction shows fifth-century calendar makers used an algorithm equivalent to continued fractions, which would produce 355/113 naturally. Zu also computed Daming calendar with a precession term and, with his son Zu Geng, a sphere's volume. His bounds stood until Madhava and Jamshid al-Kashi.

sources.title: Chen, Guo and Qu, Anjing, 'How did Zu Chongzhi calculate pi = 355/113? A reconstruction of an ancient Chinese algorithm', Archive for History of Exact Sciences (2026)
sources.author: Chen, Guo; Qu, Anjing
sources.venue: Archive for History of Exact Sciences
sources.confirms: Shows that fifth-century Chinese calendar makers used an algorithm equivalent to continued fractions and reconstructs how 355/113 could be derived.

sources.title: Wei Zheng et al., 'Suishu 16, Treatise on Pitch-pipes and Calendar' (636), digitized at Wikisource
sources.author: Wei Zheng
sources.confirms: Records Zu Chongzhi's upper and lower bounds for pi and the ratios 355/113 and 22/7.

sources.title: Martzloff, Jean-Claude, 'A History of Chinese Mathematics', Springer (1997; corrected 2006)
sources.author: Martzloff, Jean-Claude
sources.confirms: Discusses Zu Chongzhi's pi bounds, the lost Zhui shu and the Daming calendar.

zu-chongzhi-pi-480.verification_note: Year is approximate within the span given in the summary.
zu-chongzhi-pi-480.detail: No date for his pi computation survives; 480 is approximate within Zu's active years (Daming calendar presented 462, adopted 510). Suishu is a seventh-century source. A hypothesis that he extended Liu Hui's polygon method to 24,576 sides is a modern conjecture; Chen and Qu's algorithmic reconstruction offers an alternative. Zhui shu was prescribed for four years of study in Tang's mathematics college before being dropped, and no copy survived Song. His Daming calendar used 391 years with 144 intercalary months and gave a tropical year of 365.2428 days. Zu Geng's sphere derivation uses a principle equivalent to Cavalieri's.

picture.alt: Modern bronze statue of Zu Chongzhi (modern statue)
picture.credit: 三猎, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

aryabhata-499.summary: Aryabhata states he was 23 years old when 3,600 years of the Kali era had passed, fixing composition in 499 CE at Kusumapura near Pataliputra. In 121 verses he gives a table of sine differences, an algorithm (kuttaka) for linear indeterminate equations, rules for square and cube roots, arithmetic and geometric series, and states that 'the circumference of a circle of diameter 20,000 is approximately 62,832', pi to 3.1416. He explains eclipses by shadows, attributes apparent rotation of stars to Earth's spin, and gives planetary periods. Decimal place value assumed in his verses underlies later Indian work on zero and reaches Baghdad through Brahmagupta and al-Khwarizmi.

sources.title: Hayashi, Takao, 'Aryabhata's Rule and Table for Sine-Differences', Historia Mathematica 24 (1997)
sources.author: Hayashi, Takao
sources.confirms: Analyses the sine-difference rule and table in the Aryabhatiya (499 CE) and its numerical basis.

sources.title: Shukla, Kripa Shankar and Sarma, K. V. (eds), 'Aryabhatiya of Aryabhata', Indian National Science Academy (1976)
sources.author: Aryabhata; Shukla, K. S.; Sarma, K. V.
sources.confirms: Critical edition and translation; Kalakriya verse 10 gives the author's age of 23 when 3,600 Kali years had elapsed, Ganita verse 10 gives the circumference 62,832 for diameter 20,000.

sources.title: Plofker, Kim, 'Mathematics in India', Princeton University Press (2009)
sources.author: Plofker, Kim
sources.confirms: Standard history placing the Aryabhatiya in 499 and discussing decimal place value, zero and the kuttaka algorithm.

aryabhata-499.detail: Bakhshali manuscript's claim to India's earliest written zero turns on its date. Bodleian radiocarbon tests in 2017 gave one folio a date of 224 to 383 CE; a 2024 Oxford report found that determination inaccurate, and five folios now date 773 to 1032 CE with production modelled between 799 and 1102, in line with Kim Plofker's textual argument for a later text. Firmly dated zeros remain Gwalior's inscription of 876 and Cambodian K-127 of 683. Aryabhata's own system names numbers with consonant-vowel syllables rather than digit signs, so his verses imply place value without writing a zero symbol.

picture.alt: Modern statue of Aryabhata at IUCAA, Pune
picture.credit: Unknown photographer, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

hagia-sophia-dome-anthemius-537.summary: Justinian's church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, begun in 532 after riots burned its predecessor, was dedicated on 27 December 537. Its designers, Anthemius of Tralles, author of a treatise on burning mirrors and conic sections, and Isidore of Miletus, editor of Archimedes, carried a brick dome about 31 metres across on four pendentives above an open nave, with thick lime mortar joints that let masonry creep as loads shifted. First dome fell in 558 after earthquakes; Isidore's nephew rebuilt it higher with a steeper curve, finished 562. Mark and Çakmak's structural analysis traces how mortar, buttressing and later Ottoman repairs kept this span standing for fourteen centuries.

sources.title: Mark, Robert and Çakmak, Ahmet S. (eds), Hagia Sophia from the Age of Justinian to the Present (Cambridge University Press, 1992); reviewed by Terry in Technology and Culture 35 (1994)
sources.author: Mark, Robert; Çakmak, Ahmet S.
sources.confirms: Structural and historical chapters confirm dedication in 537, dome collapse in 558 and rebuilding by 562, and analyse mortar creep and buttressing.

sources.title: Mainstone, Rowland J., Hagia Sophia: Architecture, Structure and Liturgy of Justinian's Great Church (Thames and Hudson, 1988); reviewed in Journal of Hellenic Studies
sources.author: Mainstone, Rowland J.
sources.venue: Thames and Hudson / Journal of Hellenic Studies
sources.confirms: Survey of fabric, construction sequence and later deformations; review confirms scope and dating.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Hagia Sophia'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms construction 532 to 537 under Anthemius and Isidore and dome rebuilding after 558 collapse.

hagia-sophia-dome-anthemius-537.detail: Procopius, writing shortly after dedication, describes dome appearing suspended from heaven and names both architects as mechanikoi, specialists in applied geometry rather than master masons. Mainstone's survey measured ribs, windows and deformations and concluded builders worked partly by trial, thickening piers and adding buttresses as cracks appeared. Later Ottoman architect Sinan studied this building before his own domes. Dedication date comes from contemporary chronicles and is not disputed; collapse and rebuilding dates likewise rest on Malalas, Agathias and Theophanes.

picture.alt: Interior of Hagia Sophia, Istanbul, looking up into the dome rebuilt after 558
picture.credit: Ronan Reinart, via Wikimedia Commons

plague-of-justinian-541.summary: In 541 a lethal epidemic appeared at Pelusium in Egypt, reached Constantinople in spring 542, and moved along grain and trade routes through Syria, Italy, Gaul and Ireland, recurring in waves until about 750. Procopius and John of Ephesus describe buboes, mass graves and urban breakdown. Ancient DNA from sixth-century cemeteries at Aschheim and Altenerding in Bavaria recovered complete Yersinia pestis genomes, settling a long argument about causation; further strains sequenced from Britain, France, Germany and Spain show one lineage diversifying across Europe. Mortality estimates run from catastrophic to modest, and historians disagree on how far this pandemic reshaped late Roman economy and settlement.

sources.title: Feldman, Michal et al., 'A High-Coverage Yersinia pestis Genome from a Sixth-Century Justinianic Plague Victim', Molecular Biology and Evolution 33 (2016)
sources.author: Feldman, Michal; Harbeck, Michaela; Keller, Marcel; et al.
sources.confirms: Confirms Y. pestis as cause of Justinianic plague from Altenerding burial dated to sixth century.

sources.title: Keller, Marcel et al., 'Ancient Yersinia pestis genomes from across Western Europe reveal early diversification during the First Pandemic (541-750)', PNAS 116 (2019)
sources.author: Keller, Marcel; Spyrou, Maria A.; et al.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Dates first pandemic 541 to 750 and documents strain diversification across Britain, France, Germany and Spain.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Plague of Justinian'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gives 541 to 542 outbreak and Pelusium origin from Procopius.
sources.qualifies: Repeats high mortality figures that recent revisionist scholarship questions.

plague-of-justinian-541.detail: Debate over scale matters for technology history because plague has been invoked to explain labour shortages, abandoned fields and later adoption of labour-saving machinery. Mordechai and others argue written, papyrological and pollen evidence show little demographic break, while Sarris defends high mortality from legal and literary records. Genomic work confirms pathogen identity and spread but cannot measure deaths. Dates are secure from Procopius, who gives Pelusium as origin and places Constantinople's outbreak in Justinian's fifteenth year.

picture.alt: Mosaic of Justinian I and his retinue, San Vitale, Ravenna, consecrated 547
picture.credit: Steven Zucker, via Wikimedia Commons

teotihuacan-burning-collapse-550.summary: Teotihuacan in central Mexico, a planned city with apartment compounds, obsidian workshops and avenues aligned to astronomical bearings, suffered selective burning of temples, palaces and sculpture along its Avenue of the Dead. Wiggle-matched radiocarbon dates from charred beams put destruction near 550, shortening earlier chronologies. Manzanilla and others read targeted fire on elite buildings as internal revolt against a ruling cooperative rather than foreign invasion; outer neighbourhoods stayed occupied for generations. Obsidian distribution networks that had tied highland Mexico to Maya lowlands reorganised, and later Toltec and Aztec rulers treated ruins as a place of origin.

sources.title: Beramendi-Orosco, Laura E. et al., 'High-resolution chronology for the Mesoamerican urban center of Teotihuacan derived from Bayesian statistics of radiocarbon and archaeological data', Quaternary Research 71 (2009)
sources.author: Beramendi-Orosco, Laura E.; Gonzalez-Hernandez, Galia; et al.
sources.confirms: Bayesian radiocarbon model dates burning of central structures to about 550 CE.

sources.title: Cowgill, George L., Ancient Teotihuacan: Early Urbanism in Central Mexico (Cambridge University Press, 2015)
sources.author: Cowgill, George L.
sources.confirms: Synthesises evidence for selective burning of civic core and internal political crisis.
sources.qualifies: Cowgill keeps a range of roughly 550 to 650 for collapse pending further dating.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Teotihuacán'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Describes city layout and population and its decline in mid first millennium.
sources.qualifies: Britannica gives a later destruction date near 750 following older ceramic chronology.

teotihuacan-burning-collapse-550.verification_note: Burning is well documented; its calendar date differs between radiocarbon models near 550 and ceramic chronologies up to 750.
teotihuacan-burning-collapse-550.detail: George Cowgill argues against single-cause explanations and favours a political crisis within a state whose rulership left few named individuals. Burning concentrated on about one hundred structures along main avenue, with residential compounds largely spared, a pattern inconsistent with sack by outsiders. Radiocarbon models place burning near 550 and older ceramic chronologies place it as late as 750; ceramic phase boundaries differ between research groups by as much as a century.

picture.alt: Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan, Mexico
picture.credit: Peachseltzer, via Wikimedia Commons

teotihuacan-burning-collapse-550.dating_note: Radiocarbon wiggle-matching places burning of central structures around 550, earlier than older ceramic chronologies that favoured 650 to 750.

byzantine-sericulture-silkworm-eggs-552.summary: Procopius reports that monks from Serinda, probably Central Asia, brought Bombyx mori eggs hidden in hollow canes to Justinian, along with knowledge of mulberry feeding, so that Byzantium could stop paying Persian middlemen for raw silk. Sericulture took root in Syria, Asia Minor and Greece, and imperial workshops in Constantinople wove purple silks whose export was restricted by law. Muthesius traced surviving weaves and showed that domestic reeling and weaving had become routine by eighth century. A 2023 mapping study assembles textual and archaeological evidence for where mulberries and cocoons were raised across Byzantine lands. Transmission of a living organism and its husbandry, rather than a device, made this an early documented transfer of agricultural biotechnology.

sources.title: Muthesius, Anna, 'From Seed to Samite: Aspects of Byzantine Silk Production', Textile History 20 (1989)
sources.author: Muthesius, Anna
sources.confirms: Describes introduction of sericulture under Justinian and growth of domestic reeling and weaving.

sources.title: Wu, 'Mapping Byzantine Sericulture in the Global Transfer of Technology', Journal of Global History 18 (2023)
sources.author: Wu
sources.confirms: Maps textual and archaeological evidence for Byzantine mulberry and cocoon production from sixth century onward.

sources.title: Jacoby, David, 'Silk in Western Byzantium before the Fourth Crusade', Byzantinische Zeitschrift 84/85 (1992)
sources.author: Jacoby, David
sources.confirms: Traces regulation and spread of silk manufacture in Byzantine provinces.

byzantine-sericulture-silkworm-eggs-552.verification_note: Smuggling story rests on Procopius and Theophanes; date about 552 is conventional and archaeology confirms only later production.
byzantine-sericulture-silkworm-eggs-552.detail: Chinese sericulture had been practised for millennia; what crossed was a complete production package, eggs, hatching regime, mulberry cultivation and reeling, held as a state monopoly. Jacoby's work on silk in western Byzantium shows how guild regulation in Book of Eparch later controlled raw silk purchase and dyeing. Silk production spread onward to Islamic Spain and Sicily and then to Lucca and Venice, so this moment stands at head of a European industry.

picture.alt: Silkworm cocoons (Bombyx mori), modern photograph
picture.credit: Fumikas Sagisavas, via Wikimedia Commons

byzantine-sericulture-silkworm-eggs-552.dating_note: Procopius places smuggling of eggs in Justinian's reign about 552; Theophanes of Byzantium gives a Persian intermediary; exact year is unknown.

bow-and-arrow-eastern-woodlands-600.summary: Across eastern North America, Late Woodland assemblages shift from heavy dart points to small triangular and notched arrow points. Blitz's survey dates widespread bow adoption to roughly 600, spreading south and east from Arctic and Plains after much earlier use there. Nassaney and Pyle tested dart and arrow point metrics from Arkansas and placed that transition in sixth and seventh centuries. A weapon with higher rate of shot and smaller projectiles changed deer hunting, warfare and village defence; several archaeologists link it to settlement nucleation and palisades before Mississippian maize farming took hold. No single inventor or site marks this change; it is read from thousands of stone points.

sources.title: Blitz, John H., 'Adoption of the Bow in Prehistoric North America', North American Archaeologist 9 (1988)
sources.author: Blitz, John H.
sources.confirms: Dates spread of bow across eastern North America to about 600 CE and discusses social effects.

sources.title: Nassaney, Michael S. and Pyle, Kendra, 'The Adoption of the Bow and Arrow in Eastern North America: A View from Central Arkansas', American Antiquity 64 (1999)
sources.author: Nassaney, Michael S.; Pyle, Kendra
sources.confirms: Metric analysis places dart-to-arrow transition in sixth to seventh centuries in central Arkansas.

bow-and-arrow-eastern-woodlands-600.verification_note: Adoption is a regional process spanning two centuries; 600 is a central estimate.
bow-and-arrow-eastern-woodlands-600.detail: Point size is a proxy, since wooden bows seldom survive; researchers use shoulder width and neck thickness thresholds to separate dart from arrow tips, a method open to overlap. Regional timing differs, with Great Basin and Arctic adoption centuries earlier. Blitz framed adoption as an episode with social consequences, including intensified conflict visible in later fortified towns of Cahokia's era.

picture.alt: Levanna triangular arrow point, central New York, Late Woodland period
picture.credit: PAR, via Wikimedia Commons

bow-and-arrow-eastern-woodlands-600.dating_note: Small triangular points appear in Eastern Woodlands assemblages between about 500 and 700; dates rest on stratified sites and associated radiocarbon ages.

garima-gospels-ethiopia-600.summary: Two Ge'ez gospel books kept at Abba Garima monastery near Adwa in Tigray carry painted evangelist portraits, canon tables under arches and a round temple image. Radiocarbon tests on parchment, reported by McKenzie and Watson and reassessed in a 2026 study, give dates between fourth and seventh centuries, making them among earliest surviving illuminated Christian codices anywhere and earliest in sub-Saharan Africa. Their bindings, pigments and canon-table design link Aksumite scriptoria to Syriac and Byzantine book culture through Red Sea trade. Monks rather than courts preserved them, and they remained in liturgical use into modern times.

sources.title: Bulakh, Maria, 'Early Geez orthography in the Abba Garima Gospels and in the Aksumite Epigraphic Geez', Bulletin of SOAS (2026)
sources.author: Bulakh, Maria
sources.venue: Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies
sources.confirms: Treats Garima orthography as Aksumite-period, consistent with radiocarbon ranges of about 330 to 650.

sources.title: Bausi, Alessandro, review of McKenzie and Watson, The Garima Gospels, Aethiopica 20 (2018)
sources.author: Bausi, Alessandro
sources.confirms: Summarises radiocarbon dating and codicological findings of 2016 monograph.

sources.title: Winslow, Sean, review of McKenzie and Watson, The Garima Gospels, Speculum 94 (2019)
sources.author: Winslow, Sean
sources.confirms: Accepts early date while noting debate over painting chronology.

garima-gospels-ethiopia-600.verification_note: Radiocarbon brackets are wide; a date near 600 is a midpoint, not a fixed year.
garima-gospels-ethiopia-600.detail: Codex technology, folded parchment quires sewn and boarded, had replaced papyrus roll across Mediterranean by fourth century; Garima shows that Aksum, which also struck gold coinage and raised monolithic stelae, took part in that shift with its own script. Dating is debated because radiocarbon ranges are broad and later rebinding mixed leaves; Bausi and Winslow's reviews accept an Aksumite-period date while urging caution on painting chronology.

picture.alt: Portrait of Eusebius preceding the canon tables in the Garima Gospels, Ethiopia
picture.credit: Michael Gervers, via Wikimedia Commons

garima-gospels-ethiopia-600.dating_note: Radiocarbon ranges for parchment fall between about 330 and 650; stylistic dating once put these books in eleventh century.

gregory-great-images-books-illiterate-60.summary: In letters of 599 and 600 Gregory I rebuked Serenus, bishop of Marseille, for smashing church paintings to stop their veneration. Gregory agreed that images must not be worshipped but argued they should stay, because what writing offers readers, a picture offers people who cannot read, who learn from it what they ought to follow. Chazelle's study shows later medieval writers turned these lines into a general theory of visual media as instruction for laity. Letters are preserved in Gregory's register and are securely dated by indiction. This exchange records an early policy ruling on a medium's permitted use.

sources.title: Chazelle, Celia, 'Pictures, books, and the illiterate: Pope Gregory I's letters to Serenus of Marseilles', Word and Image 6 (1990)
sources.author: Chazelle, Celia
sources.confirms: Analyses both letters, their dates of 599 and 600, and their later reception.

sources.title: Woods, Kim, 'Gregory the Great's Letters to Serenus (599 CE) and Secundinus (769 CE)', in Fifty Key Texts in Art History (Routledge, 2013)
sources.author: Woods, Kim
sources.confirms: Confirms dating and content of letters to Serenus.

sources.title: Britannica, 'St. Gregory the Great'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms pontificate 590 to 604 and survival of his letter register.

gregory-great-images-books-illiterate-60.detail: Serenus had acted out of fear of idolatry; Gregory's reply distinguished adoring a picture from learning through it. Later defenders of images at Second Nicaea in 787 and during Carolingian debates cited him, and his phrase about pictures as books of the unlettered shaped justification for stained glass and wall painting. Chazelle cautions that Gregory wrote about one dispute and did not offer a programme for pictorial catechesis.

picture.alt: Ivory panel of Gregory the Great with scribes, Lorraine, late 10th century (later depiction)
picture.credit: Vassil, via Wikimedia Commons

xing-kiln-white-porcelain-600.summary: Kiln sites at Neiqiu and Lincheng in Hebei show that potters of late Northern Dynasties and Sui, around 600, fired fine white wares from kaolinitic clays at temperatures above 1,250 degrees, yielding translucent bodies with clear glazes. Late sixth-century Xing sherds have firing technology and composition that meet modern definitions of porcelain. By eighth century Lu Yu compared Xing ware to silver and snow, and tribute lists name it; Ding kilns nearby followed and became dominant under Song. White porcelain reached Abbasid Iraq by ninth century, where potters imitated it with tin glaze, and Belitung cargo of 826 included Xing-type bowls.

sources.title: Zong, Lu, Li et al., 'Firing technology and physicochemical basis for porcelain from the Xing kiln in the late sixth century', Archaeometry 66 (2024)
sources.author: Zong; Lu; Li; et al.
sources.confirms: Dates and characterises earliest Xing porcelain to late sixth century with firing analysis.

sources.title: 'Tracing the origin of Chinese early white porcelain in the late 6th century: evidence from ...', Archaeometry (2023)
sources.author: Archaeometry authors
sources.confirms: Supports late sixth-century origin of white porcelain in Hebei kilns.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Chinese pottery: The Sui and Tang dynasties'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: States white porcelain perfected early in seventh century, Hebei kilns and Lu Yu's ranking of Xing ware.

xing-kiln-white-porcelain-600.detail: Earlier Chinese stoneware and celadon were high-fired, but white body required iron-poor clays and reducing-then-oxidising kiln control. Excavated Xing kilns include mantou-type structures with saggars. Dating by stratified kiln deposits and tomb finds places first true porcelain in Sui or late Northern Qi, with sherd analysis supporting late sixth century. Xing to Ding shift came as Lincheng clays and fuel declined in late Tang.

picture.alt: White teaware, probably Xing kilns, Hebei, Sui to Tang period
picture.credit: Zunkir, via Wikimedia Commons

xing-kiln-white-porcelain-600.dating_note: Archaeometric studies date earliest Xing white porcelain to late sixth century; Tang texts of eighth century describe mature production.

sui-grand-canal-605.summary: Between 605 and 610 Sui Yangdi ordered a sequence of canals: Tongji Canal from Luoyang to Huai River in 605, Hangou link to Yangzi, Yongji Canal north toward Zhuo commandery in 608, and Jiangnan Canal to Hangzhou in 610, joining earlier channels into a waterway of roughly 2,000 kilometres. Xiong's biography, drawing on Sui shu and Zizhi tongjian, records levies in hundreds of thousands and imperial barge processions along finished reaches. Canal moved southern grain tax to northern capitals and armies, and under Tang it fed Chang'an through transshipment granaries. Forced labour and expense helped bring Sui down within a decade, while successor dynasties kept and extended its course for thirteen centuries.

sources.title: Xiong, Victor Cunrui, Emperor Yang of the Sui Dynasty: His Life, Times, and Legacy (SUNY Press, 2006)
sources.author: Xiong, Victor Cunrui
sources.venue: State University of New York Press
sources.confirms: Documents canal sections ordered in 605, 608 and 610 with labour levies from Sui sources.

sources.title: Wright, Arthur F., 'The Sui dynasty (581-617)', in Cambridge History of China vol. 3 (Cambridge University Press, 1979)
sources.author: Wright, Arthur F.
sources.confirms: Narrates canal building under Yangdi and its political cost.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Grand Canal'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms Sui construction 605 to 610 and later Yuan rerouting.

sui-grand-canal-605.detail: Hydraulic works included flash locks, towpaths lined with willows and granaries such as Hanjia and Luokou. Needham's volume on civil engineering treats Sui canal as largest artificial waterway of premodern world, built mostly by linking and widening older cuts across low watersheds. Routing changed under Yuan to run directly north to Beijing, with pound locks added by Song engineers. Contemporary criticism of Yangdi's extravagance became a standard trope in later Chinese historiography.

picture.alt: Beijing to Hangzhou Grand Canal at Changzhou, modern photograph of a route first linked under the Sui
picture.credit: Fumikas Sagisavas, via Wikimedia Commons

sui-jinshi-examination-605.summary: Sui emperors abolished Nine Ranks recommendation and under Yangdi, about 605, added a jinshi category to examinations for office, testing candidates on classics, policy essays and literary composition. Tang expanded it, Song made it main road to high office, and it ran until 1905. Elman's history of civil examinations traces how written selection shaped a bureaucratic elite and a vast market for copied and later printed texts, from rhyming dictionaries to model essays. Chinese printing history links woodblock expansion in Tang and Five Dynasties to examination demand. Debate persists over whether Sui jinshi matched later form or whether Tang built most of system.

sources.title: Elman, Benjamin A., A Cultural History of Civil Examinations in Late Imperial China (University of California Press, 2000)
sources.author: Elman, Benjamin A.
sources.confirms: Chapter 1 traces origins of civil examinations to Sui and Tang and their relation to text production.

sources.title: 'The Imperial Examination, Schools and Woodblock Printing: Sui, Tang and Five Dynasties', in A History of Books in Ancient China (Springer, 2024)
sources.author: Springer chapter authors
sources.confirms: Links examination demand to manuscript and woodblock book production from Sui onward.

sources.title: Wright, Arthur F., 'The Sui dynasty (581-617)', Cambridge History of China vol. 3 (1979)
sources.author: Wright, Arthur F.
sources.confirms: Describes Sui abolition of Nine Ranks and introduction of examination categories.
sources.qualifies: Wright notes that evidence for a Sui jinshi comes from Tang-compiled histories.

sui-jinshi-examination-605.verification_note: Existence of a jinshi category under Sui is reported in Tang sources; its early form is debated.
sui-jinshi-examination-605.detail: Examinations required standardised texts, so Tang court issued authorised classics on stone and later Feng Dao's printed edition of 953. Anonymised grading and recopying of papers came under Song. Scholars such as Herbert and Elman stress that Tang recruitment still favoured aristocratic families; meritocratic effects grew after 1000. Dating problem is noted in Wright's account of Sui, where Yangdi's innovation is recorded in sources compiled under Tang.

picture.alt: Imperial examination cells in Beijing, 19th-century engraving (much later depiction of the system)
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

sui-jinshi-examination-605.dating_note: Traditional accounts date jinshi degree to Yangdi's reign about 605; some historians place its institutional form only under early Tang.

zhaozhou-anji-bridge-li-chun-605.summary: Anji Bridge over Xiao River at Zhaoxian in Hebei carries a single segmental arch of 37.4 metres span with a rise of only 7.2 metres, and two pairs of small arches pierce each spandrel to pass floodwater and save weight. A Tang inscription by Zhang Jiazhen credits craftsman Li Chun under Sui. Needham's survey of Chinese civil engineering treats it as earliest surviving open-spandrel segmental arch, a form European builders reached only in fourteenth century. Twenty-eight parallel limestone ribs are tied with iron dovetail cramps so damaged ribs could be replaced singly. It still stands after floods and earthquakes.

sources.title: Needham, Joseph, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 3: Civil Engineering and Nautics (Cambridge University Press, 1971); reviewed in Isis 64 (1973)
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang Ling; Lu Gwei-Djen
sources.confirms: Describes Anji Bridge as earliest open-spandrel segmental arch and attributes it to Li Chun about 610.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Great Stone Bridge' (Zhaozhou Bridge)
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gives 37 metre span, 7 metre rise, construction between 589 and 618 and Li Chun attribution.

zhaozhou-anji-bridge-li-chun-605.verification_note: Attribution and date rest on a Tang inscription; precise year within 595 to 605 is unknown.
zhaozhou-anji-bridge-li-chun-605.detail: Segmental, rather than semicircular, arches let a road cross with a low gradient; open spandrels reduce dead load and flood pressure. Comparable Chinese bridges followed in Hebei and Shanxi. Dating rests on literary sources rather than excavation, so a Sui date of about 595 to 605 is accepted but not fixed; Needham and later Chinese engineering histories concur. Restoration in 1950s replaced some ribs and recovered original carved balustrade panels from riverbed.

picture.alt: Anji (Zhaozhou) Bridge, Hebei, open-spandrel stone arch of c. 605
picture.credit: crazlei, via Wikimedia Commons

zhaozhou-anji-bridge-li-chun-605.dating_note: Tang inscriptions attribute Anji Bridge to Li Chun under Sui; conventional date range is 595 to 605.

nendrum-tide-mill-619.summary: Excavation at Nendrum monastery, County Down, uncovered a stone dam enclosing a millpond, a wooden flume and a horizontal-wheeled mill whose timbers were felled in 619 by tree-ring dating, with a successor mill of 787. Tidewater filled pond at high tide and drove wheel on ebb through a tapered chute. McErlean and Crothers' monograph records wheel paddles, a millstone and timber flume preserved in estuary mud. It is earliest securely dated tide mill known, and one of earliest dated water mills in Ireland, where monastic sites adopted horizontal mills widely in seventh and eighth centuries.

sources.title: McErlean, Thomas and Crothers, Norman, Harnessing the Tides: The Early Medieval Tide Mills at Nendrum Monastery, Strangford Lough (Stationery Office, Belfast, 2007); reviewed in Antiquaries Journal 89 (2009)
sources.author: McErlean, Thomas; Crothers, Norman
sources.confirms: Excavation report with dendrochronological felling dates of 619 and 787 for two mills.

sources.title: McErlean, Thomas, Earwood, Caroline and Moore, Dermot, 'The Sequence of Early Christian Period Horizontal Tide Mills at Nendrum Monastery: An Interim Statement', Historical Archaeology 41 (2007)
sources.author: McErlean, Thomas; Earwood, Caroline; Moore, Dermot
sources.confirms: Interim report confirming two tide mills with dendrochronological dates of 619 and 787.

sources.title: Rynne, Colin, 'Waterpower in Medieval Ireland', in Squatriti, Paolo (ed.), Working with Water in Medieval Europe (Brill, 2000)
sources.author: Rynne, Colin
sources.confirms: Surveys Irish horizontal mills, their dendrochronological dates and monastic contexts.

nendrum-tide-mill-619.detail: Horizontal mills need no gearing: wheel turns on a vertical shaft fixed directly to upper millstone, suited to small flows. Irish dendrochronology from Queen's University Belfast dates dozens of such mills from about 630 onward, so Nendrum heads a dense series. Tide mills recur in Domesday and along Atlantic coasts into nineteenth century. Monastic estates had grain, labour and legal control of foreshore, which explains why a church settlement built it.

picture.alt: Nendrum monastery on Mahee Island, Strangford Lough, site of the excavated tide mills
picture.credit: Ardfern, via Wikimedia Commons

isidore-etymologiae-625.summary: Isidore, bishop of Seville, assembled a twenty-book digest of ancient learning organised by word origins, covering grammar, medicine, law, mathematics, ships, buildings, tools, agriculture and war. His friend Braulio of Zaragoza arranged books after Isidore died in 636. Close to a thousand manuscripts survive, making it among most copied secular works of Latin Middle Ages and a main channel through which Roman technical vocabulary reached Carolingian and later schools. Book 19 describes ships, looms and craft tools; book 20 covers domestic utensils and farm implements. Its method, explaining a tool by its name, shaped how medieval readers classified technology.

sources.title: Barney, Stephen A., Lewis, W. J., Beach, J. A. and Berghof, Oliver, The Etymologies of Isidore of Seville (Cambridge University Press, 2006)
sources.author: Barney, Stephen A.; Lewis, W. J.; Beach, J. A.; Berghof, Oliver
sources.confirms: Introduction dates composition to 620s and 630s, describes Braulio's editing and counts surviving manuscripts.

sources.title: Isidorus Hispalensis, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX, ed. W. M. Lindsay (Oxford, 1911), digitised at Bill Thayer's LacusCurtius
sources.author: Isidore of Seville; Lindsay, W. M. (ed.)
sources.confirms: Primary Latin text of all twenty books including books 19 and 20 on ships, tools and utensils.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Saint Isidore of Sevilla'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms death in 636 and Etymologiae as his chief work.

isidore-etymologiae-625.detail: Isidore drew on Pliny, Servius, Solinus and lost grammarians, often at second hand, and his errors spread as widely as his facts. Carolingian scriptoria produced many copies; Lindsay's 1911 Oxford edition remains standard text. Dating here follows a letter exchange with Braulio dated to 620s and 630s. Etymologiae also transmitted a short account of abacus and of Roman numerals, later displaced by Hindu-Arabic numerals that arrive in Spain in 976.

picture.alt: Title page of an 8th-century manuscript of Isidore's Etymologiae, Brussels KBR MS II 4856
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

isidore-etymologiae-625.dating_note: Isidore worked on Etymologiae until his death in 636; Braulio edited and divided it into twenty books afterwards.

sutton-hoo-ship-burial-625.summary: Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk, opened in 1939, held impression of a clinker-built rowing ship about 27 metres long and a chamber with a helmet, pattern-welded sword, shoulder clasps and purse lid set with thousands of cut garnets over gold foil, Byzantine silver dishes, a Coptic bowl and a lyre. Coins date deposit to about 625. Carver's excavations and British Museum analyses show goldsmiths controlling cloisonné at a scale matching Frankish and Byzantine courts, and a 2016 study identified lumps of bitumen among grave goods as Middle Eastern in origin, adding to evidence of long-distance supply. Ship impression documents rowed, keel-less clinker construction a century before sailing Viking vessels.

sources.title: Carver, Martin, Sutton Hoo: Burial Ground of Kings? (British Museum Press, 1998)
sources.author: Carver, Martin
sources.confirms: Excavation synthesis dating Mound 1 to about 625 and describing ship and grave goods.

sources.title: Burger, Pauline, Stacey, Rebecca J., Bowden, Stephen A. et al., 'Identification, Geochemical Characterisation and Significance of Bitumen among the Grave Goods of the 7th Century Mound 1 Ship-Burial at Sutton Hoo', PLOS ONE 11 (2016)
sources.author: Burger, Pauline; Stacey, Rebecca J.; Bowden, Stephen A.; et al.
sources.confirms: Identifies Middle Eastern bitumen among Mound 1 grave goods, confirming long-distance exchange and seventh-century date.

sources.title: British Museum collection, 'Helmet, Sutton Hoo ship burial', object 1939,1010.93
sources.author: British Museum
sources.confirms: Catalogue entry dating burial to early seventh century with object description.

sutton-hoo-ship-burial-625.detail: Pattern-welded blade, iron helmet with tinned bronze panels and chainmail represent north-west European metalwork at its peak before Carolingian reforms. Bitumen study used biomarkers and isotopes to trace tar-like fragments to Dead Sea region sources, linking an English grave to Mediterranean and Near Eastern exchange. No body survived in acidic sand; phosphate traces mark its position. Attribution to Raedwald rests on Bede's account of East Anglian kings and coin dates.

picture.alt: Sutton Hoo helmet, British Museum, from the Mound 1 ship burial
picture.credit: Geni, via Wikimedia Commons

sutton-hoo-ship-burial-625.dating_note: Merovingian gold coins in purse give a deposition date about 610 to 635; identification with King Raedwald, died about 624, is a hypothesis.

brahmagupta-brahmasphutasiddhanta-zero-6.summary: At Bhillamala in Rajasthan in 628, Brahmagupta completed an astronomical treatise whose chapters 12 and 18 lay down arithmetic of zero and negative quantities: a debt minus zero is a debt, zero times anything is zero, and sums of fortunes and debts follow sign rules, with division by zero left undefined. Plofker's history of Indian mathematics treats this as earliest surviving systematic treatment of zero as a number, and also notes his cyclic quadrilateral formula, kuttaka method for linear indeterminate equations and work on Pell-type equations. Translated into Arabic at Baghdad around 770 as Sindhind, it carried decimal place-value and sine tables westward.

sources.title: Plofker, Kim, Mathematics in India (Princeton University Press, 2009)
sources.author: Plofker, Kim
sources.confirms: Chapter 5 dates Brahmasphutasiddhanta to 628 and analyses its rules for zero, negatives and indeterminate equations.

sources.title: Brahmagupta and Bhaskara, Algebra, with Arithmetic and Mensuration, trans. H. T. Colebrooke (London, 1817; Cambridge reissue 2013)
sources.author: Colebrooke, Henry Thomas (trans.)
sources.confirms: English translation of chapters 12 and 18 including sign rules for zero and negatives.

sources.title: MacTutor, 'Brahmagupta'
sources.author: O'Connor, J. J.; Robertson, E. F.
sources.confirms: Confirms composition in 628 and summarises rules for zero.

brahmagupta-brahmasphutasiddhanta-zero-6.detail: Colebrooke's 1817 translation introduced these chapters to European readers for first time. Brahmagupta also gave an interpolation formula for sines and second-order differences. His date is secure from his own statement of composition in Saka 550 at age thirty under king Vyaghramukha. Arabic reception through al-Fazari's Sindhind underlies al-Khwarizmi's astronomical tables; al-Biruni later discussed Brahmagupta's views on earth's rotation in his book on India.

picture.alt: Annotated copy of Prthudaka's 10th-century commentary on Brahmagupta's Brahmasphutasiddhanta
picture.credit: Prthudaka commentary manuscript, via Wikimedia Commons

nalanda-xuanzang-visit-637.summary: Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang reached Nalanda in Magadha about 637 and studied under Silabhadra for several years. His travel record and his biography by Huili describe a walled campus of brick monasteries, lecture halls, a library and some ten thousand residents supported by revenue of a hundred villages, teaching Buddhist philosophy alongside logic, grammar, medicine and astronomy. Excavations since 1915 have exposed eleven monasteries and temples in rows matching his account. Asher's study and a 2014 Modern Asian Studies article on Nalanda's modern revival trace how this site became a reference point for institutional learning in Asia before Baghdad's House of Wisdom or European universities.

sources.title: Asher, Frederick M., Nalanda: Situating the Great Monastery (Marg, 2015); Asher, 'Nalanda', Grove Art Online (Oxford University Press, 2003)
sources.author: Asher, Frederick M.
sources.confirms: Describes excavated monasteries and temples and Gupta foundation.

sources.title: Pinkney, Andrea Marion, 'Looking West to India: Asian education, intra-Asian renaissance, and the Nalanda revival', Modern Asian Studies 49 (2015)
sources.author: Pinkney, Andrea Marion
sources.confirms: Summarises Xuanzang's testimony and Nalanda's historical role as basis for later revival claims.

sources.title: Xuanzang, Si-yu-ki: Buddhist Records of the Western World, trans. Samuel Beal (London, 1884)
sources.author: Xuanzang; Beal, Samuel (trans.)
sources.confirms: Primary description of Nalanda's buildings, population and curriculum.

nalanda-xuanzang-visit-637.detail: Nalanda issued clay sealings naming a community of venerable monks, manufactured bronze images and copied manuscripts that Tibetan translators later carried north. Xuanzang returned to Chang'an in 645 with 657 texts, launching a state-funded translation bureau. Dating of his stay is reconstructed from his itinerary; precise years vary by a year or two between scholars. Site declined after twelfth century and was excavated from 1915 onward.

picture.alt: Excavated Monastery 5 at Nalanda Mahavihara, Bihar
picture.credit: Sumitsurai, via Wikimedia Commons

nalanda-xuanzang-visit-637.dating_note: Xuanzang's stay at Nalanda falls between about 637 and 642; monastery was founded under Gupta rule in fifth century.

cheomseongdae-silla-observatory-647.summary: In Gyeongju, capital of Silla, a 9-metre tower of 362 cut granite blocks in 27 courses rises from a square base to a square top, with a window facing south. Thirteenth-century Samguk yusa dates it to Queen Seondeok's reign, which ended in 647. Korean historians since Rufus in 1936 have read its numbers as calendrical, 27 courses for Seondeok as twenty-seventh ruler, 12 courses above and below window for months, and its top as a platform for observers. A 2009 Nexus Network Journal study examined its geometry; others argue it was a Buddhist or shamanic altar. Whatever its use, it stands as earliest surviving purpose-built astronomical structure in East Asia and documents Silla's court astronomy.

sources.title: Kim, Jang Hoon and Park, Sang Hun, 'Mathematical Interpretation of a Thirteen Hundred Year Old Stone Masonry Observatory', Nexus Network Journal 11 (2009)
sources.author: Kim, Jang Hoon; Park, Sang Hun
sources.confirms: Analyses geometry and numerical symbolism of Cheomseongdae and accepts seventh-century Silla date.

sources.title: Chang, 'Who Proposed to Build Cheomseongdae?', Journal of the Research Institute for Silla Culture 49 (2017)
sources.author: Chang
sources.venue: Journal of the Research Institute for Silla Culture
sources.confirms: Reviews textual basis for attribution to Queen Seondeok's reign.
sources.qualifies: Korean scholarship disputes whether structure functioned as an observatory or as an altar.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Gyeongju'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Describes Cheomseongdae as a Silla-era seventh-century stone structure thought to be an observatory.

cheomseongdae-silla-observatory-647.verification_note: Date rests on a thirteenth-century chronicle; function is disputed.
cheomseongdae-silla-observatory-647.detail: Silla kept astronomical records from fourth century and sent students to Tang; Samguk sagi lists eclipses, comets and meteors by reign year. Cheomseongdae's hollow interior is packed with rubble to window level, which supports idea that observers climbed inside and out onto top. Earthquake of 2016 tilted it slightly without collapse. Debate on function continues in Korean journals, and no instrument has been found.

picture.alt: Cheomseongdae observatory tower, Gyeongju, Silla, 7th century
picture.credit: Bernard Gagnon, via Wikimedia Commons

cheomseongdae-silla-observatory-647.dating_note: Samguk yusa places construction under Queen Seondeok, who died in 647; purpose as observatory is debated against altar or symbolic readings.

umayyad-barid-postal-relay-660.summary: After taking power in 661, Mu'awiya is credited by Arabic historians with setting up barid, a state courier service with relay stations, mounts and route lists inherited from Byzantine cursus publicus and Sasanian post. Silverstein's study of pre-modern Islamic postal systems reconstructs stations spaced roughly twelve miles apart, seals and passes for riders, and barid's second role as intelligence service reporting on governors. Under Abbasids a Diwan al-Barid kept itineraries that fed geographical writing by Ibn Khurradadhbih in ninth century. Service carried state letters only; merchants used pigeons and private couriers. It is an early case of an empire funding communication infrastructure as a tool of political control.

sources.title: Silverstein, Adam J., Postal Systems in the Pre-Modern Islamic World (Cambridge University Press, 2007)
sources.author: Silverstein, Adam J.
sources.confirms: Chapter 2 reconstructs Umayyad barid, its stations, personnel and Byzantine and Sasanian antecedents.

sources.title: Silverstein, Adam, 'The origins and early development of the Islamic postal system (al-Barid), until ca. 846 CE', PhD thesis, University of Cambridge
sources.author: Silverstein, Adam
sources.confirms: Detailed sourcing of early barid accounts and dating under Mu'awiya.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Mu'awiyah I'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms reign 661 to 680 and administrative reforms including postal service.

umayyad-barid-postal-relay-660.verification_note: Attribution to Mu'awiya comes from later Abbasid historians; a start date about 660 is conventional.
umayyad-barid-postal-relay-660.detail: Silverstein argues that barid blended Roman and Persian practice rather than inventing new technique, and that its surveillance role made postmasters powerful. Papyri from Egypt show Umayyad officials requisitioning mounts and fodder. Route lists compiled by postal officials became earliest Arabic road books, so a communications bureau produced geographical knowledge. Pigeon post for state use appears later, by tenth century, and expanded under Mamluks.
umayyad-barid-postal-relay-660.dating_note: Arabic sources credit Mu'awiya, caliph from 661, with organising barid; details come from later Abbasid compilations.

greek-fire-kallinikos-672.summary: Theophanes records that Kallinikos, an architect from Heliopolis in Syria, brought to Constantinople a sea fire that Byzantine dromons projected through bronze siphons against Arab ships during blockade of 670s. Haldon and Byrne's 1977 reconstruction proposed crude oil from Black Sea seepages, heated under pressure in a sealed cauldron and forced through a swivelling tube, with a flame lit at nozzle. Later Byzantine manuals and Leo VI's Taktika confirm siphon-armed warships, and Emperor Constantine VII told his son never to reveal its formula. Pryor and Jeffreys' naval history treats it as a tactical weapon of limited range dependent on calm seas, decisive mainly in harbour defence.

sources.title: Haldon, John and Byrne, Maurice, 'A Possible Solution to the Problem of Greek Fire', Byzantinische Zeitschrift 70 (1977)
sources.author: Haldon, John; Byrne, Maurice
sources.confirms: Reconstructs apparatus as heated pressurised petroleum projected through siphon.

sources.title: Pryor, John H. and Jeffreys, Elizabeth M., The Age of the Dromon: The Byzantine Navy ca 500-1204 (Brill, 2006)
sources.author: Pryor, John H.; Jeffreys, Elizabeth M.
sources.confirms: Appendix on Greek fire reviews Theophanes' account, dates of 670s and tactical limits.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Greek fire'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gives Kallinikos attribution and first use in 670s.

greek-fire-kallinikos-672.verification_note: Attribution and date derive from Theophanes writing about 815; composition is reconstructed.
greek-fire-kallinikos-672.detail: Haldon later tested a working apparatus using a pump, pressure vessel and heated oil, producing a jet of several metres. Secrecy kept composition unknown even to Arab enemies who imitated it with naphtha pots. Use declined after twelfth century as formula knowledge apparently lapsed. Historians caution that Theophanes wrote over a century later and that first siege of Constantinople may have been a series of raids rather than one event.

picture.alt: Greek fire used against a ship, Madrid Skylitzes manuscript, 12th century (later depiction)
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

greek-fire-kallinikos-672.dating_note: Theophanes dates Kallinikos's arrival and first naval use to about 672 to 678; composition and projection method remain reconstructed from fragments.

avar-stirrup-europe-controversy-700.summary: Paired iron stirrups, attested in Chinese tombs from fourth century and in Avar graves in Hungary from about 570, appear in Byzantine and Frankish contexts through seventh and eighth centuries. In 1962 Lynn White argued that stirrup enabled mounted shock combat and that Charles Martel's land grants to support armoured horsemen set feudal society in motion. Sawyer and Hilton's 1963 reply in Past and Present showed stirrups were rare in Frankish graves, that shock tactics are not documented before eleventh century, and that military explanation of feudalism rested on thin evidence. This Great Stirrup Controversy became a standard case against single-device explanations of social change.

sources.title: Sawyer, P. H. and Hilton, R. H., 'Technical Determinism: The Stirrup and the Plough', Past and Present 24 (1963)
sources.author: Sawyer, P. H.; Hilton, R. H.
sources.confirms: Critique of White's stirrup thesis on archaeological and documentary grounds.

sources.title: Penn, Russell and Wilson, 'On the Roman-Byzantine adoption of the stirrup once more: a new find from seventh-century Anatolia', Anatolian Studies 71 (2021)
sources.author: Penn; Russell; Wilson
sources.confirms: Publishes a seventh-century Byzantine stirrup and reviews adoption chronology from Avar contact.

sources.title: White, Lynn Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (Oxford University Press, 1962)
sources.author: White, Lynn Jr.
sources.confirms: States thesis linking stirrup, mounted shock combat and Frankish feudal grants.
sources.qualifies: White's causal chain is now regarded as unproven by most medievalists.

avar-stirrup-europe-controversy-700.detail: Recent archaeology refines dating: a seventh-century stirrup from Anatolia published in Anatolian Studies in 2021 shows Byzantine adoption soon after Avar contact, and Maurice's Strategikon of about 600 already prescribes iron stirrups for cavalry. Debate now centres on adoption speed and on separating technical possibility from military practice. White's thesis remains taught as a textbook example of technological determinism and of its critique.

picture.alt: Avar iron stirrups, 7th to 8th century, Hungary
picture.credit: Bjoertvedt, via Wikimedia Commons

avar-stirrup-europe-controversy-700.dating_note: Iron stirrups appear in Avar graves in Pannonia from late sixth century and in Frankish contexts by eighth; scholars dispute when and why western armies adopted them.

wari-empire-roads-terraces-700.summary: From Huari near Ayacucho, Wari state expanded between about 600 and 1000 across highland and coastal Peru, founding rectilinear administrative compounds such as Pikillacta near Cuzco and Cerro Baúl on Tiwanaku frontier. McEwan's excavations at Pikillacta document a grid of hundreds of rooms, storage and canals, built to a plan and never fully occupied. Williams' work at Cerro Baúl describes a mesa-top colony fed by a contour canal and irrigated terraces. Wari roads and waystations foreshadow Inca systems, and khipu cord records with Wari-style wrapped colours have been radiocarbon dated to this period. Wari state built this infrastructure without writing.

sources.title: McEwan, Gordon F. (ed.), Pikillacta: The Wari Empire in Cuzco (University of Iowa Press, 2005)
sources.author: McEwan, Gordon F.
sources.confirms: Excavation volume documenting planned compound, canals and radiocarbon chronology.

sources.title: Williams, Patrick Ryan, 'Cerro Baúl: A Wari Center on the Tiwanaku Frontier', Latin American Antiquity 12 (2001)
sources.author: Williams, Patrick Ryan
sources.confirms: Describes Wari colony with canal and terrace agriculture dated about 600 to 1000.

sources.title: Isbell, William H. and McEwan, Gordon F. (eds), Huari Administrative Structure (Dumbarton Oaks, 1991); reviewed in Latin American Antiquity
sources.author: Isbell, William H.; McEwan, Gordon F.
sources.confirms: Analysis of orthogonal administrative architecture as state instrument.

wari-empire-roads-terraces-700.verification_note: Wari dates are ranges; 700 is a consolidation estimate.
wari-empire-roads-terraces-700.detail: Isbell's analysis of administrative architecture argues that standardised orthogonal compounds served as instruments of control and storage. Agricultural terracing on steep slopes with canal feed, maize beer production for feasting, and weft-faced tunics woven at extreme thread counts mark Wari technology. Chronology relies on radiocarbon series with wide ranges; onset and end dates vary by a century between researchers. Wari collapse about 1000 preceded Inca rise by centuries.

picture.alt: Pikillacta, a planned Wari administrative centre near Cusco, Peru
picture.credit: Cusqueandobydenko, via Wikimedia Commons

wari-empire-roads-terraces-700.dating_note: Wari expansion is dated by radiocarbon and ceramics to roughly 600 to 1000; 700 marks consolidation of provincial centres such as Pikillacta.

lindisfarne-gospels-715.summary: On Holy Island off Northumbria, a single scribe-artist, identified by a later colophon as Bishop Eadfrith, produced a Latin gospel book of 259 vellum leaves with carpet pages, evangelist portraits and decorated initials. Michelle Brown's study for British Library examined ruling by lead point, back-lit design drawing, compass pricking and a palette of some forty tints from local minerals and plants, with lapis-like blue now identified as indigo. Brown argues for a single hand working over several years about 715 to 720. In tenth century Aldred added an Old English gloss between lines, earliest surviving English translation of gospels.

sources.title: Brown, Michelle P., The Lindisfarne Gospels: Society, Spirituality and the Scribe (British Library / University of Toronto Press, 2003); reviewed in Speculum 80 (2005)
sources.author: Brown, Michelle P.
sources.confirms: Codicological and pigment study supporting single scribe about 715 to 720 and describing ruling and design methods.

sources.title: Ganz, David, review of Brown, The Lindisfarne Gospels, The Library 5 (2004)
sources.author: Ganz, David
sources.confirms: Summarises Brown's dating and technical findings and notes alternative earlier dates.

sources.title: British Library Archives and Manuscripts Catalogue, 'Cotton MS Nero D IV, Gospel-book (Lindisfarne Gospels)'
sources.author: British Library
sources.confirms: Catalogue description of contents, Eadfrith attribution and Aldred's gloss.

lindisfarne-gospels-715.verification_note: Attribution and date rest on a colophon added two centuries later.
lindisfarne-gospels-715.detail: Codex was planned as a whole: text spacing, lettering in insular half-uncial and illumination were designed together, which Brown treats as evidence for drafting on wax tablets and backlit tracing. Pigment analysis by Raman spectroscopy revised earlier claims of imported lapis lazuli. Dating depends on trusting Aldred's colophon; some scholars prefer a date closer to 698 for Cuthbert's translation. Manuscript survived Viking raids and is now Cotton MS Nero D.IV.

picture.alt: Carpet page before Matthew, Lindisfarne Gospels fol. 26v, British Library
picture.credit: Eadfrith, via Wikimedia Commons

lindisfarne-gospels-715.dating_note: A tenth-century colophon names Eadfrith, bishop 698 to 721, as scribe; dates proposed range from about 698 to 721.

yi-xing-meridian-survey-724.summary: In 724 and 725 Tang court ordered a survey under monk-astronomer Yi Xing and official Nangong Yue, measuring noon shadow lengths of standard eight-foot gnomons and pole-star altitudes at stations from Jiaozhou near modern Hanoi to Tiele territory north of Great Wall, spanning about 3,800 kilometres. Records in Jiu Tang shu give a derived value of 351 li 80 bu per degree of polar altitude, and a demonstration that shadow length does not change linearly with distance, overturning an old rule of one inch per thousand li. It was earliest large-scale geodetic survey on record anywhere.

sources.title: Beer, A., Ho Ping-Yü, Lu Gwei-Djen, Needham, J., Pulleyblank, E. G. and Thompson, G. I., 'An 8th-century meridian line: I-Hsing's chain of gnomons and the pre-history of the metric system', Vistas in Astronomy 4 (1961)
sources.author: Beer, A.; Ho Ping-Yü; Lu Gwei-Djen; Needham, Joseph; Pulleyblank, E. G.; Thompson, G. I.
sources.confirms: Translates and analyses survey records, stations, dates 724 to 725 and derived degree length.

sources.title: Needham, Joseph, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 3: Mathematics and the Sciences of the Heavens and the Earth (Cambridge University Press, 1959)
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang Ling
sources.confirms: Discusses Yi Xing's meridian survey and gnomon shadow tables.

sources.title: 'Yixing', in The Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer, 2007)
sources.author: Springer
sources.confirms: Confirms Yi Xing's dates 683 to 727 and his astronomical survey and calendar work.

yi-xing-meridian-survey-724.detail: Four stations on a north-south line across Henan plain were levelled and measured with cords, giving a baseline about 250 kilometres long. Results fed Yi Xing's Dayan calendar of 728. Recomputation shows accuracy modest by later standards but method sound. Abbasid astronomers under al-Ma'mun repeated such a measurement near Sinjar a century later. Dates come from official histories and are undisputed.

picture.alt: Gaocheng observatory at Dengfeng (built 1276), on the Yangcheng site used as the central station of Yi Xing's 724 survey
picture.credit: Gary Lee Todd, via Wikimedia Commons

yi-xing-liang-lingzan-escapement-clock-7.summary: In 725 Buddhist monk Yi Xing and engineer Liang Lingzan completed for Tang court a bronze celestial globe turned by water pouring into scoops on a wheel, checked by a mechanism that released wheel at regular intervals, with jacks striking a drum each quarter and a bell each hour. Jiu Tang shu describes it. Needham, Wang and Price argued in Heavenly Clockwork that this linkwork escapement, slowing a continuous drive into counted steps, is earliest known escapement, six centuries before European verge mechanisms. Device corroded within years and was stored, but its principle passed through Zhang Sixun's mercury-driven tower of 979 to Su Song's clock of 1092.

sources.title: Needham, Joseph, Wang Ling and Price, Derek J. de Solla, Heavenly Clockwork: The Great Astronomical Clocks of Medieval China (Cambridge University Press, 1960; 2nd ed. 1986)
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang Ling; Price, Derek J. de Solla
sources.confirms: Translates Jiu Tang shu account of 725 clock and argues for an escapement mechanism.

sources.title: Needham, Joseph, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 2: Mechanical Engineering (Cambridge University Press, 1965); reviewed in Isis 58 (1967)
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang Ling
sources.confirms: Section on astronomical clockwork repeats dating and mechanism analysis.

sources.title: 'Yixing', in The Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer, 2007)
sources.author: Springer
sources.confirms: Credits Yi Xing and Liang Lingzan with water-driven astronomical instrument in 725.

yi-xing-liang-lingzan-escapement-clock-7.detail: Mechanism used a counterweighted trip lever that held wheel until a filled scoop tipped it, so timekeeping depended on constant water flow regulated by a float tank. Needham's claim that this constitutes an escapement in modern sense has been debated; some horologists treat it as a water-flow regulator rather than an oscillator. Later Chinese sources also credit a horizontal ring-and-globe arrangement for demonstrating moon phases. Dating is secure from dynastic history.

picture.alt: Su Song's astronomical clock tower, illustration from Xinyi Xiangfayao (1092), the later successor to Yi Xing's escapement clock
picture.credit: PericlesofAthens, via Wikimedia Commons

byzantine-iconoclasm-726.summary: According to Theophanes, after a volcanic eruption at Thera in 726 Leo III ordered removal of a Christ icon from Chalke gate of Constantinople's palace, and in 730 decreed against images, deposing Patriarch Germanos. Council of Hieria in 754 condemned icons; Second Nicaea in 787 restored them; a second ban ran from 815 to 843. Brubaker and Haldon's history argues that scale and violence of destruction were exaggerated by later iconophile writers and that argument turned on theology of representation, whether a painted image could carry presence of its subject. For media history, it is best documented early debate over regulating a visual medium.

sources.title: Brubaker, Leslie and Haldon, John, Byzantium in the Iconoclast Era, c. 680-850: A History (Cambridge University Press, 2011)
sources.author: Brubaker, Leslie; Haldon, John
sources.confirms: Reassesses sources for 726 and 730, arguing policy developed mainly under Constantine V.
sources.qualifies: Authors doubt a formal edict in 726 and treat Theophanes' narrative as iconophile reconstruction.

sources.title: 'Secrecy, Politics, Monasteries, and Byzantine Iconoclasm', Religions 17 (2026)
sources.author: Religions authors
sources.confirms: Reviews current scholarship on origins and politics of iconoclasm.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Iconoclastic Controversy'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gives 726 start, 787 restoration, 815 to 843 second phase.

byzantine-iconoclasm-726.verification_note: Traditional date of 726 is questioned by Brubaker and Haldon.
byzantine-iconoclasm-726.detail: Iconoclast emperors kept secular imagery and imperial portraits; cross replaced figural images in churches. Writers such as John of Damascus, outside imperial reach in Umayyad territory, defended images as matter sanctified by incarnation. Brubaker and Haldon stress that evidence for 726 edict is weak and that policy coalesced in 750s. Western reaction in Libri Carolini of 790s rejected both veneration and destruction, echoing Gregory's position.

picture.alt: Iconoclasts whitewashing an image of Christ, Chludov Psalter fol. 67r, 9th century
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

byzantine-iconoclasm-726.dating_note: Theophanes dates Leo III's first move against images to 726 and a formal edict to 730; Brubaker and Haldon argue sustained imperial policy began only under Constantine V.

mugujeonggwang-dharani-sutra-751.summary: In 1966 repair workers found inside Seokgatap pagoda at Bulguksa in Gyeongju a mulberry-paper scroll about 6 metres long printed from woodblocks with Chinese text of Great Dharani Sutra of Immaculate Pure Light. Pagoda was raised around 751, so print predates that; use of characters coined under Empress Wu places it after 704. Sohn Pow-key announced it as world's oldest printed text. Debate continues: Chinese scholars argue printing took place in Tang China around 706 and scroll travelled to Silla, while Korean scholars defend local printing. Either way it shows woodblock printing of Buddhist spells in use a century before Diamond Sutra of 868.

sources.title: Deyong, 'Revisiting the Origin of Printing: Birthplace, Time, and Social Factors', Chinese Annals of History of Science and Technology 5 (2021)
sources.author: Deyong
sources.venue: Chinese Annals of History of Science and Technology
sources.confirms: Reviews Seokgatap scroll, its date after 704 and before 751, and competing origin claims.
sources.qualifies: Argues printing originated in Tang China, with scroll possibly printed there.

sources.title: Sohn, Pow-key, 'Early Korean Printing', Journal of the American Oriental Society 79 (1959)
sources.author: Sohn, Pow-key
sources.venue: Journal of the American Oriental Society
sources.confirms: Background on Silla and Goryeo printing by scroll's discoverer.

sources.title: Britannica, 'printing: Origins in China'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Notes dharani scroll found in Korea printed before 751.

mugujeonggwang-dharani-sutra-751.verification_note: Terminus of 751 is firm; place of printing and precise date are disputed.
mugujeonggwang-dharani-sutra-751.detail: Dharani sutra prescribes copying and enshrining its text in pagodas, a devotional demand that drove multiplication of short texts by stamping and block printing in Tang and Silla, as it did in Japan in 770. Paper and ink analysis by Korean conservators supports an eighth-century date. A 2021 article in Chinese Annals of History of Science and Technology reviews birthplace claims and favours seventh-century Chinese origins of woodblock printing with this scroll as earliest extant example.

picture.alt: Replica of the Mugujeonggwang Great Dharani Sutra woodblock print, Korea (replica)
picture.credit: Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons

mugujeonggwang-dharani-sutra-751.dating_note: Scroll was sealed in Seokgatap pagoda, built about 751; Chinese character forms date it after 704, and some scholars argue for Chinese printing and a date near 706.

samarkand-paper-making-751.summary: Eleventh-century writer al-Tha'alibi reported that Chinese captives from battle of Talas in 751 taught paper making in Samarkand. Bloom's Paper Before Print shows that Sogdian merchants and Buddhist communities already used paper in Central Asia and that Samarkand's contribution was large-scale production from flax and hemp rags using water-powered stamping. By about 794 a paper workshop operated in Baghdad under vizier Ja'far al-Barmaki, and Abbasid chancery switched from papyrus and parchment to paper, which could not be erased without trace. Paper then spread to Damascus, Cairo, Fez and Islamic Spain, reaching Xativa by twelfth century and Italy after.

sources.title: Bloom, Jonathan M., Paper Before Print: The History and Impact of Paper in the Islamic World (Yale University Press, 2001)
sources.author: Bloom, Jonathan M.
sources.confirms: Chapter 2 dates Samarkand production to eighth century, Baghdad workshop to about 794, and critiques Talas story.
sources.qualifies: Bloom rejects Talas captives as origin of Central Asian paper.

sources.title: Tsien, Tsuen-Hsuin, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 1: Paper and Printing (Cambridge University Press, 1985); reviewed in Isis 79 (1988)
sources.author: Tsien, Tsuen-Hsuin
sources.confirms: Discusses westward transmission of papermaking to Samarkand and Baghdad after 751.

sources.title: Britannica, 'papermaking: History of papermaking'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gives traditional 751 Samarkand date and Baghdad mill about 793.
sources.qualifies: Repeats Talas captive story without Bloom's qualification.

samarkand-paper-making-751.verification_note: Eighth-century spread is secure; 751 and Talas origin story are traditional, not documented.
samarkand-paper-making-751.detail: Bloom links paper to growth of bookshops, libraries and translation in Baghdad, since a cheap writing surface made copying long scientific works affordable. Arab paper differed from Chinese in using rag fibre pounded by trip hammers, sized with starch and polished with stone. Dating of Baghdad mill rests on Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist and later accounts. Talas anecdote remains repeated in surveys despite Bloom's correction.

picture.alt: Peeling mulberry bark at the Meros paper workshop, Koni Ghil near Samarkand, a modern revival of the craft
picture.credit: Enric, via Wikimedia Commons

samarkand-paper-making-751.dating_note: Tradition links paper making in Samarkand to Chinese prisoners taken at Talas in 751; Bloom shows paper was already known in Central Asia and that Talas story is a later anecdote.

todaiji-great-buddha-casting-752.summary: Emperor Shomu's vow of 743 led to casting of Vairocana Buddha at Todai-ji in Nara, completed in 749 and dedicated with an eye-opening ceremony in 752 attended by envoys from Tang, Silla and India. Court chronicle Shoku Nihongi records casting in eight stages over three years around an earthen core, followed by gilding with mercury amalgam using gold newly discovered in Mutsu province. Estimates from temple records give about 500 tonnes of copper and tin and 400 kilograms of gold. Japanese Journal of Religious Studies articles discuss the project as a state-wide mobilisation of labour, metal and faith. The hall built around it remains among the world's largest wooden buildings.

sources.title: Chiyonobu, Yoshimasa, 'Recent Archaeological Excavations at the Todai-ji', Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 19 (1992)
sources.author: Chiyonobu, Yoshimasa
sources.confirms: Reports excavation evidence for eighth-century casting site and temple layout.

sources.title: 'The oldest gold diggings in Japan', Journal of the Geological Society of Japan 114 (2008)
sources.author: Journal of the Geological Society of Japan authors
sources.venue: Journal of the Geological Society of Japan
sources.confirms: Confirms Mutsu gold discovery of 749 used for gilding Great Buddha.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Todai Temple'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms 752 dedication and statue dimensions.

todaiji-great-buddha-casting-752.detail: Casting method piled earth ramps around a clay model, pouring bronze in horizontal bands; seams remain visible. Mercury gilding released fumes that chroniclers do not mention but modern scholars suspect poisoned workers. Statue was damaged by earthquake in 855 and fires in 1180 and 1567; present head is seventeenth century. Dating of dedication to 752 is secure from Shoku Nihongi and from dedicatory objects stored in Shosoin.

picture.alt: Great Buddha of Todaiji, Nara (head recast in later centuries)
picture.credit: Balon Greyjoy, via Wikimedia Commons

copan-hieroglyphic-stairway-755.summary: At Copán in Honduras, Structure 10L-26 carries a stairway of 63 steps whose risers bear more than 2,000 glyph blocks narrating dynastic history from founder K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' to mid eighth century. Begun under Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil and finished by fifteenth ruler in 755, with a dedication date carved in Long Count, it is longest known Maya text. William Fash's excavations and reassembly of displaced blocks recovered its sequence and showed it rewrote history after a defeat by Quiriguá in 738. Copán's scribes also recorded lunar and eclipse tables and corrected calendrical reckonings. Carving on soft tuff has weathered badly, and digital documentation now preserves it.

sources.title: Fash, William L., Williamson, Richard V., Larios, Carlos Rudy and Palka, Joel, 'The Hieroglyphic Stairway and its Ancestors: Investigations of Copan Structure 10L-26', Ancient Mesoamerica 3 (1992)
sources.author: Fash, William L.; Williamson, Richard V.; Larios, Carlos Rudy; Palka, Joel
sources.confirms: Excavation and epigraphic study dating stairway's completion to 755 and reconstructing its sequence.

sources.title: Doehne, Eric, Simon, Stefan and Mueller, Ursula, 'Characterization of Carved Rhyolite Tuff: The Hieroglyphic Stairway of Copán, Honduras', Restoration of Buildings and Monuments 11 (2005)
sources.author: Doehne, Eric; Simon, Stefan; Mueller, Ursula
sources.confirms: Material study of stairway stone and its weathering.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Copán'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms stairway as longest Maya inscription and eighth-century dating.

copan-hieroglyphic-stairway-755.detail: Maya writing combined logograms and syllabic signs, written by scribes trained in court workshops. Stairway's monumental scale made dynastic record a public medium while stelae and codices served narrower audiences. Copán astronomers' work includes Altar Q and a corrected lunar count on Stela A; Aveni's surveys measured building alignments to solstice and Venus points. Reconstruction order of blocks remains partly uncertain after nineteenth-century collapse.

picture.alt: Hieroglyphic Stairway, Copán, Honduras
picture.credit: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium, via Wikimedia Commons

shosoin-treasures-nara-756.summary: On 21 June 756, forty-nine days after Emperor Shomu's death, Empress Komyo dedicated about 650 of his belongings to Todai-ji with an inventory, Kokka chinpo cho, that survives. Objects were stored in Shosoin, a raised azekura log storehouse, and remained under imperial seal with periodic airing. Collection holds some 9,000 items: Persian cut glass, Tang mirrors, a five-stringed biwa inlaid with mother-of-pearl, go boards, medicines, textiles, writing brushes and documents. Hayashi's Silk Road and Shoso-in traces origins across Asia. A 2016 Journal of Cultural Heritage study analysed materials in collection. It is a dated time capsule of eighth-century domestic and court technology.

sources.title: Hayashi, Ryoichi, The Silk Road and the Shoso-in, trans. Robert Ricketts (Weatherhill/Heibonsha, 1975); reviewed in Monumenta Nipponica 32 (1977)
sources.author: Hayashi, Ryoichi
sources.confirms: Describes 756 dedication, inventory and provenance of objects.

sources.title: Nakamura, Rikako and Naruse, Masako, 'Scientific analysis of Japanese ornamental adhesives found in Shosoin treasures stored since the mid-eighth century', Journal of Cultural Heritage 17 (2016)
sources.author: Nakamura, Rikako; Naruse, Masako
sources.confirms: Analyses adhesives on treasures stored since mid-eighth century, confirming repository's antiquity.
