yashodharapura-angkor-founded-889.summary: After his accession in 889, Khmer king Yasovarman I moved his capital from Hariharalaya to a site centred on Phnom Bakheng hill, naming it Yashodharapura, and ordered Yashodharatataka, East Baray, an embanked reservoir about 7.5 by 1.8 kilometres fed by Siem Reap river. Inscriptions on stelae at its corners date it. Radar and ground survey mapped a low-density urban complex of roughly 1,000 square kilometres with canals, embankments and ponds developing from this foundation; its water network diverted rivers, stored monsoon flow and eventually silted. Angkor Wat and West Baray of twelfth century built on this template.

sources.title: Evans, Damian et al., 'A comprehensive archaeological map of the world's largest preindustrial settlement complex at Angkor, Cambodia', PNAS 104 (2007)
sources.author: Evans, Damian; Pottier, Christophe; Fletcher, Roland; et al.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Maps Angkor's low-density urban complex and water network from ninth-century foundation onward.

sources.title: Fletcher, Roland, Penny, Dan, Evans, Damian et al., 'The water management network of Angkor, Cambodia', Antiquity 82 (2008)
sources.author: Fletcher, Roland; Penny, Dan; Evans, Damian; et al.
sources.confirms: Analyses East Baray and later reservoirs as a river-diverting water system.

sources.title: Dumarçay, Jacques and Royère, Pascal, 'Phnom Bakheng', in Cambodian Architecture, Eighth to Thirteenth Centuries (Brill, 2001)
sources.author: Dumarçay, Jacques; Royère, Pascal
sources.confirms: Dates Phnom Bakheng and Yashodharapura to Yasovarman I's reign from 889.

yashodharapura-angkor-founded-889.detail: Barays have been read as rice irrigation and as ritual and urban water supply; Roland Fletcher and Damian Evans find both uses with changing emphasis. Hundred temples ordered by Yasovarman, ashrama inscriptions in Sanskrit and Khmer, and a road system radiating from capital are documented epigraphically. Lidar surveys since 2012 revealed further grid patterns within and beyond walls.

picture.alt: Phnom Bakheng, state temple of Yasovarman I at Yashodharapura, Angkor
picture.credit: Ms Sarah Welch, via Wikimedia Commons

yashodharapura-angkor-founded-889.dating_note: Yasovarman I came to throne in 889; inscriptions record his capital at Phnom Bakheng and East Baray, completed in 890s.

al-battani-zij-900.summary: Muhammad ibn Jabir al-Battani, working at Raqqa on Euphrates between 877 and 918, produced a zij, a set of astronomical tables with explanatory chapters, based on his own observations with large instruments. He measured solar year at 365 days 5 hours 46 minutes 24 seconds, within about two minutes of modern value, found solar apogee had moved since Ptolemy, refined obliquity of ecliptic and precession, and used sines, tangents and cotangents with trigonometric identities in place of Greek chords. Nallino's Latin edition of 1899 to 1907 made it accessible. Translated into Latin by Plato of Tivoli as De motu stellarum, it was cited by Copernicus and used by Kepler.

sources.title: Nallino, Carlo Alfonso (ed.), Al-Battani sive Albatenii Opus astronomicum, 3 vols (Milan, 1899-1907)
sources.author: al-Battani; Nallino, Carlo Alfonso (ed.)
sources.venue: Pubblicazioni del Reale Osservatorio di Brera
sources.confirms: Arabic text with Latin translation and commentary, dating observations 877 to 918.

sources.title: van Dalen, Benno, 'Battani', in Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer, 2014)
sources.author: van Dalen, Benno
sources.confirms: Summarises observations, parameters and Latin transmission.

sources.title: MacTutor, 'Abu Abdallah Mohammad ibn Jabir Al-Battani'
sources.author: O'Connor, J. J.; Robertson, E. F.
sources.confirms: Gives year-length value and observation period at Raqqa.

al-battani-zij-900.detail: Al-Battani showed annular solar eclipses were possible because apparent solar diameter varies, and he gave improved lunar and planetary parameters. His tables mark a shift from translating Ptolemy to correcting him by observation, a pattern continued by Ibn Yunus in Cairo and al-Zarqali in Toledo. Manuscript at Escorial underlies Nallino's edition. Biographical details beyond his Sabian origin at Harran are sparse.

picture.alt: Phases of the Moon from Nallino's edition of al-Battani's Opus astronomicum
picture.credit: Carlo Alfonso Nallino edition of al-Battani, via Wikimedia Commons

al-battani-zij-900.dating_note: Al-Battani observed at Raqqa from 877 to 918; his Zij al-Sabi' was compiled around 900 and revised later.

laguna-copperplate-inscription-900.summary: A thin copper sheet found in 1989 near Lumban on Laguna de Bay carries ten lines in Kawi script and a language mixing Old Malay, Sanskrit, Old Javanese and Old Tagalog, dated by its text to fourth day of waning moon of Vaisakha in Saka 822, which Postma converted to 21 April 900. It certifies that a named official, Namwaran, and his descendants are cleared of a gold debt of one kati and eight suwarna by authorities of Tondo and other places. Postma's 1992 edition and Santos's 2012 redating check make it earliest dated written document from Philippines, linking Luzon to Srivijayan and Javanese legal and scribal practice centuries before Spanish contact.

sources.title: Postma, Antoon, 'The Laguna Copper-Plate Inscription: Text and Commentary', Philippine Studies 40 (1992)
sources.author: Postma, Antoon
sources.confirms: Edition, translation and dating to Saka 822, 900 CE.

sources.title: Santos, Hector, 'The Date of the Laguna Copperplate Inscription', Philippine Studies 44 (1996)
sources.author: Santos, Hector
sources.confirms: Verifies calendrical conversion to 21 April 900.

sources.title: Clavé, Elsa; Griffiths, Arlo, 'The Laguna Copperplate Inscription: Tenth-Century Luzon, Java, and the Malay World', Philippine Studies 70 (2022) 167-242
sources.author: Clavé, Elsa; Griffiths, Arlo
sources.confirms: Reassesses language, place names and regional context.

laguna-copperplate-inscription-900.detail: Place names Pailah, Puliran and Binwangan are identified with sites around Laguna de Bay and possibly Bulacan; Mdang may be Medang in Java. Document shows weights, calendar and titles of maritime Southeast Asian trade world in use in Luzon. Plate is held by National Museum of Philippines. Authenticity is accepted; readings of some names remain debated. Oceania here follows brief's inclusion of Southeast Asian islands.

picture.alt: Laguna Copperplate Inscription, National Museum of the Philippines
picture.credit: Gary Lee Todd, via Wikimedia Commons

mississippian-maize-american-bottom-900.summary: In Mississippi floodplain below modern St Louis, Terminal Late Woodland villagers added maize to a diet of native seed crops, squash and fish during tenth century. Isotopes in human remains show maize consumption rising sharply around 900 and intensifying through eleventh century, coinciding with population growth that produced Cahokia's mounds and plazas after 1050. Earlier claims of substantial maize in Middle Woodland were rejected by direct dating. Maize varieties adapted to shorter northern seasons, stored in pits and granaries, underwrote nucleated towns, chunkey yards and a hierarchy that spread Mississippian culture across Southeast and Midwest.

sources.title: Emerson, Thomas E., Hedman, Kristin M., Simon, Mary L., Fort, Mathew A. and Witt, Kelsey E., 'Isotopic Confirmation of the Timing and Intensity of Maize Consumption in Greater Cahokia', American Antiquity 85 (2020)
sources.author: Emerson, Thomas E.; Hedman, Kristin M.; Simon, Mary L.; Fort, Mathew A.; Witt, Kelsey E.
sources.confirms: Dates onset of intensive maize consumption to about 900 from isotopes.

sources.title: 'Early Maize in Northeastern North America: A Comment on Emerson and Colleagues', American Antiquity 86 (2021)
sources.author: American Antiquity authors
sources.confirms: Comment debating earlier maize evidence elsewhere in Northeast.
sources.qualifies: Argues maize was present earlier in some northeastern regions, though not as a staple.

sources.title: Byers, A. Martin, Cahokia: A World Renewal Cult Heterarchy (University Press of Florida, 2006), chapter on Terminal Late Woodland transition
sources.author: Byers, A. Martin
sources.confirms: Describes Terminal Late Woodland settlement and subsistence change.

mississippian-maize-american-bottom-900.detail: Carbon isotope ratios distinguish maize, a C4 plant, from native C3 crops. Dated burials across greater Cahokia carry no significant maize signal before 900. Beans arrived later, around 1200, so early Mississippian diet paired maize with fish, deer and native starchy seeds. Some hold that maize adoption drove political centralisation, others that it followed. A 2021 comment argues maize was present earlier in some northeastern regions, though not as a staple.

picture.alt: Monks Mound at Cahokia, the later centre of the American Bottom (built after 1050)
picture.credit: QuartierLatin1968, via Wikimedia Commons

mississippian-maize-american-bottom-900.dating_note: Isotopic and macrobotanical evidence places intensive maize consumption in American Bottom after about 900; earlier scattered maize finds are rare.

sican-arsenical-bronze-900.summary: In La Leche valley of northern Peru, Middle Sicán society from about 900 operated clusters of small furnaces fed by blowpipes, smelting copper ores with arsenic-bearing minerals to make arsenical bronze for tools, naipes, I-shaped currency blanks, and sheet metal. Shimada, Epstein and Craig's 1982 Science report on Batán Grande described furnaces, slag heaps and workshops indicating specialised production over centuries, with gold-silver-copper tumbaga alloys hammered into masks and beakers for elite tombs. Arsenical bronze spread along Andean coast ahead of tin bronze, which Inca later standardised. Sicán metalworkers' depletion gilding gave copper-rich alloys a gold surface.

sources.title: Shimada, Izumi, Epstein, Stephen and Craig, Alan K., 'Batan Grande: A Prehistoric Metallurgical Center in Peru', Science 216 (1982)
sources.author: Shimada, Izumi; Epstein, Stephen; Craig, Alan K.
sources.confirms: Describes furnaces, slag and arsenical bronze production dated to Middle Sicán.

sources.title: Shimada, Izumi and Merkel, John F., 'Copper-Alloy Metallurgy in Ancient Peru', Scientific American 265 (1991)
sources.author: Shimada, Izumi; Merkel, John F.
sources.confirms: Experimental reconstruction of Sicán smelting and alloying.

sources.title: Shimada, Izumi and McLeod, 'Batan Grande', Grove Art Online (Oxford University Press, 2003)
sources.author: Shimada, Izumi; McLeod
sources.confirms: Summary of site chronology and metallurgy.

sican-arsenical-bronze-900.detail: Furnace reconstructions and experiments by Shimada's team showed batches of a few hundred grams, repeated many times, with slag crushed to recover prills. Charcoal from algarrobo forests was a limiting resource. Huaca Loro tombs, excavated in 1990s, held over a tonne of metal goods. Dating relies on radiocarbon of furnace charcoal and association with Middle Sicán ceramics; onset is given variously as 850 to 950.

picture.alt: Sicán (Lambayeque) gold funerary mask, Metropolitan Museum of Art
picture.credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons

sican-arsenical-bronze-900.dating_note: Middle Sicán metallurgy at Batán Grande is dated about 900 to 1100 by radiocarbon and ceramic association.

sistan-windmills-900.summary: Tenth-century geographers al-Masudi and al-Istakhri report that in Sistan, on border of Iran and Afghanistan, wind of 120 days drives mills that grind flour and raise water. These mills set a vertical shaft carrying reed or cloth sails inside a walled chamber with an opening that admits wind on one side only, turning millstones directly below. Needham's survey of mechanical engineering treats Sistan machines as earliest attested windmills, distinct in principle from horizontal-axis European mills that appear after 1180. A 2022 Scientific Reports study analysed surviving Nashtifan mills' aerodynamics. Earlier Arabic anecdotes about windmills under caliph Umar are not accepted as evidence.

sources.title: Needham, Joseph, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 2: Mechanical Engineering (Cambridge University Press, 1965); reviewed in Isis 58 (1967)
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang Ling
sources.confirms: Section on windmills cites al-Masudi and al-Istakhri on Sistan vertical-axis mills.

sources.title: 'Effect of resilient architecture in an ancient windmill in the Sistan region on natural ventilation', Scientific Reports 12 (2022)
sources.author: Scientific Reports authors
sources.confirms: Analyses surviving Sistan windmill structures and summarises their historical attestation.

sources.title: Britannica, 'windmill'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms earliest known windmills in Persia with vertical sails, seventh to tenth century.
sources.qualifies: Britannica repeats a seventh-century date that rests on later anecdote.

sistan-windmills-900.verification_note: Windmills are attested from tenth-century texts; ninth-century origin is inferred.
sistan-windmills-900.detail: Vertical-axis design needs no gearing to drive a horizontal stone, like Irish horizontal water mills, but captures wind from one direction only, which suits Sistan's steady seasonal wind. Mills spread to Central Asia and China, where sail-driven pumps of Yuan period may descend from them. Whether European post mills owe anything to Persian examples is disputed; most historians favour independent invention. Dates rest on tenth-century descriptions of an existing practice.

picture.alt: Vertical-axis windmills at Nashtifan, Khorasan, Iran
picture.credit: Ali Vaseghnia, via Wikimedia Commons

sistan-windmills-900.dating_note: Al-Masudi about 947 and al-Istakhri about 950 describe windmills in Sistan; a seventh-century anecdote about a Persian millwright is legendary.

kana-kokin-wakashu-905.summary: In 905 Emperor Daigo commissioned Kokin wakashu, an anthology of 1,111 Japanese poems, and Ki no Tsurayuki wrote its preface in Japanese using kana, cursive phonetic signs derived from Chinese characters. Seeley's History of Writing in Japan and Frellesvig's linguistic history trace how man'yogana of eighth century simplified into hiragana during ninth century in private letters and poetry, and how this imperial anthology gave phonetic script official standing beside Chinese. Katakana developed in parallel from abbreviated characters used by monks glossing sutras. Kana made vernacular prose possible, culminating in Tale of Genji a century later, and gave women writers a medium outside Chinese learning.

sources.title: Seeley, Christopher, A History of Writing in Japan (Brill, 1991)
sources.author: Seeley, Christopher
sources.confirms: Chapters on ninth and tenth centuries trace kana development and Kokinshu's role.

sources.title: Frellesvig, Bjarke, A History of the Japanese Language (Cambridge University Press, 2010)
sources.author: Frellesvig, Bjarke
sources.confirms: Describes Early Middle Japanese writing and emergence of hiragana and katakana.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Kokinshu'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms 905 commission and Tsurayuki's kana preface.

kana-kokin-wakashu-905.detail: A syllabary of about 48 signs mapped Japanese moras far more economically than borrowed characters used for sound alone. Earliest dated hiragana texts include a land document of 867 and pottery inscriptions from ninth-century Kyoto excavations. Tsurayuki also wrote Tosa Diary about 935 in kana in a woman's voice. Mixed script of kanji with kana, standardised much later, remains Japan's writing system, and kana's forms were fixed by decree only in 1900.

picture.alt: Kokin Wakashu, first volume, Kamakura-period manuscript copy
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

chichen-itza-el-caracol-906.summary: On a double platform at Chichén Itzá in Yucatán stands El Caracol, a cylindrical tower with an interior spiral stair and a small upper chamber pierced by narrow shafts. Aveni, Gibbs and Hartung's 1975 Science study surveyed 29 alignments from windows, doorways and platform corners and found that several match extreme northern and southern setting points of Venus and sunset at equinox, consistent with Dresden Codex Venus tables. A stela dated 906 and ceramic phases place construction in Terminal Classic, when northern cities flourished as southern lowlands emptied. Round plan is rare in Maya architecture and recalls Gulf Coast wind-god temples.

sources.title: Aveni, Anthony F., Gibbs, Sharon L. and Hartung, Horst, 'The Caracol Tower at Chichen Itza: An Ancient Astronomical Observatory?', Science 188 (1975)
sources.author: Aveni, Anthony F.; Gibbs, Sharon L.; Hartung, Horst
sources.confirms: Surveys alignments and argues for Venus and solar sightlines.

sources.title: Aveni, Anthony F., Skywatchers of Ancient Mexico (University of Texas Press, 1980); reviewed in Ethnohistory 29 (1982)
sources.author: Aveni, Anthony F.
sources.confirms: Extended treatment of Caracol dating and Venus tables.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Chichén Itzá'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Describes Caracol as observatory and gives Terminal Classic dating.

chichen-itza-el-caracol-906.verification_note: Construction spans two centuries; 906 is one dated stela, and observatory function is argued, not proven.
chichen-itza-el-caracol-906.detail: Aveni's method, measuring every available sightline and testing against astronomical targets, became a model and a point of criticism for archaeoastronomy, since many alignments allow chance matches. Upper chamber is partly ruined, leaving three of original windows. Venus mattered to Maya as a war and calendrical star; its 584-day cycle is tabulated in codices. Later Chichén structures such as Castillo show solar hierophanies at equinox.

picture.alt: El Caracol at Chichén Itzá, Yucatán
picture.credit: Coral2712, via Wikimedia Commons

chichen-itza-el-caracol-906.dating_note: Caracol's construction phases span about 800 to 1000; a stela associated with it carries a date read as 906, and Aveni's alignments relate to Venus extremes.

al-razi-smallpox-measles-910.summary: Abu Bakr al-Razi, director of hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad, wrote a short treatise distinguishing smallpox from measles by onset, fever pattern, rash and prognosis, with advice on nursing, diet and eye protection. Pormann and Savage-Smith place it among his clinical works alongside case notebooks later compiled as al-Hawi, which record individual patients, treatments and outcomes and include a controlled trial of bloodletting for meningitis. Greenhill's 1848 English translation for Sydenham Society made smallpox treatise a classic of descriptive medicine. Al-Razi also wrote on doubts about Galen, on charlatans and on why skilled physicians cannot cure every disease.

sources.title: Pormann, Peter E. and Savage-Smith, Emilie, Medieval Islamic Medicine (Edinburgh University Press, 2007)
sources.author: Pormann, Peter E.; Savage-Smith, Emilie
sources.confirms: Discusses al-Razi's smallpox treatise, case notes and clinical experiment.

sources.title: Rhazes, A Treatise on the Small-Pox and Measles, trans. William Alexander Greenhill (Sydenham Society, London, 1848)
sources.author: al-Razi; Greenhill, William Alexander (trans.)
sources.confirms: English translation of full treatise with differential signs.

sources.title: Britannica, 'al-Razi'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms dates about 865 to 925 and smallpox-measles treatise.

al-razi-smallpox-measles-910.detail: Smallpox and measles had been conflated in Greek medicine; al-Razi's text gave differential signs still cited in eighteenth-century Europe, with over forty Latin editions after 1498. His empirical temperament is visible in reported experiment comparing meningitis patients bled and not bled. Alchemy writings describe distillation apparatus and classify substances by observed properties. Biographical dates vary by a few years between sources.

picture.alt: Al-Razi in a Latin medical manuscript from Naples, Torino D.I.14 (later depiction)
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

al-razi-smallpox-measles-910.dating_note: Al-Razi, about 865 to 925, wrote Kitab al-Jadari wa-l-hasba during his Baghdad and Rayy hospital years; 910 is a conventional midpoint.

nastulus-dated-astrolabe-927.summary: A brass planispheric astrolabe now in Kuwait's Dar al-Athar al-Islamiyyah bears signature of Nastulus, also read Bastulus, and date 315 of Hijra, corresponding to 927 or 928. King's studies of early Islamic instruments identify Nastulus as a Baghdad maker also credited with an astrolabe showing mean and true positions. Astrolabe, a flattened model of heavens with rotating star map over latitude plates, had Greek origins and a treatise by Theon, but Islamic makers of eighth and ninth centuries, among them al-Fazari and Ali ibn Isa, standardised its construction and added prayer-time scales. This dated instrument anchors chronology of a craft later carried to al-Andalus and Latin Europe.

sources.title: King, David A., In Synchrony with the Heavens: Studies in Astronomical Timekeeping and Instrumentation in Medieval Islamic Civilization, vol. 2: Instruments of Mass Calculation (Brill, 2005)
sources.author: King, David A.
sources.confirms: Catalogue of earliest Islamic astrolabes including Nastulus's dated instrument of 315 AH.

sources.title: Berggren, J. L., review of King, In Synchrony with the Heavens, Isis 98 (2007)
sources.author: Berggren, J. L.
sources.confirms: Summarises King's catalogue of early instruments.

sources.title: Oxford Art Online, 'Astrolabe' (Grove)
sources.author: Grove Art Online
sources.confirms: Describes astrolabe construction and early Islamic makers.

nastulus-dated-astrolabe-927.detail: King's catalogue of early astrolabes lists only a handful before 1000, with Nastulus's piece earliest dated; others attributed to ninth-century Baghdad lack dates. Instrument served for telling time by sun or stars, finding qibla and casting horoscopes. Al-Zarqali's universal astrolabe of 1060s and Latin treatises of Gerbert's circle follow. Reading of maker's name remains uncertain between Nastulus and Bastulus, since Arabic script leaves initial letter ambiguous without diacritics.

picture.alt: Replica astrolabes, Istanbul Museum of the History of Science and Technology in Islam (replicas)
picture.credit: Dosseman, via Wikimedia Commons

al-uqlidisi-decimal-fractions-952.summary: In 952 or 953 Abu al-Hasan al-Uqlidisi completed in Damascus Kitab al-Fusul fi al-Hisab al-Hindi, earliest surviving Arabic arithmetic text. Saidan's 1966 Isis article and later edition showed that he replaced dust board, where digits were erased as calculation proceeded, with ink on paper, so steps could be checked, and that he used a mark over a digit to separate whole from fractional part, halving numbers repeatedly to produce decimal fractions. Saidan argued this is earliest known use of decimal fractions, centuries before al-Kashi and Stevin. Book also explains Indian numerals for readers suspicious of them, noting that calculators in markets were mocked as astrologers.

sources.title: Saidan, A. S., 'The Earliest Extant Arabic Arithmetic: Kitab al-Fusul fi al Hisab al-Hindi of Abu al-Hasan, Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Uqlidisi', Isis 57 (1966)
sources.author: Saidan, Ahmad Salim
sources.confirms: Describes manuscript, date of 952 to 953, pen-and-paper method and decimal fractions.

sources.title: Saidan, A. S., The Arithmetic of Al-Uqlidisi (Reidel, 1978)
sources.author: al-Uqlidisi; Saidan, Ahmad Salim (trans.)
sources.confirms: Full translation with commentary.

sources.title: MacTutor, 'Abu'l Hasan Ahmad ibn Ibrahim Al-Uqlidisi'
sources.author: O'Connor, J. J.; Robertson, E. F.
sources.confirms: Summarises Saidan's findings and debate over decimal fractions.

al-uqlidisi-decimal-fractions-952.detail: Al-Uqlidisi's name suggests a copyist of Euclid. His treatise survives in a single manuscript in Istanbul. Earlier scholarship credited al-Kashi in 1427 with decimal fractions; Saidan's reading of al-Uqlidisi's marker as a decimal point is accepted by most historians though its generality is debated. Text also includes multiplication shortcuts and checks by casting out nines. Paper's availability in Syria made pen-and-paper method practical.

picture.alt: Diagram of the evolution of Hindu-Arabic numeral forms
picture.credit: Karl Menninger, Frank Swetz, via Wikimedia Commons

feng-dao-printed-confucian-classics-953.summary: In 932 chief minister Feng Dao, serving Later Tang court at Kaifeng, proposed that Guozijian, National Academy, cut woodblocks for nine Confucian classics with commentaries, using text of Tang stone classics as copy. Work continued through four short dynasties and was presented complete in 953 under Later Zhou, in 130 volumes. Tsien's history of Chinese printing treats this as first state-sponsored printing of canonical texts, shifting woodblock from Buddhist charms and almanacs to orthodox literature and examination curriculum. Private and Sichuan editions followed, and Song government extended printing to histories, medical texts and dynastic law.

sources.title: Tsien, Tsuen-Hsuin, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 part 1: Paper and Printing (Cambridge University Press, 1985)
sources.author: Tsien, Tsuen-Hsuin
sources.confirms: Documents Feng Dao's proposal of 932 and completion in 953.

sources.title: Twitchett, Denis, Printing and Publishing in Medieval China (Wynkyn de Worde Society, 1983)
sources.author: Twitchett, Denis
sources.confirms: Discusses Feng Dao edition and change in scholarly attitude to printing.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Feng Dao'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms 932 to 953 printing of classics.

feng-dao-printed-confucian-classics-953.detail: Feng Dao's memorial cited printed books he had seen in Sichuan and Jiangnan; Shu kingdom's minister Wu Zhaoyi had privately printed classics around same decades. Edition set a standard for page layout with commentary in smaller characters. No copy survives, but later editions descend from it. Twitchett notes that Confucian scholars had earlier disdained printing as fit only for popular texts, so 953 marks a change in attitude.

picture.alt: Song printed edition of the Shangshu with commentary, later than Feng Dao's edition
picture.credit: Jin, Lüxiang 1232-1303, via Wikimedia Commons

al-sufi-book-of-fixed-stars-964.summary: At Buyid court of Adud al-Dawla in Isfahan, Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi completed in 964 Kitab Suwar al-Kawakib, revising Ptolemy's catalogue of 1,025 stars from his own observations, correcting magnitudes, adding precession of 12 degrees 42 minutes, and pairing each of 48 constellations with two drawings, as seen in sky and on a globe. He recorded a little cloud in Andromeda, earliest known note of a galaxy beyond our own, and identified Bedouin star names alongside Greek figures. Hafez, Stephenson and Orchiston's study reassessed his magnitude estimates and found them accurate. Copies made by his son and later Persian and Latin versions carried Arabic star names into European use.

sources.title: Hafez, Ihsan, Stephenson, F. Richard and Orchiston, Wayne, 'Abdul-Rahman al-Sufi and His Book of the Fixed Stars: A Journey of Re-discovery', in Highlighting the History of Astronomy in the Asia-Pacific Region (Springer, 2011)
sources.author: Hafez, Ihsan; Stephenson, F. Richard; Orchiston, Wayne
sources.confirms: Dates book to 964 and assesses its magnitudes, nomenclature and Andromeda note.

sources.title: Hafez, Ihsan, Stephenson, F. Richard and Orchiston, Wayne, 'The Investigation of Stars, Star Clusters and Nebulae in al-Sufi's Book of the Fixed Stars', in New Insights From Recent Studies in Historical Astronomy (Springer, 2015)
sources.author: Hafez, Ihsan; Stephenson, F. Richard; Orchiston, Wayne
sources.confirms: Analyses non-stellar objects recorded by al-Sufi.

sources.title: Digital Bodleian, 'Arabic Manuscripts and Maps' collection page, noting MS. Marsh 144, al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars
sources.author: Bodleian Libraries
sources.confirms: Identifies MS. Marsh 144 as an illustrated copy of al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars held in Marsh bequest.

al-sufi-book-of-fixed-stars-964.detail: Oldest surviving manuscript, Bodleian Marsh 144, dated 1009, was copied by al-Sufi's son. Al-Sufi also wrote on astrolabe use with over a thousand applications. His magnitudes became a benchmark for detecting long-term stellar variability. Al-Biruni and Ulugh Beg relied on his catalogue, and Alfonsine astronomers in Castile used a Latin translation. Date of 964 appears in his dedication, and his star positions are given for that epoch.

picture.alt: Ursa Major from al-Sufi's Book of Fixed Stars, Bodleian Library Marsh 144
picture.credit: Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi, via Wikimedia Commons

cordoba-al-hakam-library-970.summary: Al-Hakam II, Umayyad caliph of Córdoba from 961 to 976, sent agents to Cairo, Damascus and Baghdad to buy and copy books, employed scribes, binders and illuminators in palace, and annotated volumes in his own hand. Later chroniclers put collection at 400,000 volumes with a catalogue of 44 registers, figures Wasserstein treats as symbolic of scale rather than exact. Library, with Madinat al-Zahra workshops, made al-Andalus a centre for transmission of Arabic science that reached Latin scholars through Catalonia within a generation. After caliph's death, chamberlain al-Mansur had books on philosophy and astronomy burned to appease jurists, and remainder dispersed during civil wars after 1009.

sources.title: Wasserstein, David, 'The Library of al-Hakam II al-Mustansir and the Culture of Islamic Spain', Manuscripts of the Middle East 5 (1990-1991), reprinted in The Formation of al-Andalus, Part 2 (Routledge, 1998)
sources.author: Wasserstein, David
sources.confirms: Assesses sources for library's size and its dispersal.
sources.qualifies: Argues 400,000 figure is conventional, not a count.

sources.title: Hamerly, Ulrike, 'The Córdovan Library of Caliph al-Hakam II', in Libraries: Traditions and Innovations (De Gruyter, 2017)
sources.author: Hamerly, Ulrike
sources.confirms: Surveys al-Hakam's acquisitions, scriptorium and al-Mansur's purge.

sources.title: Britannica, 'al-Hakam II'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms reign dates and library patronage.

cordoba-al-hakam-library-970.verification_note: Reign and library are secure; size figures are literary.
cordoba-al-hakam-library-970.detail: Surviving manuscripts with al-Hakam's notes are rare; one copy of a work by Ibn Qutayba bears his autograph. Court also sponsored Arabic translation of Orosius and medical work of Ibn Juljul, who revised Dioscorides with help of a Byzantine monk. Figure of 400,000 appears in Ibn Hazm's circle and Maqqari's seventeenth-century compilation. Gerbert's studies in Catalonia around 967 drew on this Andalusi learning.

picture.alt: Dome before the mihrab of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, al-Hakam II's extension of the 960s
picture.credit: Roldan, via Wikimedia Commons

cordoba-al-hakam-library-970.dating_note: Al-Hakam II reigned 961 to 976; library grew throughout his reign and was purged under al-Mansur after 976.

codex-vigilanus-numerals-976.summary: Codex Vigilanus, a compilation of church councils and canon law finished in 976 at monastery of San Martín de Albelda in Rioja by scribe Vigila, contains on a folio near Isidore's chapter on arithmetic a row of nine numeral forms, one to nine, written in Western Arabic or ghubar style, with a note that Indians have subtle minds and excel in arithmetic and geometry. No zero appears. Burnett and Folkerts treat this as earliest dated appearance of Hindu-Arabic numerals in a Latin manuscript, a century and a half after al-Khwarizmi's Arabic treatise, arriving through Christian scriptoria in contact with Córdoba. Numerals then spread through abacus treatises of Gerbert's circle and Latin translations after 1100.

sources.title: Burnett, Charles, 'The Semantics of Indian Numerals in Arabic, Greek and Latin', Journal of Indian Philosophy 34 (2006)
sources.author: Burnett, Charles
sources.confirms: Discusses Codex Vigilanus of 976 as earliest Latin witness to numerals.

sources.title: Folkerts, Menso, 'Early Texts on Hindu-Arabic Calculation', Science in Context 14 (2001)
sources.author: Folkerts, Menso
sources.confirms: Surveys transmission of numerals and arithmetic to Latin West, citing Vigilanus and Aemilianensis.

sources.title: Smith, David Eugene and Karpinski, Louis Charles, The Hindu-Arabic Numerals (Ginn, Boston, 1911)
sources.author: Smith, David Eugene; Karpinski, Louis Charles
sources.confirms: Reproduces and discusses numeral folio of 976.

codex-vigilanus-numerals-976.detail: Companion manuscript Codex Aemilianensis of 992 repeats numerals. Forms resemble those on apices of Gerbertian abacus counters rather than Eastern Arabic shapes. Smith and Karpinski's 1911 study first publicised the folio; Burnett has traced how Western forms differ from those in later Latin translations of al-Khwarizmi. Manuscript is in Escorial library as d.I.2. Isidore's text, which the numerals annotate, discusses number without them.

picture.alt: Western Arabic numerals in the Codex Vigilanus fol. 12v, 976
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

gerbert-aurillac-abacus-980.summary: Gerbert, a monk from Aurillac who studied mathematics in Catalonia from 967 to 970, taught quadrivium at cathedral school of Reims from 972. His pupil Richer describes an abacus of 27 columns with a thousand counters marked with numerals, armillary spheres for showing celestial circles, a sighting tube for finding pole star, and a monochord for teaching musical ratios. Darlington's 1947 study and Gerbert's own Regulae de numerorum abaci rationibus show how his counting board used nine Western Arabic numeral signs on counters, apices, replacing piles of pebbles, so that multiplication and division of large numbers could be taught. He became Pope Sylvester II in 999.

sources.title: Darlington, Oscar G., 'Gerbert, the Teacher', American Historical Review 52 (1947)
sources.author: Darlington, Oscar G.
sources.confirms: Analyses Richer's account of Gerbert's abacus, spheres and teaching at Reims.

sources.title: Burnett, Charles, 'The Names and Forms of the Numerals on the Abacus in the Gerbert Tradition', in Essays on Early Medieval Mathematics (Routledge, 2024)
sources.author: Burnett, Charles
sources.confirms: Studies numeral forms on apices and their relation to Spanish manuscripts.

sources.title: Richer of Saint-Rémi, Historiae, book III, chapters 43-54, ed. Hoffmann, MGH Scriptores 38 (2000)
sources.author: Richer of Saint-Rémi; Hoffmann, Hartmut (ed.)
sources.confirms: Contemporary description of Gerbert's abacus and instruments.

gerbert-aurillac-abacus-980.detail: Gerbert's letters request copies of Boethius and astronomical texts, and he corresponded with Lupitus of Barcelona about an astrolabe treatise. Legends later made him a sorcerer who built a talking brazen head, an attitude to his learning recorded by William of Malmesbury around 1125. His abacus method spread through treatises by Bernelinus, Heriger and Abbo of Fleury. No zero was used; empty columns served instead.

picture.alt: Gerbert of Aurillac's Geometriae Isagoge, 12th-century Bavarian manuscript
picture.credit: Unknown author, via Wikimedia Commons

gerbert-aurillac-abacus-980.dating_note: Gerbert taught at Reims from 972 to about 989; Richer's account of his abacus and instruments describes this period, and his treatise on abacus is undated.

al-zahrawi-kitab-al-tasrif-1000.summary: Abu al-Qasim Khalaf ibn Abbas al-Zahrawi, physician at Madinat al-Zahra near Córdoba, compiled a thirty-volume medical encyclopaedia, Kitab al-Tasrif li-man ajiza an al-ta'lif. Its final book on surgery, edited and translated by Spink and Lewis in 1973, treats cautery, incision, bone-setting and midwifery and includes drawings of about two hundred instruments, among them scalpels, forceps, syringes, catheters and a concealed knife for tonsils. He describes ligature of arteries, catgut sutures, lithotomy and removal of thyroid goitre, and warns students against operating beyond their skill. Gerard of Cremona's Latin translation in twelfth century made Albucasis a standard surgical text in European universities for five centuries.

sources.title: Spink, M. S. and Lewis, G. L. (eds), Albucasis on Surgery and Instruments: A Definitive Edition of the Arabic Text with English Translation and Commentary (Wellcome Institute and University of California Press, 1973)
sources.author: al-Zahrawi; Spink, M. S.; Lewis, G. L. (eds)
sources.confirms: Full edition of surgical book with instrument drawings.

sources.title: Hamarneh, Sami, review of Spink and Lewis, Albucasis on Surgery and Instruments, Speculum 51 (1976)
sources.author: Hamarneh, Sami
sources.confirms: Assesses edition and dates al-Zahrawi's work.

sources.title: Pormann, Peter E. and Savage-Smith, Emilie, Medieval Islamic Medicine (Edinburgh University Press, 2007)
sources.author: Pormann, Peter E.; Savage-Smith, Emilie
sources.confirms: Places al-Zahrawi's surgery within Islamic medical practice and Latin reception.

al-zahrawi-kitab-al-tasrif-1000.detail: Illustrations in Arabic manuscripts are earliest known systematic depiction of surgical instruments. Other volumes cover pharmacology, diet and a treatise on distillation. Al-Zahrawi records his own cases, including a failed tracheotomy performed by another and a successful one he observed. Region is europe because al-Andalus lies in Iberia; intellectual context is Islamic, with Arabic sources from Baghdad and Cairo reaching Córdoba.

picture.alt: Surgical instruments of Albucasis, plate from Gurlt 1893 after al-Tasrif manuscripts
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, via Wikimedia Commons

al-zahrawi-kitab-al-tasrif-1000.dating_note: Al-Zahrawi died about 1013; Kitab al-Tasrif was completed late in his life, conventionally around 1000.

k2-bambandyanalo-1000.summary: At Bambandyanalo, known as K2, below Mapungubwe hill at confluence of Limpopo and Shashe rivers, Leopard's Kopje people settled around 1000, replacing Zhizo population of Schroda. Huffman's excavations show a central cattle byre that filled with ash and refuse as wealth shifted from herds to trade, with thousands of imported glass beads, locally made garden-roller beads from remelted glass, ivory working and early gold. Wood's chemical analysis of beads links them to Persian Gulf and later Indian sources carried through Swahili ports such as Chibuene. By about 1220 elite moved onto Mapungubwe hill, a precursor of Great Zimbabwe's stone-built kingship.

sources.title: Huffman, Thomas N., 'Leokwe and K2: Ethnic Stratification during the Middle Iron Age in Southern Africa', Journal of African Archaeology 5 (2007)
sources.author: Huffman, Thomas N.
sources.confirms: Dates K2 occupation from about 1000 and analyses its social layout.

sources.title: Huffman, Thomas N., 'Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe: The origin and spread of social complexity in southern Africa', Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 28 (2009)
sources.author: Huffman, Thomas N.
sources.confirms: Sequence Schroda, K2, Mapungubwe with radiocarbon chronology.

sources.title: Robertshaw, Peter, Wood, Marilee et al., 'Southern African glass beads: chemistry, glass sources and patterns of trade', Journal of Archaeological Science 37 (2010)
sources.author: Robertshaw, Peter; Wood, Marilee; Melchiorre, Erik; Popelka-Filcoff, Rachel S.; Glascock, Michael D.
sources.confirms: Chemical sourcing of K2 and Mapungubwe beads to Indian Ocean glassmaking.

k2-bambandyanalo-1000.detail: K2 marks earliest evidence in southern African interior of long-distance trade altering settlement layout, as byre gave way to a court and cattle moved outside. Radiocarbon dates cluster between tenth and thirteenth centuries. Debate concerns whether class distinction began at K2 or only at Mapungubwe. Human remains excavated in 1930s were repatriated and reburied in 2007 after negotiations with descendant communities.

picture.alt: Mapungubwe Hill, Limpopo, near the K2 (Bambandyanalo) settlement
picture.credit: Marius Loots, via Wikimedia Commons

k2-bambandyanalo-1000.dating_note: K2 was occupied from about 1000 to 1220 on radiocarbon and ceramic grounds, after Zhizo-phase Schroda; Mapungubwe hill followed from about 1220.

tale-of-genji-1008.summary: An entry in Murasaki Shikibu's diary for eleventh month of 1008 describes Fujiwara no Kinto asking for a young Murasaki, a character in her tale, showing that chapters of Genji monogatari were circulating in manuscript among courtiers of Empress Shoshi. Bowring's study of text and its author sets this as earliest external date for work, a prose narrative of 54 chapters following Prince Genji and his descendants through love, politics and loss. Written in kana by a woman in service, copied by hand and passed between salons, it shows a literary market working through private copying before print. Diary also records Shoshi's household assembling a presentation copy with fine paper and bindings.

sources.title: Bowring, Richard, Murasaki Shikibu: The Tale of Genji, 2nd ed. (Cambridge University Press, 2003)
sources.author: Bowring, Richard
sources.confirms: Dates circulation from 1008 diary entry and describes text's transmission.

sources.title: Murasaki Shikibu, Her Diary and Poetic Memoirs, trans. Richard Bowring (Princeton University Press, 1982); reviewed in Journal of Asian Studies 42 (1983)
sources.author: Murasaki Shikibu; Bowring, Richard (trans.)
sources.confirms: Translation of diary entries for 1008 mentioning the tale.

sources.title: Britannica, 'The Tale of Genji'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Confirms early eleventh-century date and authorship.

tale-of-genji-1008.detail: Genji's length, about 750,000 characters, and its psychological interiority have no parallel in earlier narrative. Earliest surviving manuscripts date from twelfth and thirteenth centuries, with Fujiwara no Teika's recension becoming standard. Chapter order and authorship of some later chapters are debated. Illustrated handscrolls of about 1130 survive in fragments. Murasaki's own dates are uncertain, about 973 to about 1014, and her personal name is unknown.

picture.alt: Azumaya scene from the 12th-century Genji Monogatari Emaki
picture.credit: Imperial court in Kyoto, via Wikimedia Commons

goryeo-tripitaka-first-carving-1011.summary: In 1011, with Khitan Liao armies occupying the capital Kaegyong, King Hyeonjong vowed to have entire Buddhist canon cut on woodblocks, a project that continued for decades and produced some 6,000 fascicles based on Northern Song Kaibao canon printed from 971 to 983. Lancaster's catalogue traces this first Goryeo Tripitaka through prints preserved in Japan, since blocks were burned by Mongols in 1232 and replaced by second Tripitaka Koreana of 1236 to 1251 at Haeinsa. Undertaking turned woodblock printing, used for charms since Mugujeonggwang dharani, into a state project of textual preservation and protective ritual, rivaling Chinese imperial canons.

sources.title: Lancaster, Lewis R. and Park, Sung-bae, The Korean Buddhist Canon: A Descriptive Catalogue (University of California Press, 1979)
sources.author: Lancaster, Lewis R.; Park, Sung-bae
sources.confirms: Introduction dates first carving from 1011 and traces its destruction and replacement.

sources.title: 'A Study on the Bottom Book of the Tripitaka Koreana: the First Tripitaka Koreana, the Second Tripitaka Koreana', Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies 48 (2011)
sources.author: Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies author
sources.venue: Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies
sources.confirms: Compares base texts of first and second carvings.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World, 'Printing woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana and miscellaneous Buddhist scriptures'
sources.author: UNESCO
sources.confirms: Confirms first carving in eleventh century and loss in 1232.

goryeo-tripitaka-first-carving-1011.detail: Supplementary carving under monk Uicheon in 1090s added commentaries collected from Song, Liao and Japan. Prints of first canon survive in Nanzenji in Kyoto and elsewhere, allowing textual comparison with Kaibao edition. Second canon's 81,258 blocks remain at Haeinsa and are UNESCO listed. Motive combined piety, merit-making for defence and competition with Liao's own canon, which Khitan court was printing in same decades.

picture.alt: Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks at Haeinsa (the 13th-century second carving)
picture.credit: Bernard Gagnon, via Wikimedia Commons

champa-rice-zhenzong-1012.summary: In 1012, after drought in Jiangnan and Huainan, Song emperor Zhenzong ordered 30,000 bushels of Champa rice seed, an early-ripening variety from Champa in central Vietnam already grown in Fujian, sent to farmers of lower Yangzi with printed instructions for cultivation. Ho Ping-ti's 1956 article traced how this variety, maturing in about sixty days and tolerating poorer and higher ground, allowed double cropping and expansion onto hillsides, underpinning population growth to over 100 million by 1100. Later selection shortened maturation further. Episode shows state agronomy using print and distribution networks to move a crop across regions.

sources.title: Ho, Ping-ti, 'Early-Ripening Rice in Chinese History', Economic History Review 9 (1956)
sources.author: Ho, Ping-ti
sources.confirms: Documents 1012 distribution and argues for long-term agrarian effects.

sources.title: Bray, Francesca, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 6 part 2: Agriculture (Cambridge University Press, 1984)
sources.author: Bray, Francesca
sources.confirms: Discusses Champa rice varieties and qualifies Ho's thesis.

sources.title: Elvin, Mark, The Pattern of the Chinese Past (Stanford University Press, 1973)
sources.author: Elvin, Mark
sources.confirms: Places Champa rice within Song agricultural change.

champa-rice-zhenzong-1012.detail: Song shi and Zhenzong's edicts record distribution; agricultural writers such as Chen Fu in 1149 describe varieties and planting schedules. Ho's thesis of a Champa rice-led agrarian transformation has been qualified by scholars noting that early-ripening varieties existed in China before 1012 and that yields of Champa types were lower. Role of terracing, irrigation pumps and wet-field tools alongside seed is emphasised in later work.

picture.alt: Terraced rice fields in Hunan, photograph from Farmers of Forty Centuries (1911)
picture.credit: Underwood & Underwood, N. Y, via Wikimedia Commons

ibn-al-haytham-kitab-al-manazir-1021.summary: In Cairo under Fatimid caliph al-Hakim and his successor, Ibn al-Haytham wrote Kitab al-Manazir in seven books, rejecting extramission theories of Euclid and Ptolemy and showing that rays travel from each point of a lit object into eye, where they form an image in a point-to-point order. He set out controlled experiments with dark chambers, apertures and screens, described camera obscura, studied reflection in curved mirrors and refraction, and analysed psychology of perception and optical illusions. Sabra's edition and translation and Smith's edition of Latin De aspectibus trace how work, translated around 1200, shaped Roger Bacon, Witelo, Kepler's retinal image and European understanding of experimental argument.

sources.title: Sabra, A. I., The Optics of Ibn al-Haytham, Books I-III: On Direct Vision, 2 vols (Warburg Institute, London, 1989); reviewed in Isis 82 (1991)
sources.author: Ibn al-Haytham; Sabra, A. I. (trans.)
sources.confirms: English translation with commentary dating composition and analysing experimental method.

sources.title: Smith, A. Mark, Alhacen's Theory of Visual Perception: A Critical Edition of the First Three Books of Alhacen's De Aspectibus, Transactions of the American Philosophical Society 91 (2001)
sources.author: Smith, A. Mark
sources.venue: Transactions of the American Philosophical Society
sources.confirms: Latin edition with introduction on intromission theory and later influence.

sources.title: Smith, A. Mark, From Sight to Light: The Passage from Ancient to Modern Optics (University of Chicago Press, 2015); reviewed in Isis 107 (2016)
sources.author: Smith, A. Mark
sources.confirms: Surveys Ibn al-Haytham's optics and its transmission to Kepler.

ibn-al-haytham-kitab-al-manazir-1021.verification_note: Content is secure; composition date is disputed between 1011-1021 and 1028-1038.
ibn-al-haytham-kitab-al-manazir-1021.detail: Ibn al-Haytham's phrase for experiment, i'tibar, denotes testing a claim by arranged observation, repeated for each case. Problem of Alhazen, finding reflection point on a spherical mirror, occupied mathematicians until seventeenth century. He also wrote on moonlight, on atmospheric refraction and twilight, and a critique of Ptolemy's astronomy. Biographical stories of feigned madness to escape al-Hakim after a failed Nile project come from later sources.

picture.alt: Opticae thesaurus, Risner's 1572 Latin edition of Ibn al-Haytham's Optics
picture.credit: Alhazen, via Wikimedia Commons

ibn-al-haytham-kitab-al-manazir-1021.dating_note: Sabra dates composition of Kitab al-Manazir to between 1028 and 1038 in Cairo; older accounts place it between 1011 and 1021, and this record follows brief's convention while noting dispute.

lanse-aux-meadows-norse-1021.summary: At L'Anse aux Meadows on northern tip of Newfoundland, eight turf-walled buildings, iron rivets, a bronze pin and bog-iron smelting mark a Norse base identified by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad in 1960. In 2021 three pieces of wood from different trees, each bearing clean metal-tool cuts, were found to carry a radiocarbon spike caused by a solar storm of 993 in their rings, and counting outer rings fixed felling year at 1021. This gave first exact calendar date for Europeans in Americas, consistent with Vinland sagas' voyages of Leif Eriksson and Thorfinn Karlsefni around 1000. Peat evidence points to activity over a longer span.

sources.title: Kuitems, Margot et al., 'Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021', Nature 601 (2022)
sources.author: Kuitems, Margot; Wallace, Birgitta L.; Lindsay, Charles; et al.
sources.confirms: Dates wood cut by Norse tools to 1021 using 993 cosmic-ray marker.

sources.title: Ledger, Paul M., Girdland-Flink, Linus and Forbes, Véronique, 'New horizons at L'Anse aux Meadows', PNAS 116 (2019)
sources.author: Ledger, Paul M.; Girdland-Flink, Linus; Forbes, Véronique
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Peat-bog evidence of Norse and indigenous activity and site chronology.

sources.title: Parks Canada, 'L'Anse aux Meadows National Historic Site'
sources.author: Parks Canada
sources.confirms: Describes site, buildings and finds.

lanse-aux-meadows-norse-1021.detail: Site served as a gateway for exploring Gulf of St Lawrence, where butternuts not native to Newfoundland were found. Norse clinker-built ships, descending from Oseberg and Gokstad types, made such crossings from Greenland. Occupation was brief, a few years to a decade or so, and sagas record conflict with indigenous people. Site is a UNESCO World Heritage property managed by Parks Canada.

picture.alt: Mounds of the original Norse longhouse at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland
picture.credit: Acunsolo, via Wikimedia Commons

lanse-aux-meadows-norse-1021.dating_note: Kuitems and colleagues dated three wood pieces cut with metal tools to exactly 1021 using a cosmic-ray spike of 993 in tree rings; site occupation may have spanned several years.

jiaozi-paper-money-chengdu-1024.summary: In Sichuan, where heavy iron coins made large payments cumbersome, sixteen merchant houses of Chengdu had issued printed deposit notes called jiaozi around 1000. After defaults, prefect Zhang Yong ordered private issue closed, and in 1023 Song court established a Jiaozi Office in Yizhou, Chengdu, which in 1024 issued first government notes, printed from woodblocks with seals, serial marks and multicolour designs against a reserve of iron cash, in issues valid for three years. Von Glahn's monetary history traces how this convertible, time-limited currency later spread to other circuits and inflated under military pressure, leading to huizi of 1160s and Yuan paper money seen by Marco Polo.

sources.title: von Glahn, Richard, Fountain of Fortune: Money and Monetary Policy in China, 1000-1700 (University of California Press, 1996)
sources.author: von Glahn, Richard
sources.confirms: Traces private jiaozi, 1023 office and 1024 issue, and later paper currencies.

sources.title: 'Jiaozi', in Chinese Economic History dictionary entry (Springer, 2023)
sources.author: Springer
sources.confirms: Summarises jiaozi issue dates and reserve system.

sources.title: Yang, Lien-sheng, Money and Credit in China: A Short History (Harvard University Press, 1952), chapter VI, Paper Money to the End of the Sung Dynasty
sources.author: Yang, Lien-sheng
sources.confirms: Traces Sichuan jiaozi from private notes to government issue in 1020s.

jiaozi-paper-money-chengdu-1024.detail: Jiaozi built on Tang flying cash and on Sichuan's printing industry, which also produced Buddhist texts and almanacs. Reserve ratio was initially about 28 percent of issue; notes were redeemable for a fee. Over-issue under Huizong in early twelfth century and renaming as qianyin showed limits of trust. Counterfeiting was punished by death, and notes carried printed warnings to that effect alongside images of buildings and figures.

picture.alt: Northern Song banknote printing plate, China Printing Museum, Beijing
picture.credit: Popolon, via Wikimedia Commons

ibn-sina-canon-of-medicine-1025.summary: Ibn Sina (born near Bukhara, 980) began al-Qanun fi al-Tibb in Gorgan and finished it in Hamadan around 1025. Five books cover general principles, about 760 simple drugs, organ diseases, whole-body diseases and compound remedies. Book II sets out seven rules for drug testing, among them trial on human disease rather than animals and consistent effect in many cases. Gerard of Cremona's Latin translation from twelfth-century Toledo stayed on syllabi at Montpellier and Louvain into the 1600s. It opens: "Medicine is a science from which one learns the states of the human body with respect to what is healthy and what is not, in order to preserve good health when it exists and restore it when it is lacking."

sources.title: Nasser, Mona; Tibi, Aida; Savage-Smith, Emilie, 'Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine: 11th century rules for assessing the effects of drugs', Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine 102 (2009)
sources.author: Nasser, Mona; Tibi, Aida; Savage-Smith, Emilie
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine
sources.confirms: Confirms the Canon was begun in Gorgan and completed in Hamadan, its five-book structure, the seven rules for drug testing, and its six centuries as the leading textbook.

sources.title: 'Avicenna', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Confirms birth in 980 near Bukhara, death in 1037 in Hamadan, about 760 drugs in Book II, and use as a European textbook into the mid-17th century.

sources.title: National Library of Medicine, 'Islamic Medical Manuscripts: Catalogue, Avicenna', NLM digital collections
sources.author: National Library of Medicine
sources.confirms: Confirms the Gerard of Cremona Latin translation, Alpago revision, teaching at Louvain and Montpellier, and the opening sentence quoted.

ibn-sina-canon-of-medicine-1025.verification_note: Completion year is given as c.1025 by Nasser, Tibi and Savage-Smith and other scholars; some sources say 1024 or spread composition over 1012 to 1024. Marked approximate.
ibn-sina-canon-of-medicine-1025.detail: Published completion dates range from 1024 to 1025 and manuscript tradition does not fix a single year. Latin editions appeared in Venice and elsewhere; Andrea Alpago revised Gerard's translation in early sixteenth century. Across Islamic lands and Europe, Ibn Sina's Canon remained a principal medical textbook for roughly six centuries.

picture.alt: Page from a 15th-century manuscript of Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine showing a pharmacy, Ferrara
picture.credit: Unknown illuminator, 15th-century manuscript, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

polynesian-east-settlement-1025.summary: After a pause of nearly two millennia in Samoa and Tonga, Polynesians using double-hulled sailing canoes and star, swell and bird navigation settled central East Polynesia. A reanalysis of over 1,400 radiocarbon dates, keeping only reliable short-lived samples, placed Society Islands colonisation at about 1025 to 1120, followed within a century or two by Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand. Lake sediment from Atiu in Cook Islands holds human indicators by about 900, so earlier arrival is possible. Polynesians dispersed across a vast ocean within a few centuries without compass.

sources.title: Wilmshurst, Janet M., Hunt, Terry L., Lipo, Carl P. and Anderson, Atholl J., 'High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia', PNAS 108 (2011)
sources.author: Wilmshurst, Janet M.; Hunt, Terry L.; Lipo, Carl P.; Anderson, Atholl J.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Dates Society Islands settlement to about 1025 to 1120.

sources.title: Sear, David A. et al., 'Human settlement of East Polynesia earlier, incremental, and coincident with prolonged South Pacific drought', PNAS 117 (2020)
sources.author: Sear, David A.; Allen, Melinda S.; Hassall, Jonathan D.; et al.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Argues from lake sediments for settlement by about 900.
sources.qualifies: Contradicts short chronology; earlier arrival possible.

sources.title: Wilmshurst, Janet M. et al., 'Reply to Mulrooney et al.: Accepting lower precision radiocarbon dates results in longer colonization chronologies for East Polynesia', PNAS 108 (2011)
sources.author: Wilmshurst, Janet M.; Hunt, Terry L.; Lipo, Carl P.; Anderson, Atholl J.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Defends short chronology against criticism.

polynesian-east-settlement-1025.verification_note: Settlement date is actively disputed between about 900 and about 1025.
polynesian-east-settlement-1025.detail: Short chronology rests on excluding dates from long-lived wood and unidentified charcoal, which inflate ages. Sweet potato from South America reached Polynesia by about 1200, implying a voyage to or from Americas. Rapa Nui's settlement is now placed around 1200, later than Society Islands colonisation. Pacific rat, dog and chicken arrived with settlers. Radiocarbon on short-lived samples supports settlement from about 1025; lake sediment supports about 900.

picture.alt: Hokule'a, a modern reconstruction of a Polynesian voyaging canoe, arriving in Honolulu 1976
picture.credit: Phil Uhl, via Wikimedia Commons

polynesian-east-settlement-1025.dating_note: Wilmshurst and colleagues' 2011 short chronology places Society Islands settlement at 1025 to 1120; Sear and colleagues in 2020 argue from lake sediments for arrival in Atiu by about 900, so date remains contested.

guido-arezzo-staff-notation-1026.summary: Between about 1026 and 1028 Guido of Arezzo, a Benedictine monk teaching at Arezzo's cathedral school, wrote Micrologus, a manual that spread his way of writing music on a staff of lines. Earlier neumes showed only a melody's rise and fall; Guido's lines, spaced a third apart with letters as clefs and C and F lines picked out in yellow and red, fixed every pitch so a singer could learn a chant without hearing it first. He said his boys learned in months what had taken years. After Boethius, Micrologus was the Middle Ages' most copied music treatise, and his staff is the direct ancestor of written music today.

sources.title: Guido of Arezzo
Micrologus
Grier, James, 'Guido of Arezzo', Oxford Bibliographies in Music (Oxford University Press, 2011)
sources.author: Grier, James
sources.venue: Oxford Bibliographies in Music, Oxford University Press
sources.confirms: Grier dates Guido's four authentic writings to the third and fourth decades of the eleventh century and credits them with introducing solmization and staff notation equipped with clefs.
sources.qualifies: It dates the writings as a group to the 1020s and 1030s and gives no single year for the Micrologus.

sources.title: Babb, Warren (trans.) and Palisca, Claude V. (ed.), Hucbald, Guido, and John on Music: Three Medieval Treatises (Yale University Press, 1978), Micrologus with introduction
sources.author: Babb, Warren; Palisca, Claude V.
sources.confirms: The standard English edition of the Micrologus with Palisca's introduction; the Internet Archive record lists the Micrologus translation among its contents.

guido-arezzo-staff-notation-1026.verification_note: Grier (Oxford Bibliographies) dates Guido's writings as a group to the 1020s and 1030s; Micrologus is conventionally placed about 1026 to 1028.

picture.alt: Manuscript page of Guido of Arezzo's Micrologus with a Guidonian hand drawn in the margin, a medieval copy held at Leiden.
picture.credit: Leiden University Libraries, Public domain, via Europeana

wang-weiyi-bronze-acupuncture-figures-10.summary: In 1026 the Song court ordered imperial physician Wang Weiyi (987 to 1067) to standardise acupuncture points, and he produced his Illustrated Manual of Acupuncture Points on the Bronze Figure. In 1027 he cast two life-size hollow bronze figures, about 170 cm tall, marked with channels and points. For examinations a figure was coated in wax and filled with water or mercury; a student who needled a correct point drew liquid, a wrong one drew none. He also had the manual carved on stone tablets in Kaifeng for public consultation. These figures made point location a tested skill rather than a matter of lineage, and later dynasties cast copies, including a Ming figure of 1443.

sources.title: Li, Min; Liang, Yongxuan, 'Wang Weiyi, acupuncture expert of the Song Dynasty', Journal of Traditional Chinese Medical Sciences 2 (2015)
sources.author: Li, Min; Liang, Yongxuan
sources.venue: Journal of Traditional Chinese Medical Sciences
sources.confirms: Confirms the 1026 imperial order, the 1027 casting of two bronze figures about 170 cm tall, the wax and liquid examination method, and the stone tablets.
sources.qualifies: Gives 365 points on the figures, whereas the Library of Congress record gives 354.

sources.title: Library of Congress, 'Tong ren shu xue zhen jiu tu jing' (Illustrated Manual of Acupuncture Points on the Bronze Figure), catalogue record
sources.author: Library of Congress
sources.confirms: Confirms Wang Weiyi (987 to 1067), the manual commissioned in 1026, and the two bronze figures of 1027 used for examinations with wax and mercury.
sources.qualifies: States 354 points, against 365 in Li and Liang.

wang-weiyi-bronze-acupuncture-figures-10.verification_note: Sources disagree on how many points the figures carry (354 versus 365); year and method are consistent.

picture.alt: Ming-period bronze acupuncture figure of 1443, successor to Wang Weiyi's Song figures, National Museum of China
picture.credit: Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

al-biruni-india-1030.summary: Around 1030 al-Biruni measured Earth's size from a single hill, to within 2 percent. The same year he finished his book on India. He had spent years in India during Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns. It described Indian religion and customs so even-handedly that scholars called him al-Ustadh, the Master. He also devised a way to find Earth's radius from a single hill: measure its height, then how far the horizon dips below level when seen from its top. He carried this out at Nandana in present-day Pakistan, on a date not known; one modern reckoning puts his result about 2 percent above Earth's true mean radius.

sources.title: Al-Biruni - Wikipedia

Sachau, Edward C. (ed. and trans.), Alberuni's India: an account of the religion, philosophy, literature, geography, chronology, astronomy, customs, laws and astrology of India about AD 1030, 2 vols (Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner, 1910)
sources.author: al-Biruni, Abu Rayhan; Sachau, Edward C.
sources.confirms: Sachau's edition dates the Kitab al-Hind to about AD 1030, written after Mahmud of Ghazna's death that year.

sources.title: 'Al-Biruni (973 - 1048) - Biography', MacTutor History of Mathematics
sources.confirms: The page says Mahmud died in 1030 and India “appeared at this time”; it does not say al-Biruni finished it around 1030.
sources.qualifies: It does not say al-Biruni finished it around 1030. It gives Earth’s radius as 6339.6 km and says he used triangulation to measure Earth and distances, but does not mention Nandana, measuring from a hill, or the claim that the result was within about 2 percent.

al-biruni-india-1030.verification_note: Page supports c.1030 for the India treatise; the Earth-radius measurement at Nandana (Salt Range, present-day Pakistan) is undated and Nandana/India sit in south-asia, so middle-east is a loose fit for this entry.

picture.alt: Illustrated page from a 1307 copy of al-Biruni's Chronology of Ancient Nations, a different work by the same author.
picture.credit: University of Edinburgh Library, CC BY 3.0, via Europeana

chola-bronze-casting-1030.summary: Under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I, bronze casters in Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram produced solid copper-alloy icons of Shiva, Parvati and saints by lost-wax casting. A sculptor modelled each figure in beeswax, coated it in clay, melted out wax and poured alloy into a single-use mould, so every image is unique. Temple inscriptions record donors, weights and jewellery for processional images carried through streets on festival days. Casting lineages (sthapatis) in Swamimalai still follow this workflow. Chola bronzes became one of premodern India's most widely traded metal technologies in later collections and in museum study of alloy composition.

sources.title: Vidya Dehejia, The Thief Who Stole My Heart: The Material Life of Sacred Bronzes from Chola India, 855-1280 (Princeton University Press, 2021)
sources.author: Vidya Dehejia
sources.confirms: Chola processional bronzes, lost-wax method, inscriptions on donors and temple use

sources.title: Sharada Srinivasan, 'Shiva as cosmic dancer: on Pallava origins for the Nataraja bronze', World Archaeology 36 (2004)
sources.author: Sharada Srinivasan
sources.qualifies: Nataraja form originates under Pallavas, 7th to mid-9th century, not as a 10th-century Chola invention

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Great Living Chola Temples'
sources.confirms: Chola bronzes at Gangaikondacholapuram named as masterpieces of Chola metal icons

chola-bronze-casting-1030.verification_note: Dehejia confirmed through publisher record and reviews, not read to page. Srinivasan abstract read; she dates Nataraja origins earlier than Chola. Year 1030 is a chosen midpoint for Rajendra I's reign.
chola-bronze-casting-1030.detail: Dehejia reads temple inscriptions and donor records to reconstruct how patrons, often women, commissioned processional bronzes and how workshops organised casting. Srinivasan's lead-isotope and trace-element study argues that dancing Shiva (Nataraja) bronzes begin under Pallava rule in the seventh to mid-ninth century rather than as a tenth-century Chola invention, so Chola casters scaled and refined an older practice. Dating here is approximate and marks mature production during Rajendra I's reign.

picture.alt: Chola bronze Nataraja, Shiva dancing within a ring of flames, cast by the lost-wax method, Cleveland Museum of Art
picture.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, 1930.331 (CC0)

gangaikondacholapuram-temple-1035.summary: Rajendra I built a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram, after his northern campaign and finished its Brihadisvara temple around 1035. Its sanctum tower rises 53 metres with recessed corners and an upward curve, a deliberate contrast to his father's straight-sided tower at Thanjavur. Builders moved and dressed granite without local quarries nearby, cut a lion-well and sub-shrines to a single plan, and installed bronzes of Bhogasakti and Subrahmanya. Stone was shaped with corbelled courses rather than true arches, carrying mass through pure compression. Chola engineers also dug a large reservoir, Cholagangam, beside this city to supply water and display royal control over irrigation.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Great Living Chola Temples', World Heritage List 250
sources.confirms: completed in 1035; 53 m vimana; bronzes of Bhogasakti and Subrahmanya; lion-well

sources.title: 'Excavation at Gangaikondacholapuram, the Imperial Capital of Rajendra Chola, and its Significance', in Hermann Kulke, K. Kesavapany and Vijay Sakhuja (eds), Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa: Reflections on the Chola Naval Expeditions to Southeast Asia (ISEAS, 2009), chapter 6
sources.confirms: Rajendra's campaigns and new capital as part of Chola expansion

gangaikondacholapuram-temple-1035.verification_note: UNESCO page read in full for date and dimensions. ISEAS chapter confirmed through publisher record.
gangaikondacholapuram-temple-1035.detail: UNESCO's listing gives completion in 1035 and vimana height of 53 m. Scholars in an ISEAS volume on Chola maritime expansion connect this capital with Rajendra's Ganga and Srivijaya campaigns, reading its name (city of the Chola who took the Ganga) as part of a wider programme of monumental assertion funded by trade and tribute.

picture.alt: Granite vimana of the Gangaikondacholapuram temple rising above its courtyard
picture.credit: simianwolverine

bi-sheng-movable-type-1040.summary: Around 1040 Bi Sheng printed with reusable clay characters, so a page no longer had to be carved whole. Gutenberg came 400 years later. Under the Song dynasty he made single characters from baked clay that could be set in an iron frame, inked, printed and reused. He tried wooden type too, but grain and swelling made it uneven. Shen Kuo described his method in Dream Pool Essays. After Bi Sheng's death clay type may have spread to Western Xia; Wang Zhen improved on it with wooden type around 1300, and Hua Sui cast bronze type by 1490, though movable type never displaced woodblock printing in China.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bi Sheng
Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 pt. 1: Paper and Printing (Cambridge University Press, 1985)
sources.author: Tsien, Tsuen-Hsuin
sources.confirms: Quotes Shen Kua's contemporary record: in the Chhing-li reign (1041-48) Pi Sheng, a commoner, made movable type of baked sticky clay set in an iron frame on a resin-wax-ash bed.

sources.title: Carter, Thomas Francis, The Invention of Printing in China and Its Spread Westward (Columbia University Press, 1925), chronological table and ch. 'The Invention of Movable Type'
sources.author: Carter, Thomas Francis
sources.confirms: Dates Pi Sheng's invention of earthenware movable type set in an iron form to 1041-1049.

sources.title: Di Doménico, Luciano Agustín, 'The invention of Movable-Type Printing in the work of Shen Kuo (1031-1095)', Sinología hispánica. China Studies Review 13 (2022)
sources.author: Di Doménico, Luciano Agustín; Mina, Federico Daniel; Santillán, Gustavo E.
sources.confirms: The page identifies Shen Kuo (1031-1095) and the Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127). It says jotting no.
sources.qualifies: It supports the general association with movable-type printing but does not state the specific details in the claim.

picture.alt: Museum display of clay movable type set in a frame beside a printed sheet, a reconstruction of Bi Sheng's method photographed in 2011.
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

wujing-zongyao-gunpowder-1044.summary: In 1044 a Chinese military manual wrote down gunpowder's first recipes. That mixture would end the age of castles and knights. Wujing Zongyao, finished for Emperor Renzong of Song, gives mixtures of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal with many added ingredients. Renzong, at war with Western Xia and worried that his officials knew too little of the military classics, had scholars led by Zeng Gongliang compile all known military knowledge between 1040 and 1044. The book gives recipes for several bomb types, including an explosive bomb and a poison-smoke bomb, and describes low-nitrate incendiaries lowered from city walls onto besiegers, an early compass and a double-piston flamethrower that shot a continuous jet of flame.

sources.title: Wujing Zongyao
Needham, Joseph, with Ho Ping-Yu, Lu Gwei-Djen and Wang Ling, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 pt. 7: Military Technology; The Gunpowder Epic (Cambridge University Press, 1986)
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Ho, Ping-Yu; Lu, Gwei-Djen; Wang, Ling
sources.confirms: Wu Ching Tsung Yao ch. 12 pp. 58a-b (1044) holds the earliest specifications of the gunpowder formula, three recipes for bombs and incendiaries.

sources.title: Early Gunpowder Warfare (The Gunpowder Age, 2016)
sources.confirms: The page identifies “nitrates, sulfur, and charcoal” and says heat triggers “a terrific conflagration.” It states oxygen and nitrogen were discovered in the late 18th century and the reaction was understood during the following century.
sources.qualifies: The ingredient types are partly supported, but the claimed manual, date, and other details are absent.

sources.title: 'Gunpowder', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says black powder “is thought to have originated in China” and was used in fireworks and signals “by the 10th century”; it also describes a 9th-century invention by Chinese alchemists.
sources.qualifies: It does not mention 1044, the Wujing Zongyao, or that it recorded the first formulas.

picture.alt: Printed page of the Wujing Zongyao giving a gunpowder formula, from a later edition of the 1044 text.
picture.credit: PericlesofAthens, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

cahokia-1100.summary: Around 1100 Cahokia, in today's Illinois, held up to 20,000 people, as many as London, a city of earth mounds. It was the Mississippian culture's largest city, which had developed across much of what is now the central and southeastern United States from about 1000. Workers raised its mounds by carrying earth in woven baskets; Monks Mound alone covers 14 acres and rises 100 feet, and Woodhenge, rings of upright posts, was among features of its 1050 to 1100 period. Cahokia was abandoned by about 1350.

sources.title: Cahokia
'Cahokia Mounds', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Cahokia flourished “c. 950-1350” and reached “as many as 20,000” people;
sources.qualifies: The population and mound facts are supported, but the specific 1050-1100 peak dates are not given, and the page says more than 14 acres.

sources.title: Benson, Larry V.; Pauketat, Timothy R.; Cook, Edward R., 'Cahokia's Boom and Bust in the Context of Climate Change', American Antiquity 74 (2009), pp. 467-483
sources.author: Benson, Larry V.; Pauketat, Timothy R.; Cook, Edward R.
sources.confirms: The abstract dates the abrupt planned construction of central Cahokia and a large-scale influx of people to the Lohmann phase, AD 1050-1100, says a 20,000-log palisade was built around Monks Mound about 1150, population fell by half by 1200, and Cahokia was abandoned by AD 1350.

sources.title: Schilling, Timothy, 'The Chronology of Monks Mound', Southeastern Archaeology 32 (2013), pp. 14-28
sources.author: Schilling, Timothy
sources.confirms: Crossref metadata confirms a peer-reviewed study dating the construction stages of Monks Mound; the publisher page itself was behind a bot wall, so its findings were not read.

cahokia-1100.verification_note: Britannica confirms Cahokia as largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, with Monks Mound and a peak about 1050 to 1150; other sources put its peak at 1050 to 1100, so a 1050 start suits this span, and Pauketat's Alabama monograph is cited as supporting literature.

picture.alt: Monks Mound at Cahokia with the site reconstruction model in view, photographed in 2019.
picture.credit: Thank You (24 Millions ) views, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

chaco-canyon-roads-1050.summary: Around 1050 Chaco Canyon in present-day New Mexico stood at its height as administrative, economic and ceremonial centre of Ancestral Pueblo people, active there from about 850 to 1250 by Britannica's dating. Pueblo Bonito, its largest great house, went up in stages from about 850 and by this period held about 800 rooms and 39 kivas; straight engineered roads, some 400 miles in all, ran from its canyon to dozens of outlying settlements. Wesley Bernardini (KIVA, 1999) reassessed what those rooms mean: Pueblo Bonito probably never housed more than 12 households, about 70 people, while holding over 200 nonresidential rooms, so its mass records gatherings hosted inside its walls rather than resident population. Drought from about 1130 preceded Chaco's decline.

sources.title: Pueblo Bonito - Wikipedia
Chaco Culture National Historical Park - Wikipedia
Bernardini, Wesley, 'Reassessing the Scale of Social Action at Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon, New Mexico', KIVA 64 (1999)
sources.author: Bernardini, Wesley
sources.confirms: The page dates the Chaco Canyon social system to A.D. 850-1150.
sources.qualifies: The page supports the 850-1150 period but does not provide the other claimed details.

sources.title: 'Chaco Culture National Historical Park', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Pueblo Bonito was “built mainly in the 10th century” and “contained about 800 rooms.” Chaco was an administrative, economic, and ceremonial centre from 850 to 1250. It does not state that Pueblo Bonito was built in stages, that Chaco peaked from 900 to 1150, or that it declined after a drought from 1130.
sources.qualifies: It does not state that Pueblo Bonito was built in stages, that Chaco peaked from 900 to 1150, or that it declined after a drought from 1130.

chaco-canyon-roads-1050.verification_note: Pueblo Bonito's building ran in stages from about 850, so 1050 marks Chaco's peak; Bernardini (KIVA, 1999) reads its 800 rooms as mostly nonresidential space for perhaps 70 residents.
chaco-canyon-roads-1050.detail: Bernardini estimated population from residential suites and found residential use of Pueblo Bonito neither as intensive nor as continuous as most researchers had presumed. Chaco's social system, dated 850 to 1150, matters for reconstructions of later change across northern Southwest.

picture.alt: Great house of Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon seen from the canyon rim, photographed in 2024.
picture.credit: JacobCarr06, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

heavy-plough-three-field-rotation-1050.summary: Across northern Europe, farmers working heavy clay soils adopt an iron-tipped plough with coulter, asymmetric share and mouldboard that cuts, lifts and turns sod in one pass, drawn by teams of up to eight oxen. Finds from Poland, Bohemia, the Rhineland and Savoy date between the 8th and 10th centuries; England and Wales see widespread use only in the 11th century.
