Economists place its agricultural breakthrough around AD 1000 and link it to urban growth in clay-soil regions. Alongside it spreads three-field rotation: winter wheat or rye on one field, spring oats, barley or legumes on a second, a third left fallow, which roughly doubled yields over two-field systems.

sources.title: Andersen, T. B., Jensen, P. S. and Skovsgaard, C. V., 'The heavy plow and the agricultural revolution in Medieval Europe', Journal of Development Economics 118 (2016), 133-149
sources.author: Andersen, Thomas Barnebeck; Jensen, Peter Sandholt; Skovsgaard, Christian Volmar
sources.confirms: Dates the heavy plough's agricultural breakthrough to around AD 1000 and estimates its effect on medieval urbanization in Denmark and Europe.
sources.qualifies: Gives no single adoption year; treats the spread as a process over the 10th and 11th centuries.

sources.title: EBSCO Research Starters, 'Heavy Plow Helps Increase Agricultural Yields'
sources.author: EBSCO
sources.confirms: Lists archaeological finds from Poland, Bohemia, Rhineland and Savoy between 8th and 10th centuries, the coulter-share-mouldboard design, ox teams and 11th century spread to England and Wales.

sources.title: Britannica, 'Three-field system'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Describes winter grain, spring grain or legumes and fallow sequence and states yields roughly doubled over two-field rotation.

heavy-plough-three-field-rotation-1050.verification_note: No single date exists; archaeology spans 8th to 11th centuries and economists place the breakthrough around AD 1000. Year 1050 marks spread into England and Wales, approximate.
heavy-plough-three-field-rotation-1050.detail: Long, narrow strips suited the heavy plough because turning eight oxen was slow, shaping open-field village landscapes that lasted into 18th-century enclosures. Surplus oats fed horses, setting up later substitution of horse for ox. Yield gain came from working deeper, better-drained soil and from legumes restoring nitrogen. No single adoption date exists: individual plough parts survive from Roman times, and spread was gradual over three centuries. Economists estimate heavy-plough suitability explains around 10 percent of medieval urbanization in Denmark, with similar effects across Europe.

picture.alt: March page of Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry: peasant guides wheeled mouldboard plough drawn by two oxen
picture.credit: Limbourg brothers / Barthélemy d'Eyck, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

ibn-ridwan-egypt-health-treatise-1050.summary: Ali ibn Ridwan, a self-taught physician born in Giza about 998 and chief physician to Fatimid Cairo until his death around 1068, wrote On the Prevention of Bodily Ills in Egypt. He treated Egypt as a medical problem in its own right: Cairo's dust, heat and crowding, water drawn from a Nile that rose and fell each year, and recurring epidemics. His advice ran to diet, housing, bathing and seasonal regimen, following Galen and Hippocratic airs-and-waters reasoning. Michael Dols and Adil Gamal edited and translated his Arabic text in 1984, making it a key witness to medical practice and urban public health in eleventh-century Egypt.

sources.title: Dols, Michael W. (tr.) and Gamal, Adil S. (ed.), Medieval Islamic Medicine: Ibn Ridwan's Treatise 'On the Prevention of Bodily Ills in Egypt' (University of California Press, 1984)
sources.author: Dols, Michael W.; Gamal, Adil S.
sources.confirms: Publisher page describes the book as a study and translation of On the Prevention of Bodily Ills in Egypt by Ali ibn Ridwan (998-1068) and the questions it addresses about medieval Islamic medical practice

sources.title: Review of Dols (tr.), Medieval Islamic Medicine: Ibn Ridwan's Treatise, Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 51 (1988)
sources.venue: Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies
sources.confirms: Scholarly review confirming the edition, translator, editor, press and 1984 date

ibn-ridwan-egypt-health-treatise-1050.verification_note: Sources do not fix this treatise's composition date; about 1050 falls within Ibn Ridwan's Cairo career (998 to 1068 per UC Press), and its content summary follows publisher description and review.
ibn-ridwan-egypt-health-treatise-1050.detail: Dols's study frames three questions through Ibn Ridwan: what it meant to be a doctor in medieval Islamic society, what medicine physicians practised, and how physician and patient related. Ibn Ridwan quarrelled in writing with Ibn Butlan of Baghdad over medical learning, and his treatise defends Egypt's environment against charges of unhealthiness while prescribing how residents could live well within it. Dating rests on his career, so this year is approximate.

picture.alt: Excavated remains of Fustat, Cairo, the city whose air, water and soils Ibn Ridwan described
picture.credit: Roland Unger

kilwa-copper-coinage-1050.summary: On Kilwa Kisiwani, off southern Tanzania, Swahili rulers minted small copper coins carrying a ruler's name on one face and a rhyming Arabic couplet on its reverse. Issues of Ali ibn al-Hasan come earliest and remain most numerous: thousands turn up at Kilwa, on Mafia, at Songo Mnara and as far inland as Great Zimbabwe. A hoard at Mtambwe Mkuu on Pemba, sealed with a Fatimid dinar of 1066, held more than 2,000 locally struck silver coins including 30 of Ali ibn al-Hasan. Stephanie Wynne-Jones and Jeffrey Fleisher read this copper coinage as money valued by local custom and a ruler's name rather than metal weight.

sources.title: Wynne-Jones, Stephanie and Fleisher, Jeffrey, 'Coins in Context: Local Economy, Value and Practice on the East African Swahili Coast', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 22 (2012)
sources.author: Wynne-Jones, Stephanie; Fleisher, Jeffrey
sources.confirms: Medieval Kilwa-type coins excavated at Songo Mnara; value created through local use and ritual rather than metal content

sources.title: Perkins, John; Fleisher, Jeffrey and Wynne-Jones, Stephanie, 'A deposit of Kilwa-type coins from Songo Mnara, Tanzania', Azania 49 (2014)
sources.author: Perkins, John; Fleisher, Jeffrey; Wynne-Jones, Stephanie
sources.confirms: Over 300 copper Kilwa-type coins in a deposit of the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century; coins of the late eleventh to early twelfth century ruler Ali ibn al-Hasan still in circulation
sources.qualifies: Dates Ali ibn al-Hasan to the late eleventh or early twelfth century

sources.title: Horton, M. C.; Brown, H. M. and Oddy, W. A., 'The Mtambwe Hoard', Azania 21 (1986)
sources.author: Horton, M. C.; Brown, H. M.; Oddy, W. A.
sources.confirms: Publication of the Pemba hoard that anchors Ali ibn al-Hasan's coins to the eleventh century
sources.qualifies: Landing page shows bibliographic record only; hoard details taken from Wynne-Jones's open-access chapter 'Money and the Everyday' citing it

kilwa-copper-coinage-1050.verification_note: Scholars date Ali ibn al-Hasan variously: tenth century (new Kilwa radiocarbon context), eleventh (Mtambwe hoard) or late twelfth (Chittick); about 1050 is a middle estimate.
kilwa-copper-coinage-1050.detail: Dating is disputed. Neville Chittick, from Kilwa stratigraphy, placed Ali ibn al-Hasan around 1180; Mtambwe's hoard pushed him back to around 1066; a silver miniature found in tenth-century context at Kilwa has prompted an even earlier claim. A deposit of more than 300 copper coins at Songo Mnara shows his issues still circulating around 1400. Copper remained dominant, with rare gold and silver strikes. Minting at Kilwa continued into the sixteenth century.

picture.alt: Great Mosque at Kilwa Kisiwani, Tanzania, coral-stone arches and domes of the Swahili port whose sultans struck copper coins
picture.credit: Richard Mortel from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

al-zarqali-universal-astrolabe-1060.summary: In Toledo, instrument maker and astronomer Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Zarqali (Azarquiel, born Cordoba 1029, died 1100) designs the azafea or al-safiha, an astrolabe plate with an equinoctial rather than polar projection. A conventional astrolabe needs a separate engraved plate for each latitude; al-Zarqali's plate works anywhere, and Britannica notes navigators used it into the 1500s. Al-Zarqali was making instruments for Toledan astronomers by 1048 and joined Qadi ibn Said's circle in 1062, which produced the Toledan Tables. Latin translations carried his design north; by Chaucer's day astrolabes were being made in England and he wrote England's first manual for one.

sources.title: King, D. A., 'A Universal Astrolabe from 17th-Century Lahore', in In Synchrony with the Heavens, vol. 2 (Brill, 2005)
sources.author: King, David A.
sources.venue: In Synchrony with the Heavens, Volume 2: Instruments of Mass Calculation (Brill)
sources.confirms: Scholarly chapter on a universal astrolabe of the al-Zarqali (shakkaziyya) type made in Lahore; bibliographic record checked through Crossref, chapter text behind Brill paywall and not opened.

sources.title: Samso, J., On Both Sides of the Strait of Gibraltar: Studies in the History of Medieval Astronomy in the Iberian Peninsula and the Maghrib (Brill, 2020)
sources.author: Samso, Julio
sources.confirms: University-level monograph on Andalusi astronomy including al-Zarqali's Toledo circle and instruments; record checked through Crossref, full text not opened.

sources.title: O'Connor, J. J. and Robertson, E. F., 'Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Yahya al-Zarqali', MacTutor History of Mathematics (University of St Andrews)
sources.author: O'Connor, John J.; Robertson, Edmund F.
sources.confirms: Born 1029 Cordoba, died 15 October 1100; instruments for the Toledo astronomers by 1048 to 1049; joined Qadi ibn Said's group in 1062; invented the azafea with projection centred on the equinoctial point; left Toledo after 1085.

sources.title: 'al-Zarqali', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: The azafea, a universal astrolabe, was widely used by navigators until the 16th century.

al-zarqali-universal-astrolabe-1060.verification_note: No source fixes this azafea's year; al-Zarqali worked in Toledo from 1040s to 1085, so 1060 marks that period's midpoint, and his biographical dates are confirmed by MacTutor and Britannica, with two Brill works cited as supporting literature.
al-zarqali-universal-astrolabe-1060.detail: David King's study of a 17th-century universal astrolabe from Lahore shows how far shakkaziyya projection travelled: Mughal India was still building this design five centuries later. Julio Samso's Brill monograph on Andalusi astronomy places al-Zarqali's instruments inside a Toledo school working under Taifa patronage after Cordoba's caliphate fell. Latin writers kept his name on both tables and instrument as Arzachel.

picture.alt: Replica of al-Zarqali's azafea, an 11th-century universal astrolabe plate, displayed in the Torre de la Calahorra museum, Cordoba.
picture.credit: Codex, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

rani-ki-vav-stepwell-patan-1063.summary: Queen Udayamati commissioned an inverted temple in Patan, Gujarat, as a memorial to Bhima I of Solanki dynasty. Masons cut seven levels of stairs down to a 9.5 by 9.4 metre tank at 23 metres depth, then sank a shaft 10 metres across and 30 metres deep. Four pillared pavilions gain storeys as they descend westward. More than five hundred principal sculptures and over a thousand minor ones line its walls. Stepwells of this kind let communities reach a falling water table through the dry season, provided cool rooms and gave sculptors a vertical canvas. Silting by Saraswati river buried it until Archaeological Survey of India excavation in the 1980s.

sources.title: Michael W. Meister and Kirit Mankodi, 'The Queen's Stepwell at Patan', Artibus Asiae 53 (1993)
sources.author: Michael W. Meister; Kirit Mankodi
sources.confirms: attribution to Udayamati, 11th-century date, architecture and sculptural programme

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat', World Heritage List 922
sources.confirms: 7 levels; tank 9.5 x 9.4 m at 23 m; well 10 m diameter, 30 m deep; over 500 principal sculptures

rani-ki-vav-stepwell-patan-1063.verification_note: UNESCO page read in full. Meister and Mankodi confirmed through JSTOR record and review of the Artibus Asiae study; page text not read.
rani-ki-vav-stepwell-patan-1063.detail: Meister and Mankodi analyse its architecture and sculptural programme in Artibus Asiae, placing construction in the 1060s under Udayamati. UNESCO's listing gives dimensions and sculpture counts and describes it as an inverted temple marking sanctity of water. Date is approximate; inscriptions do not survive for a precise year.

picture.alt: Stepped terraces and sculpted pillars descending into Rani ki Vav at Patan
picture.credit: Bernard Gagnon

nizamiyya-baghdad-1065.summary: In 1065 Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded a college in Baghdad, on the Tigris's east bank, and opened it in September 1067. An endowment paid for its building, teachers' salaries, student stipends and a library, and it taught Shafi'i law free of charge. Nizamiyya colleges formed a network across Seljuk lands, from Nishapur to Mosul, with Baghdad as flagship, and al-Ghazali taught there from 1091. This model of a funded, residential college with a set curriculum shaped later madrasas across the Islamic world. Baghdad's college was sacked along with its city in 1258.

sources.title: Nizamiyya of Baghdad
Muslim institutions of learning in eleventh-century Baghdad
Makdisi, George, 'Muslim Institutions of Learning in Eleventh-Century Baghdad', Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 24 (1961) 1-56
sources.author: Makdisi, George
sources.venue: Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies
sources.confirms: Makdisi dates the founding of the Nizamiyya madrasa in Baghdad to 457 AH (1065) under Nizam al-Mulk, with its inauguration in 1067 and a chair of Shafi'i law at its centre.

halley-comet-1066.summary: From 24 April 1066 a bright comet hung in evening skies for a week, recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle as 'the long-haired star' and in Chinese court annals as well. In England it was read as an omen; King Harold died at Hastings that October. Bayeux Tapestry embroiderers show a crowd pointing at it beneath Isti mirant stella, its first known picture. Edmond Halley identified this same body in 1705 as returning every 76 years, so 1066 records joined a run of observations longer than for any other comet.

sources.title: Halley's Comet
955 Years Ago: Halley's Comet and the Battle of Hastings
D. K. Yeomans and T. Kiang, 'The long-term motion of comet Halley', Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society 197 (1981), 633-646
sources.author: Donald K. Yeomans; Tao Kiang
sources.venue: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
sources.confirms: Integrates Halley's orbit back to 1404 BC against Chinese records and gives the 1066 perihelion on 20 March 1066.

sources.title: T. Lewis and S. Portegies Zwart, 'The significance of Halley's Comet in the Bayeux Tapestry', in Dorestad and Everything After (Sidestone Press, 2025), pp. 123-138
sources.author: Tristan Lewis; Simon Portegies Zwart
sources.confirms: The comet was visible from England from 24 April 1066 and the tapestry's placement of it beside Harold's coronation is retrospective.
sources.qualifies: The comet appeared weeks after Harold's coronation, not at it.

picture.alt: Bayeux Tapestry scene of men pointing at Halley's Comet above King Harold, embroidered in the 1070s.
picture.credit: Myrabella, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

marrakesh-khettara-irrigation-1070.summary: Marrakesh was founded on a dry plain about 1070, and its palm groves and gardens came to depend on khettaras: gently sloping tunnels, marked at the surface by lines of vertical shafts, that tap groundwater below Atlas foothills and carry it by gravity into town. Mohammed El Faïz and Thierry Ruf count hundreds of such galleries irrigating the Haouz; Dale Lightfoot mapped a 300 km network of khettaras in Morocco's Tafilalt basin, dug from about 1380 onward after Sijilmasa broke up. Marrakesh's galleries, credited by Moroccan historians to Almoravid engineers, kept Marrakesh green for nine centuries before pumped wells lowered groundwater and left most tunnels dry.

sources.title: El Faïz, Mohammed and Ruf, Thierry, 'An Introduction to the Khettara in Morocco: Two Contrasting Cases', in Water and Sustainability in Arid Regions (Springer, 2010), pp. 151-163
sources.author: El Faïz, Mohammed; Ruf, Thierry
sources.confirms: Hundreds of underground tunnels irrigated the palm groves of the Marrakesh Haouz; their use declined over the last thirty years and collapse around Marrakesh affects water supply
sources.qualifies: Abstract opened does not give the founding date or engineer; the Almoravid attribution is Moroccan historiographical tradition

sources.title: Lightfoot, Dale R., 'Moroccan khettara: Traditional irrigation and progressive desiccation', Geoforum 27 (1996)
sources.author: Lightfoot, Dale R.
sources.confirms: A 300 km khettara network with more than 75 chains in the Tafilalt basin, excavated from the late fourteenth century, and its progressive desiccation
sources.qualifies: Dates Tafilalt khettaras to the late fourteenth century, not the eleventh; abstract read via publisher index, full text not opened

marrakesh-khettara-irrigation-1070.verification_note: Lightfoot dates Morocco's best-documented khettara network (Tafilalt) to about 1380 to 1400; an eleventh-century Almoravid origin for Marrakesh's galleries is a tradition reported by Moroccan historians and is not independently confirmed.
marrakesh-khettara-irrigation-1070.detail: Khettara is Morocco's name for a qanat, a technique shared with Iran and Oman. Each gallery is dug by hand from a mother well and cleared through shafts spaced every 10 to 20 metres. Lightfoot documented more than 75 chains in Tafilalt and their progressive desiccation; El Faïz and Ruf describe collapse of Marrakesh's galleries over thirty recent years as groundwater pumping spread. A founding-era date for Marrakesh's system is traditional and approximate.

picture.alt: Line of khettara well shafts crossing the Tafilalt plain, Morocco, the same underground-channel technique used at Marrakesh
picture.credit: Sebastian Lapostol

horse-collar-harrow-bayeux-1077.summary: The Bayeux Tapestry's lower border, stitched in England in the late 1070s, shows a draught horse wearing a rigid padded collar and pulling a harrow, among Europe's earliest pictures of a horse used for field work rather than war or carriage. A padded collar rests on shoulders rather than throat, so a horse can pull at full strength without choking. Britannica traces this harness to China before AD 500 and to Europe by about 800. Horses outpace oxen and work longer days; John Langdon's studies of English manorial accounts show horses replacing oxen for hauling in the 12th and 13th centuries and for ploughing more slowly, cutting haulage time and widening how far farmers could travel to market.

sources.author: Langdon, John

sources.qualifies: Places the working shift to horses a century or more after the tapestry's 1070s depiction and questions whether it amounted to a revolution.

horse-collar-harrow-bayeux-1077.detail: Older European harnesses used breast straps or throat-and-girth bands suited to oxen; on horses they pressed on a horse's windpipe and lost much of its pull. This scene also shows seed sown by hand ahead of it, one of few images of 11th-century field routine. When collars reached Europe is unknown, so this tapestry serves as dated evidence rather than as origin. Langdon stresses that oxen stayed cheaper to feed and that replacement was slow and by no means inevitable.

song-coal-iron-1078.summary: Robert Hartwell argued in 1962 that Northern Song iron works around Cizhou, Xingzhou and Kaifeng turned to mineral coal as wood ran short, and estimated output near 125,000 tons a year by 1078, a figure larger than Europe reached before 1700. Mines, tax records and foundry sites along this belt point to large blast furnaces, state purchase quotas and a market in coal for both smelting and household heating. Donald Wagner reworked Hartwell's arithmetic in 2001 and found his annual figure unreliable, while accepting coal use and a large sector. 1078 is Hartwell's reference year, and his tonnage is contested.

song-coal-iron-1078.detail: Hartwell linked iron demand to coinage and tools and to Kaifeng's million-strong population. Wagner showed that Hartwell's production estimate rested on an assumed tax rate and could be out by a wide margin; he also stressed that coke smelting cannot be proven for Song furnaces. Both agree that Song China ran a coal-and-iron complex with no contemporary parallel, which later shrank under Jurchen conquest and river shifts.

jalali-calendar-khayyam-1079.summary: On 15 March 1079 Persia adopted Omar Khayyam's calendar, truer to the seasons than ours today. Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I took it up on advice from astronomers at Isfahan's observatory. It replaced lunar reckoning, whose 354-day year drifted relative to seasons: Jalali years began each March equinox and each month began when the sun entered its next zodiac sign, so drift never exceeded one day and no leap year was needed. Grand vizier Nizam al-Mulk had ordered this work, using observations from Isfahan, Rey and Nishapur, and its precision cost full astronomical computation for every month.

toledan-tables-al-zarqali-1080.summary: Around 1080 Toledo's astronomers finished planet tables that Europe used, in later forms, for 400 years. They also fixed calendar dates and times of eclipses. They adapted earlier Arabic tables to Toledo's meridian, drawing in part on al-Zarqali's work. Toledo fell to Christian rule soon after; Gerard of Cremona translated these Toledan Tables into Latin one century later, and their descendants, updated as Alfonsine tables in the 1270s, were late medieval Europe's most widely used astronomical tables. Copernicus still drew on their data.

domesday-book-mills-1086.summary: In 1086 England's Domesday survey counted 5,624 water mills, one for every 46 households. A century earlier there had been under 100. William the Conqueror's survey was completed that year according to its colophon; historians treat this total as too low because Domesday is incomplete. Georges Duby reads this total as one mill for every 46 peasant households, implying baked bread was replacing boiled, unground porridge.

shen-kuo-magnetic-compass-1088.summary: In 1088 Shen Kuo wrote history's first account of a magnetic needle used to find direction. Compasses would let ships leave sight of land. His Dream Pool Essays, published under Song rule, also first described Bi Sheng's movable type. Shen also set out his idea that such needles point slightly away from true north, Earth's pole, which is now called magnetic declination.

su-song-astronomical-clock-1092.summary: By 1094 Su Song's water clock ticked one step per filled scoop, an escapement two centuries before Europe's. Europe's first mechanical clocks came two centuries later. Water filled limited-size scoops set round its great wheel; whenever a scoop filled, its weight tripped an escapement that let that wheel advance by a single step, so its motion kept even time. Gearing turned its bronze armillary sphere, rings for tracking star positions, on top and its celestial globe inside, while timed figures showed plaques, rang bells or beat drums for each hour. Su Song's 1092 treatise Xinyi Xiangfayao recorded this design.

su-song-astronomical-clock-1092.detail:
An escapement is any device that halts and releases moving parts at regular intervals. Su's was of a type invented in 725 by Tang monk Yi Xing and official Liang Lingzan to drive a water-powered armillary sphere, but Su's sphere was first to be turned by mechanical clock drive. His tower also carried history's oldest known endless power-transmitting chain, called tian ti, celestial ladder, and 133 clock jacks to indicate and sound hours.

After Kaifeng fell in 1127 and Song's capital moved, his tower was dismantled and its armillary sphere carried south; attempts to reassemble it failed and it was never rebuilt. His treatise received official printed publication in 1094.

champagne-fairs-1100.summary: From the 12th century merchants settled debts across Europe on paper at the Champagne fairs. International finance began there. Six fairs a year, six weeks or longer apiece, rotated through Champagne's towns in France's northeast during the 12th and 13th centuries. They linked cloth cities of the Low Countries with Italian dyers and exporters led by Genoa. After cloth sales closed, Italian money-changers reckoned credits at their tables and settled bills of exchange written to fall due at one of these fairs. Under merchant law enforced by private judges, Champagne's fairs kept working as an international clearing house for debts even after trade routes shifted; historians date their decline to Champagne's absorption into France's royal domain after 1284.

chinampas-1100.summary: Around 1100 farmers in central Mexico built fields on lake beds, chinampas, giving up to seven harvests a year. Farmers wove reeds between stakes driven into lakebeds to make underwater fences, then piled soil and aquatic plants inside until land stood above water. Often called floating gardens, chinampas were anchored to lake beds and stayed moist, which allowed those seven harvests. Farmers used them on small plots beside their homes until Aztecs, after conquering Xochimilco, developed them for large-scale cultivation.

great-zimbabwe-1100.summary: In the 11th century stone building began at Great Zimbabwe, a city of up to 20,000, and continued for more than 300 years. Its dry-stone walls, laid without mortar, still stand 11 metres high at its Great Enclosure. After 1200 this city served as capital of Great Zimbabwe's kingdom; population estimates run from under 10,000 to about 20,000. Abandonment came in the 1500s or 1600s.

kilwa-sultanate-1100.summary: After 1100 Kilwa, an island city off Tanzania, controlled gold trade between inland Africa and Arabia, Persia and India. It flourished as an independent city-state between 1100 and 1500, largely on gold that came from Great Zimbabwe's kingdom to Sofala, Kilwa's southern outpost. It minted copper coins from the 1000s or 1100s, and at its 14th-century peak it boasted Husuni Kubwa palace, one large mosque and many fine stone buildings. Portuguese arrival soon after 1500 began to end its independence, as trade declined and merchants left.

yingzao-fashi-building-manual-1103.summary: In 1103 Song China fixed standard building parts, so any craftsman could build to plan. Li Jie, who ran the Directorate of Buildings and Construction, had revised older architectural treatises from 1097 to 1100 and presented his own to Emperor Zhezong; his successor Huizong had it published as standards for builders, craftsmen and government engineering agencies. Its 34 chapters set units of measurement, rules for moats and fortifications, standards for stonework and for greater and lesser woodwork, estimates of labour that allowed for the season, and classifications of crafts, materials and accounting.

pagan-ananda-temple-1105.summary: On a plain beside Irrawaddy in Upper Burma, masons under King Kyanzittha finished Ananda, a cruciform brick temple with corbelled and true vaults, pointed arches and a gilded shikhara, around 1105. Bagan's builders fired bricks locally, bonded them with mud mortar so tight that blades will not pass between courses, and roofed corridors with vaults at a time when such arches were uncommon elsewhere in Asia. Archaeological survey ties Bagan's urban growth to walled settlements from about the ninth century, with temple building peaking between eleventh and thirteenth centuries. UNESCO inscribed Bagan in 2019 with 3,595 recorded monuments.

Its author Zhu Yu, whose father had superintended merchant shipping at Guangzhou, wrote it between 1111 and 1117. Shen Kuo had described this needle in 1088 without mentioning use at sea.

khazini-balance-of-wisdom-1121.summary: Abd al-Rahman al-Khazini, a treasury official at Merv under Seljuk sultan Sanjar, finishes Kitab Mizan al-Hikma in 515 AH (1121 to 1122). Eight books cover centres of gravity, steelyards, water clocks and hydrostatics, and describe a five-pan balance with a graduated beam for weighing objects in air and in water. Treasury staff used it to tell pure gold and silver from alloys and genuine gems from fakes, and to compute exchange between dirhams and dinars. His tables give specific gravities for about fifty metals, stones and liquids, several within one percent of modern values. A 2020 reconstruction in Iran weighed to 0.7 percent and measured density to 1.1 percent following his instructions. N. Khanikoff translated large extracts in 1858.

sources.title: Yassi, Y. and Yassi, R., 'Al-Khazini's Balance of Wisdom', Nuncius 36 (2021), 49-71
sources.author: Yassi, Yousef; Yassi, Reza
sources.confirms: Book completed 1121 at Sanjar's court in Marv while al-Khazini served in the treasury; five-pan balance; reconstruction accuracy 0.7 percent weight, 1.1 percent density.

sources.author: Khanikoff, Nikolai
sources.venue: Journal of the American Oriental Society
sources.confirms: Partial translation of the Arabic text on the water balance, written in the twelfth century.

sources.title: Abattouy, M., 'Khazini', in Hockey, T. (ed.), Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer, 2014)
sources.author: Abattouy, Mohammed
sources.confirms: Al-Khazini flourished at Marw in the first half of the twelfth century at the court of Sanjar ibn Malik-Shah and dedicated Kitab mizan al-hikma to him.

khazini-balance-of-wisdom-1121.detail: Al-Khazini credits predecessors, including al-Biruni, Umar Khayyam and al-Isfizari, whose balance he refined, and he reproduces abridged Greek and Arabic mechanical texts, which makes his book a main witness for medieval statics. He also claims air has weight and that water grows denser nearer Earth's centre. Four manuscripts survive, three independent.

angkor-wat-baray-1122.summary: From 1122 Khmer builders raised Angkor Wat beside reservoirs that watered a city of 750,000. Construction ran from 1122 to 1150 across 162.6 hectares, and it remains the world's largest religious complex. As Khmer kings adopted Buddhism from late in the 1200s, Angkor Wat became Buddhist, serving as temple and monastery, and it has stayed in active worship ever since.

southern-song-era-1127.summary: From 1127 Southern Song China ran an economy with paper money and a standing navy. Invaders had pushed its court south, and its remaining lands were populous and fertile, sustaining a commercial economy: Song issued true paper money before any other state and was the first Chinese government to keep a permanent standing navy. Mongols conquered Jin in 1234 and ended Song rule in 1279.

southern-song-era-1127.verification_note: Sources give dates and southward move but neither economic nor naval claims; a permanent Southern Song navy is unconfirmed.

great-mosque-of-kilwa-1131.summary: From 1131 Kilwa, a Swahili port, built a Great Mosque of coral stone on gold-trade wealth. It is among the Swahili coast's earliest partly surviving mosques, on Kilwa Kisiwani island off present-day Tanzania. Its northern section went up between 1131 and 1170 with walls and columns of coral stone. Between 1294 and 1302 it was extended southward, and early in the 1300s Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman added its great dome, which Ibn Battuta described after his 1331 visit.

fire-lance-siege-of-dean-1132.summary: In 1132 Chinese soldiers first used fire lances in battle, gunpowder tubes on spears that became the first guns. Lit as close combat began, they threw flame about 3 metres, later with pellets or debris mixed in, for one shot. Evidence for them in China dates to 950, but their first recorded use in war came in 1132, when Song garrisons wielded them against Jin forces during the Siege of De'an. Before 1300 barrels had turned to metal and spear points were dropped, making these history's first hand cannons.

crossbow-ban-lateran-1139.summary: In 1139 the Church banned crossbows and bows against Christians; later writers read it as shielding knights from commoners' bolts. It was an early attempt to outlaw a weapon. Its Canon 29 forbade using crossbowmen and archers against Christians and Catholics under anathema, in Latin scholars call ambiguous, and may have served Innocent II's campaign against Roger II of Sicily; canonists exempted just wars. Rulers across Europe kept hiring crossbowmen all the same, and this ban had no lasting effect on battlefields.

saint-denis-choir-gothic-1144.summary: On 11 June 1144 (Suger's own dating; Crosby gives 14 June) Abbot Suger consecrated a new choir at Saint-Denis royal abbey, north of Paris, before King Louis VII and Queen Eleanor. Built in a little over three years, it put pointed arches, ribbed vaults, slender columns and an ambulatory of radiating chapels together for the first time, so thin walls could carry large stained-glass windows and light filled its interior. This manner spread through northern France's royal domain and then across Europe as the French style, called Gothic only centuries later. It set structural grammar for cathedrals for three hundred years after.

robert-chester-algebra-1145.summary: In 1145, in Segovia, English scholar Robert of Chester translated al-Khwarizmi's ninth-century book on completion and balancing into Latin as Liber algebrae et almucabola. It was the first algebra Latin Europe could read, and the word algebra entered European languages through its title. Its text set out how to reduce and solve equations up to second degree, with worked problems in trade, surveying and inheritance. Gerard of Cremona made a second translation at Toledo, and this text served as a university mathematics textbook into the sixteenth century. A year earlier Robert had translated the first book on alchemy to reach Europe.

chen-fu-nong-shu-rice-1149.summary: In 1149 Chen Fu (born 1075), a Jiangsu scholar who refused an official career and farmed while growing medicinal herbs, finishes Nongshu, a three-chapter manual and the first Chinese agricultural book devoted to wet-rice farming of Jiangnan rather than northern dry grain. Fourteen sections treat farm management, weather, manure and tools, three treat water buffalo, six treat sericulture. He argues soil fertility can be kept indefinitely with fertilizer, against the proverb that fields wear out in three to five years, and sorts rice into early, late, cold-water mountain and lowland types. Francesca Bray notes he wrote to refute Jia Sixie's empty words on rice. His book codifies Song rice intensification that followed 1012, when Emperor Zhenzong distributed Champa rice seed from Fujian to Yangtze and Huai farmers, allowing two crops a year on many fields.

A preface by Hong Xingzu (1090 to 1155) calls Chen expert in Buddhist, Daoist and Shen Nong texts. Bray records that Wang Zhen folded Chen's rice instructions into his 1313 Nong Shu, carrying them to the middle Yangtze and far south, and that much of Chen's advice remained valid for centuries.

bhaskara-lilavati-1150.summary: In 1150 Bhaskara II in India handled changing speeds with ideas calculus formalised 500 years later. Lilavati, named for a woman the text addresses, covers arithmetic and measurement in verse problems; Bijaganita covers algebra, including solutions to Pell's equation, which asks for whole numbers x and y with x² minus N·y² equal to one; Grahaganita covers planetary mathematics and Goladhyaya spheres. For planetary motion he worked with instantaneous speeds, found the derivative of sine, and stated principles later formalised as Rolle's theorem, some five centuries before Newton and Leibniz.

bhaskara-wheel-1150.summary: Around 1150 Bhaskara II described a wheel with mercury in its spokes that would turn forever; the dream of perpetual motion had a design. As each spoke passed over its top, mercury was meant to flow outward, so that one side would stay heavier and keep it turning on its own. No such wheel has ever worked: whatever turning force its heavier side gains is cancelled as weights shift inward on its rising side. Bhaskara's design counts as history's first documented proposal for perpetual motion, and it drew imitators for centuries.

goryeo-sanggam-celadon-1150.summary: Kiln workers on Korea's southwest coast cut designs into leather-hard clay, filled grooves with white and iron-black slips, then glazed and fired at reducing heat so cranes, clouds and chrysanthemums appeared sharp beneath a jade-green surface. This sanggam technique matured around mid-twelfth century, after Song envoy Xu Jing praised Goryeo's plain green wares in 1123. Chemical analysis published in 2002 shows glaze compositions and firing conditions tuned to keep colour contrast crisp. Inlay turned a borrowed Chinese glaze tradition into a Korean signature, supplied court and monasteries, and ended with Mongol wars and kiln dispersal in later Goryeo.

hayy-ibn-yaqzan-1150.summary: Around 1150 Ibn Tufayl wrote of a boy raised by a gazelle alone on a desert island who, without meeting another human, reasons his way to science and God; it is counted the first philosophical novel. Edward Pococke the Younger's Latin translation, Philosophus Autodidactus, appeared in 1671 and Simon Ockley's English one in 1708; it sold widely across Europe, is thought to have inspired Locke's idea of infants as blank slates, and may have inspired Defoe's Robinson Crusoe.

parakrama-samudra-1153.summary: From 1153 Sri Lanka's king Parākramabāhu I built reservoirs so that, as he had said while ruling Dakkhinadesa before his accession, no drop of rain reached the sea unused. His largest, Parakrama Samudra, held some 25 square kilometres of water (sources give 2,400 to 2,550 hectares) for irrigation beside his capital Polonnaruwa. His saying, that not one drop of rain should reach the sea without first serving humanity, is still quoted.

tabula-rogeriana-1154.summary: In 1154 al-Idrisi finished a world map unmatched in accuracy for 300 years. He built it from travellers' reports checked against each other: he interviewed experienced travellers, kept only what they agreed on, discarded what conflicted, and drew seventy sectional maps with south uppermost, as Islamic cartographers did.

weavers-company-charter-1155.summary: In 1155 London's weavers got a royal charter, making theirs the oldest of London's guilds, bodies that decided who could ply a trade. Weavers' Company, formally The Worshipful Company of Weavers, is described as older than any other City of London livery company.

nur-al-din-bimaristan-1156.summary: In 1156 Damascus opened a hospital that treated anyone free and kept patient records. It ran for 700 years. Nur al-Din Zengi founded this bimaristan, as such hospitals were called. Bimaristans in Islamic lands admitted anyone regardless of religion, origin or gender, including people with mental illness, and their endowment deeds forbade turning patients away. Al-Nuri Hospital was first to keep medical records of its patients; Sultan Qalawun was treated there, and it inspired him to found his own great hospital in Cairo.

sources.qualifies: The page supports hospital-building and the 1154 date for taking Damascus, but not the other details.

huizi-paper-money-1160.summary: In 1160 Song China began printing Huizi, which became the most heavily issued official paper money of its age. Its Ministry of Revenue issued these notes, overseen by a Paper Notes Office. Printed in three colours and backed by 280,000 strings of copper cash, they circulated widely; notes as small as 200 cash followed in 1163. As Mongol armies pressed south, military costs drove the government to print far more Huizi than it could back, so the notes lost value and people hoarded coins instead.

roman-de-troie-automata-1160.summary: Around 1160 to 1165 a French poem described four metal figures, golden in some tellings, guarding a chamber. Benoît de Sainte-Maure's 30,000-line Roman de Troie, dated between 1155 and about 1165, imagines these automata in a Chamber of Beauties: one holds a mirror showing those present their own appearance, and another plays music.

sources.qualifies: The source dates the poem to circa 1165 rather than 1160 or 1155-1160, describes four metal figures rather than golden ones, and says the mirror shows inhabitants’ appearance rather than the world.

battle-of-caishi-paddle-ships-1161.summary: In 1161 Song paddle-wheel warships with gunpowder bombs sank a Jin fleet and saved the dynasty. Jin emperor Wanyan Liang had tried to cross at Caishi on 26 and 27 November to conquer Southern Song. Song commander Yu Yunwen met him with paddle-wheel warships driven by treadmills, whose crews hurled gunpowder bombs with trebuchets; Jin's fleet was destroyed. Liang's own officers assassinated him weeks later, Jin pulled back across the Huai River, and a peace in 1165 held for forty years.

prester-john-letter-1165.summary: Around 1165 a forged letter from Prester John, a Christian king in Asia, began circulating. Explorers sought him for centuries. Europeans later placed Prester John among Central Asia's Mongols, and Portuguese explorers came to assume he ruled Ethiopia; hope of finding him shaped diplomacy and exploration for three centuries.

al-zahrawi-surgery-latin-translation-117.summary: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (c.936 to c.1013), court physician at Madinat al-Zahra near Cordoba, wrote Kitab al-Tasrif, a 30-part medical encyclopedia whose final part is a surgical manual illustrated with more than 200 instruments: scalpels, cauteries, hooks, forceps, a concealed knife for tonsils, syringes and a vaginal speculum. Such illustration was new; earlier surgical texts described tools in words only. In Toledo, in the later twelfth century, Gerard of Cremona translated the surgical part into Latin as Liber Alsaharavi de cirurgia. Printed at Venice from 1497 and used at Salerno and Montpellier, it remained the standard surgical text in European universities for about five centuries, and Guy de Chauliac cited it more than 200 times.

sources.title: Al Aloul, Adnan, 'Al-Zahrawi surgical instruments and techniques: a milestone in the history of surgery', Medicine and Pharmacy Reports (2026)
sources.author: Al Aloul, Adnan
sources.confirms: Confirms al-Zahrawi (936 to 1013), the 30-part Kitab al-Tasrif, more than 200 original instruments, and the 12th-century Latin translation that carried the text into European universities.

sources.title: 'Abu al-Qasim', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Confirms the Gerard of Cremona translation in the 12th century, the more than 200 instrument drawings, and roughly 500 years as the leading surgical text.

sources.title: National Library of Medicine, 'Islamic Medical Manuscripts: Catalogue, Surgery', NLM digital collections
sources.author: National Library of Medicine
sources.confirms: Confirms the Toledo translation and the illustrated instruments in the surgical part of al-Tasrif.

al-zahrawi-surgery-latin-translation-117.verification_note: Translation date undocumented; placed c.1170 within Gerard of Cremona's Toledo career (d. 1187). Al-Zahrawi's birth and death years are approximate.
al-zahrawi-surgery-latin-translation-117.detail: No translation year is recorded; Gerard worked in Toledo from the 1140s until his death in 1187, so c.1170 is a midpoint estimate. Al-Zahrawi's own dates are approximate, and his Arabic original dates to around 1000. Arabic manuscripts of the surgical part with instrument drawings survive in Istanbul, Oxford and Paris, and drawings vary from copy to copy.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

nur-ad-din-pigeon-post-1171.summary: In 1171 Nur al-Din Zengi set up a pigeon post across his Syrian domains, faster than any rider, fifteen years after pigeons had first linked Baniyas with Damascus; routes ran from Damascus to Cairo, Aleppo and Baalbek. Messages went on very thin paper tied to one wing feather; pigeon towers stood in major citadels, and relay stations along roads often shared sites with mounted courier posts. Caliph al-Nasir renewed the service around 1200, Mongol invasion disrupted it, and when it was abolished in the 15th century people pulled its relay stations down stone by stone.

sources.title: II. Le système administratif sous Nūr ad-Dīn

sources.qualifies: Some later sources place the creation two years earlier; no source records the number or location of stations.

gerard-of-cremona-translations-1175.summary: Around 1175 Gerard of Cremona translated Ptolemy from Arabic, one of 87 books returning Greek science to Europe. He had left Italy for Toledo to read the Almagest, then unavailable in Latin, and learned Arabic there. He went on to translate 87 Arabic books, including Euclid's Elements, Archimedes on measuring circles, Aristotle's On the Heavens and al-Khwarizmi's algebra, making Arab and ancient Greek learning in astronomy, mathematics and medicine available to Latin readers across Western Europe.

sources.title: Gerard of Cremona
Burnett, Charles, 'The Coherence of the Arabic-Latin Translation Program in Toledo in the Twelfth Century', Science in Context 14 (2001)
sources.author: Burnett, Charles
sources.confirms: The page says Gerard of Cremona was one of two principal translators in Toledo in the second half of the twelfth century, and that he “appears to have followed a clear program” in his translations. It does not mention the Almagest, a date around 1175, 87 books, his departure from Italy, or learning Arabic in Toledo.
sources.qualifies: The page supports Gerard’s role in Toledo and a translation program, but does not state the specific claims above.

sources.title: 'Gerard of Cremona', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Gerard went to Toledo to learn Arabic and remained there for life. His translation of Ptolemy’s Almagest “was finished in 1175” and was “printed in 1515.” About 80 translations, not 87, were attributed to him.
sources.qualifies: The page supports the Toledo, Almagest, 1175, and Euclid claims, but gives about 80 translations and does not mention al-Khwarizmi.

gerard-of-cremona-translations-1175.verification_note: Burnett, Science in Context 2001, describes Gerard's translation programme at Toledo in the later twelfth century; Britannica dates his Almagest translation to 1175 and credits about 80 translations, not 87.

al-hassar-fraction-bar-1180.summary: Abu Bakr al-Hassar, who taught arithmetic in twelfth-century Ceuta on Morocco's Mediterranean coast, set out in his Kitab al-Bayan wa-l-tadhkar a way of writing fractions with numerator above denominator and a horizontal line between them, using the Hindu-Arabic digits already current in the Maghreb. He extended the device to chains of numerators and denominators for compound fractions. Fibonacci took up this notation in chapter 5 of Liber Abaci in 1202, and Moses ibn Tibbon translated al-Hassar's manual into Hebrew at Montpellier in 1271. Mohamed Aballagh and Ahmed Djebbar identified a surviving part of his second book, al-Kamil, in 1987. This bar became standard notation for fractions.

sources.title: Aballagh, Mohamed and Djebbar, Ahmed, 'Découverte d'un écrit mathématique d'al-Hassar (XIIe s.): Le livre I du Kamil', Historia Mathematica 14 (1987)
sources.author: Aballagh, Mohamed; Djebbar, Ahmed
sources.confirms: Identification of al-Hassar as a twelfth-century Maghrebi mathematician and of the surviving first book of his al-Kamil
sources.qualifies: Landing page redirected without displaying text; metadata confirmed through Crossref

sources.title: Pfeffer, Jeremy I., 'An Introductory Exposition: Christ Church MS 189, the Hebrew translation of al-Hassar's Kitab al-Bayan wa-l-tadhkar' (Christ Church Library, Oxford, 2023)
sources.author: Pfeffer, Jeremy I.
sources.venue: Christ Church Library, University of Oxford
sources.confirms: Al-Hassar taught in twelfth-century Ceuta; his key contribution was a fractional notation with numerator and denominator separated by a horizontal bar, taken up by Fibonacci in Liber Abaci (1202); ibn Tibbon's Hebrew translation completed 12 May 1271 at Montpellier

al-hassar-fraction-bar-1180.detail: Al-Hassar's manual belongs to a Maghrebi school of calculation that ran from Fez and Ceuta to Marrakesh, later including Ibn al-Banna al-Marrakushi, whose Talkhis amal al-hisab summarised the tradition around 1300. Its oldest dated copy of Kitab al-Bayan comes from 1194. Exact dates for al-Hassar are unknown, so 1180 is approximate. Fibonacci's adoption carried it into Latin Europe, and printed arithmetics after 1478 fixed it as common notation.

picture.alt: Page of Fibonacci's Liber abaci (Florence manuscript) showing fractions written with a horizontal bar, a notation he took from Maghrebi arithmetic
picture.credit: Wikimedia Commons

ibn-al-awwam-kitab-al-filaha-1180.summary: In late 12th-century Seville, Abu Zakariya Ibn al-Awwam writes Kitab al-Filaha, 34 or 35 chapters covering 585 plants and more than 50 fruit trees, with sections on soils, manures, grafting, irrigation, pests and livestock. He cites 112 earlier authors about 1,900 times, drawing on Ibn Wahshiyya's Nabataean Agriculture, Greek and Byzantine writers and Andalusi predecessors Ibn Hajjaj, Ibn Bassal, Abu l-Khayr and al-Tighnari, yet insists: 'I put forward nothing that I have not first proved by experiment on repeated occasions.' Jimenez-Castillo and Camarero place his work on his own land in Aljarafe outside Seville. Josef Banqueri printed a Spanish translation in Madrid in 1802 and Clement-Mullet a French one in 1864 to 1867, feeding 19th-century European agronomy.

sources.confirms: Identifies Ibn al-Awwam as 12th to 13th century author working on his own land in Aljarafe of Seville, compiling an encyclopedic Kitab al-Filaha from Nabataean, Greco-Byzantine and Andalusi sources and testing their claims himself.
sources.qualifies: Dates him broadly to 12th to 13th centuries rather than to a single year.

ibn-al-awwam-kitab-al-filaha-1180.verification_note: Author flourished late 12th century; no exact composition year survives. Chapter count given as 34 or 35 by different sources.
ibn-al-awwam-kitab-al-filaha-1180.detail: Thirty chapters treat crops and grafting, four treat cattle, poultry and bees. British Library holds a manuscript as Add MS 10461. Nothing is known of the author beyond name and city; Al-Qantara dates him to the 12th to 13th centuries from authors he cites, so his date is approximate. His book sums up Andalusi irrigated horticulture that spread citrus, sugar cane, rice, cotton and eggplant through Iberia.

nan-madol-1180.summary: Around 1180 Pohnpei's rulers built Nan Madol, 92 artificial islands of basalt in a Pacific lagoon. No one knows how the columns were moved. Built off Pohnpei in Micronesia, its islets of stone and coral fill are separated by tidal canals. Islet building began by the 8th or 9th century, and its megalithic walls date from around 1180 to 1200, when large basalt columns were brought from a volcanic plug on Pohnpei's far side. How they were moved is not known. Nan Madol served as ceremonial and political seat of Saudeleur rulers, who united Pohnpei until about 1628.

lalibela-rock-churches-1181.summary: From 1181 Ethiopians carved eleven churches down into rock at Lalibela, a pilgrims' Jerusalem. Tradition dates them to Zagwe king Gebre Meskel Lalibela's reign, around 1181 to 1221; most are thought to have been made in the 12th and 13th centuries, though dating is disputed. Their layout and names are widely read as a symbolic Jerusalem, which leads some experts to place construction after Saladin captured Jerusalem in 1187.

sources.qualifies: The page confirms rock-cut churches at Lalibela, but does not state the claimed number, ruler, or construction chronology.
