sources.confirms: The page states that “eleven medieval monolithic churches were carved out of rock” and attributes their building to King Lalibela, who set out “in the 12th century” to construct a “New Jerusalem.” It also describes them as the 13th-century “New Jerusalem.” It does not give King Lalibela’s reign dates or more specific.
sources.qualifies: It supports the eleven churches and 12th-century attribution, but does not state the claimed reign dates and also describes the churches as 13th-century.

lalibela-rock-churches-1181.verification_note: Fauvelle-Aymar et al., Antiquity 2010: construction sequence is hard to establish and these churches may be a long-lived ritual centre refashioned over time; UNESCO attributes them to King Lalibela in the twelfth to thirteenth century without reign dates, so 1181 is conventional.

picture.alt: Rock-hewn church of Bete Giyorgis at Lalibela seen from above, photographed in 2012.
picture.credit: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

joachim-of-fiore-1184.summary: In 1184 Pope Lucius III summoned Joachim of Fiore and urged him to press on with his biblical commentary, probably his Book of Harmony of New and Old Testaments, where he worked out his reading of history as three rising ages. Acclaimed as a prophet in his lifetime, Joachim was dimmed by condemnation at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215; Spiritual Franciscans and sects down to the 16th century took up his prophecy of a third age.

sources.title: Joachim Of Fiore
Reeves, Marjorie, 'The Originality and Influence of Joachim of Fiore', Traditio 36 (1980)
sources.author: Reeves, Marjorie
sources.confirms: The article examines Joachim's doctrine of three status of history and its later influence, and its notes record his exposition before Pope Lucius III in 1184.

sources.title: Gemeinhardt, Peter, 'Joachim the Theologian: Trinitarian Speculation and Doctrinal Debate', in A Companion to Joachim of Fiore (Brill, 2017), pp. 41-87
sources.author: Gemeinhardt, Peter
sources.confirms: A Brill companion chapter on Joachim's Trinitarian reading of history; bibliographic record confirmed, chapter text not read.

joachim-of-fiore-1184.detail:
Joachim was born about 1130 to 1135 at Celico and died in 1201 or 1202. He became a Cistercian monk at Sambucina and abbot of Corazzo in 1177; about 1191 he withdrew to contemplative life, and in 1196 Pope Celestine III let him form his disciples at San Giovanni in Fiore into their own order. His Book of Harmony worked chiefly in a pattern of twos, concords between Old and New Testaments; his pattern of threes grew from that, with a final age of the spirit proceeding from both earlier ages. He prophesied two new orders of spiritual men to guide that passage, hermits on the mountaintop and a mediating order, and the Franciscan and Dominican mendicants, hailed as those men, restored his standing as prophet.

The 1215 condemnation fell on his tract against Peter Lombard's doctrine of the Trinity. His Book of Figures, discovered in 1937, carried his ideas in drawings of flowering trees and geometric figures, and his double reputation as saint and heretic is still debated.

picture.alt: Tree diagram of the ages of history from a manuscript of Joachim of Fiore's Concordia, a medieval copy.
picture.credit: Deutsche Fotothek, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Europeana

letter-of-toledo-1184.summary: In 1184 a letter credited to Toledo's astrologers, one of a genre of re-dated forgeries, foretold ruin in 1186, and Europe panicked over a forecast. People sought refuge, sold possessions and gathered in penance, in one of Europe's earliest recorded outbreaks of collective hysteria; when that week passed quietly, astrologers claimed prayer had turned disaster aside.

sources.title: The Letter from Toledo Unleashes Collective Hysteria, Canadian Library Association
Wikisource: Folk-Lore, Volume 13, The Letter of Toledo
Museum of Hoaxes: The Toledo Letter (1184)
Mentgen, Gerd, Astrologie und Öffentlichkeit im Mittelalter (Hiersemann, 2005), ch. 1 'Toledobriefe und ähnliche Prognostiken', pp. 17-135
sources.author: Mentgen, Gerd
sources.venue: Anton Hiersemann, Stuttgart (Monographien zur Geschichte des Mittelalters 53)
sources.confirms: The Letter of Toledo circulated as a forged astrological prophecy of disaster for 1186, and spawned a long series of later Toledo letters.
sources.qualifies: Mentgen treats the 1184 letter as one stage in a genre whose earliest versions and later re-datings (to 1229, 1395, 1472, 1479) spread over three centuries.

letter-of-toledo-1184.verification_note: Mentgen (2005) shows Toledo letters formed a genre of re-dated forgeries rather than one 1184 text; its 1184 to 1186 version is best known but one among several.

windmill-post-mill-europe-1185.summary: In 1185 northern Europe's earliest securely dated windmill stood at Weedley in Yorkshire, bringing power to country without streams; 1180s records also name Dinton and Amberley, and some scholars list Swineshead in 1170. Vertical windmills, sails turning in a vertical plane, appeared before 1200 across northern France, eastern England and Flanders. Europe's earliest type was the post mill: its whole body, holding all its machinery, balanced on one large upright post so it could turn to face north-western Europe's shifting winds. These first mills ground cereals.

sources.title: Windmill - Wikipedia
'Windmill', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page dates the earliest-known references to a Persian millwright to 644 CE and to windmills in Seistan, Persia, to 915 CE. It says windmill use spread in Europe from the 12th century, and calls the post mill “the earliest form of vertical mill.” The earliest-known illustration of a tower mill is dated about 1420.
sources.qualifies: Post mills are identified as the earliest vertical-mill form, but the specific northern European reference is absent.

sources.title: Bridge, Martin, Luke Bonwick, Martin Davies and David Pearce, 'What do dendrochronology and other timber-dating methods tell us about the history of English post mills?', Vernacular Architecture 53 (2022)
sources.author: Bridge, Martin; Bonwick, Luke; Davies, Martin; Pearce, David
sources.confirms: No windmills existed in England through the eleventh century, and three references from the 1180s, at Dinton, Amberley and Weedley in Yorkshire, show the post-mill design established by then.
sources.qualifies: Names three 1180s mills rather than a single first windmill, and says the origin of the post-mill design is unknown.

sources.title: Hough, Carole, 'Another Note on Windmills', Notes and Queries 53 (2006), p. 417
sources.author: Hough, Carole
sources.confirms: There is no evidence for windmills in Britain before the late twelfth century, and the Weedley mill near Beverley in the East Riding of Yorkshire is recorded in 1185.
sources.qualifies: States that the first windmill on record in England is at Swineshead, Lincolnshire, in 1170, with Weedley 1185 the next.

sources.title: Campbell, Bruce M. S., 'Adapting to change: English seigniorial agriculture, 1250-1450', in English Seigniorial Agriculture, 1250-1450 (Cambridge University Press, 2000), pp. 411-440
sources.author: Campbell, Bruce M. S.
sources.confirms: The first recorded reference to an English windmill is in 1185, and windmill construction spread widely between 1180 and 1300 after a breakthrough in woodworking.

windmill-post-mill-europe-1185.verification_note: Campbell (2000) and Bridge et al. (Vernacular Architecture 2022) treat 1180s references, Weedley among them, as England's earliest secure windmills, while Hough (Notes and Queries 2006), following Kealey and Breeze, lists Swineshead in 1170 as first on record; 1185 is therefore its earliest certain date among several candidates.

picture.alt: Great Gransden post mill in Cambridgeshire, a surviving seventeenth-century example of the type, photographed in 2014.
picture.credit: Barry Marsh from London, England, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

jayavarman-vii-hospitals-roads-1186.summary: A Sanskrit inscription at Ta Prohm, dated 1186, records that Khmer king Jayavarman VII endowed 102 arogyasala, or hospitals, dedicated to Bhaisajyaguru, each staffed with physicians, attendants and stocks of rice, honey and medicines. Another stele at Preah Khan (1191) lists 121 rest houses spaced along roads toward Phimai and Champa. Mitch Hendrickson's survey shows these routes developing from ninth century and formalised under Jayavarman with laterite bridges and stone way stations. Hospital chapels still stand at Say Fong in Laos and across northeast Thailand, which makes this one of few medieval state health networks visible in stone.

sources.title: Hendrickson, Mitch, 'Historic routes to Angkor: development of the Khmer road system (ninth to thirteenth centuries AD) in mainland Southeast Asia', Antiquity 84 (2010)
sources.author: Hendrickson, Mitch
sources.confirms: Khmer road system, rest houses, bridges; organic development across reigns
sources.qualifies: Warns against attributing whole network to Jayavarman VII

sources.title: Honda, Megumu, 'A Sanskrit inscription of Say Fong, Laos', Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies 14 (1965)
sources.author: Honda, Megumu
sources.venue: Journal of Indian and Buddhist Studies
sources.confirms: Hospital inscription text: staff, provisions, Bhaisajyaguru dedication

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Jayavarman VII'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Crowned 1181; more than 100 hospitals and rest houses; roads radiating from capital

jayavarman-vii-hospitals-roads-1186.detail: Scholars read hospital numbers as programmatic claims rather than audited counts; some chapels may have been built in later reigns. Honda's 1965 reading of Say Fong inscription established staffing details that match Ta Prohm text. Hendrickson cautions that roads grew in stages and that attribution of every bridge to Jayavarman VII is unsafe.

picture.alt: Ta Prohm Kel, a hospital chapel of Jayavarman VII near Angkor Wat
picture.credit: Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China

mesa-verde-cliff-dwellings-1190.summary: By 1190 Ancestral Puebloans were building 150-room towns into Mesa Verde's cliffs. Within a century drought emptied them. Cliff Palace, with 150 rooms and 23 kivas, is one of North America's largest and housed about 125 people. By 1285, after severe and prolonged droughts, its people had migrated south into Arizona and New Mexico.

sources.title: Mesa Verde National Park
Varien, Mark D., The Mesa Verde Region (Oxford Handbooks Online, 2012)
sources.author: Varien, Mark D.; Kohler, Timothy A.; Ortman, Scott G.
sources.confirms: The page says Pueblo people “have not lived in the MVR since the late thirteenth century AD” and research there dates from 1874. It gives no dates or facts about cliff-dwelling construction, 1190, 1285, drought, Cliff Palace’s rooms or kivas, or its population.
sources.qualifies: The late-thirteenth-century departure is stated; the specific claims are not.

sources.title: 'Mesa Verde National Park', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says the Ancestral Pueblo peoples moved into canyon alcoves and began building cliff houses “between 1150 and 1200.” Cliff Palace had 217 rooms and 23 kivas and housed up to 250 people; 150 rooms describes Long House.
sources.qualifies: Cliff Palace’s room count differs, and the page does not state that the dwellings were built around 1190-1270.

mesa-verde-cliff-dwellings-1190.verification_note: Varien (Oxford Handbook 2012) places cliff dwelling construction in late 1100s to 1200s with depopulation by 1300; Britannica gives Cliff Palace 217 rooms, while 150 rooms matches Long House.

picture.alt: Cliff Palace at Mesa Verde under its sandstone overhang, photographed in 2006.
picture.credit: Andreas F. Borchert, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

qutb-minar-delhi-1199.summary: Qutb al-Din Aibak, Ghurid commander and later first Delhi Sultan, began a minaret in 1199 beside Quwwat al-Islam mosque, Delhi's first congregational mosque. His successor Iltutmish raised it to four storeys; later rulers repaired and capped it, reaching 72.5 metres, tallest masonry tower in India. Its shaft tapers from 14.32 metres at base to 2.75 metres at top, with alternating angular and rounded flutings in red and buff sandstone and bands of Quranic calligraphy. Indian masons used corbelled construction and carved motifs from local temple practice, while Persian inscriptions name Ghurid patrons. This complex set a template for Sultanate building in Delhi for three centuries.

sources.title: Anthony Welch, Hussein Keshani and Alexandra Bain, 'Epigraphs, Scripture, and Architecture in the Early Delhi Sultanate', Muqarnas 19 (2002)
sources.author: Anthony Welch; Hussein Keshani; Alexandra Bain
sources.confirms: Qutb complex epigraphy, Aibak and Iltutmish phases

sources.title: Nayanjot Lahiri, 'Qutb Minar', in Archaeology and the Public Purpose (Oxford University Press, 2021)
sources.author: Nayanjot Lahiri
sources.confirms: Qutb complex within Delhi's medieval archaeology

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi', World Heritage List 233
sources.confirms: 72.5 m height; 14.32 m base to 2.75 m top; red and buff sandstone; begun 1199; Alai Darwaza 1311

qutb-minar-delhi-1199.verification_note: UNESCO text read in full. Muqarnas article confirmed through publisher record and abstract.
qutb-minar-delhi-1199.detail: Welch, Keshani and Bain read the complex's epigraphy in Muqarnas to show how inscriptions project Ghurid and then Delhi Sultanate authority. Lahiri's Oxford monograph on Delhi archaeology sets the minar within its medieval cityscape. UNESCO gives 72.5 m height, tapering diameters and construction between 1199 and 1503 for later repairs. Alai Darwaza (1311) added a true arch and dome to this complex.

picture.alt: Qutb Minar, a fluted red sandstone tower in Delhi, seen past a neem tree
picture.credit: Shikhers

chimu-intervalley-canal-1200.summary: Chimú rulers at Chan Chan, on Peru's north coast, ordered an intervalley canal, known as La Cumbre, to bring Chicama river water across a desert divide into Moche valley fields and city reservoirs. Surveyors held gradients over more than 70 kilometres of open channel, built aqueduct embankments across dry ravines and shaped channel cross-sections to control flow speed. Ortloff, Moseley and Feldman's 1982 hydraulic analysis found many trial alignments near its lower end where tectonic tilt had altered slopes, and concluded construction stopped before Chicama water ever reached Moche. Kus answered in 1984 that parts did run water and that drought politics, not uplift, explain abandonment. Chimú canal networks nonetheless irrigated far more land than Moche valley farmers work today.

sources.title: Ortloff, Charles R., Moseley, Michael E. and Feldman, Robert A., 'Hydraulic Engineering Aspects of the Chimu Chicama-Moche Intervalley Canal', American Antiquity 47 (1982)
sources.author: Ortloff, Charles R.; Moseley, Michael E.; Feldman, Robert A.
sources.confirms: Computer analysis of channel design, trial alignments at the distal end and the conclusion that construction stopped before Chicama water reached Moche valley.

sources.title: Kus, James S., 'The Chicama-Moche Canal: Failure or Success? An Alternative Explanation for an Incomplete Canal', American Antiquity 49 (1984)
sources.author: Kus, James S.
sources.confirms: Chimú were skilled engineers and the canal functioned in a limited manner.
sources.qualifies: Argues drought politics rather than tectonic uplift explain abandonment and that the canal did carry some water.

sources.title: Ortloff, Charles R., 'Canal Builders of Pre-Inca Peru', Scientific American 259 (1988)
sources.author: Ortloff, Charles R.
sources.confirms: Overview of Chimú canal engineering, near-critical flow design and canal length.

chimu-intervalley-canal-1200.verification_note: Ortloff, Moseley and Feldman (1982) hold that construction stopped before any Chicama water reached Moche valley; Kus (1984) holds that sections functioned in a limited manner and that abandonment followed the end of a drought. Date is by ceramic association with Chimú expansion, so approximate.
chimu-intervalley-canal-1200.detail: Ortloff's computer modelling of channel sections showed Chimú builders varying width, depth and wall slope to hold water near critical flow, a design principle not written down in Europe until the eighteenth century. Pozorski and Pozorski's 1982 comment and Kus's 1984 article dispute how much water passed and why work ended. Dating rests on ceramic association with Chimú expansion, roughly 1000 to 1400; no single construction year is known.

picture.alt: Adobe walls of Chan Chan, Chimú capital near Trujillo, Peru; a modern photograph of the city whose fields the canals served
picture.credit: Håkan Svensson, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: resized to 1200 px long edge; converted to JPEG

dresden-codex-1200.summary: Around 1200 Maya astronomers made the Dresden Codex, whose tables predict Venus and eclipses. It is one of four Maya books to survive. It comes from Chichén Itzá's region. It dates to about 1200 to 1345, though estimates range from the 12th to 14th centuries. Its 78 pages of fig-bark paper fold screen-style to 3.7 metres and carry hieroglyphs with detailed Venus tables and lunar tables whose intervals match eclipses. Long thought to be the Americas' oldest surviving book, it ceded that place in 2018 to the Maya Codex of Mexico. Librarian Ernst Förstemann published its first full facsimile in 1880 and deciphered its calendar numerals, one key step in reading Maya writing.

sources.title: Dresden Codex - Wikipedia
B. The Dresden Codex: Description and Known History (Astronomy in the Maya Codices, 2011)
sources.confirms: The page describes the Dresden Codex as “a book of 39 physical pages,” thought originally to have formed “a single screenfold object.” Its contents list a “Venus Table in the Dresden Codex” and an “Eclipse Table in the Dresden Codex.” It gives no date or date range, creator, Chichén Itzá provenance, or claim that it is one of.
sources.qualifies: Table topics are listed; the other claims are not stated).

sources.title: [PDF] 33 IDENTIFICATION OF POSTCLASSIC MAYA CONSTELLATIONS ...
sources.confirms: The page says the Dresden Codex “tells us about the cyclic appearance of the Venus and lunar eclipses” (p. 36) and is one of “only four codices remaining in existence today”: Paris, Madrid, Dresden, and Grolier (p.
sources.qualifies: Venus and lunar eclipses and survival as one of four are supported; origin and production-date claims are not stated.

sources.title: 'Dresden Codex', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The codex is “thought to date from the 11th or 12th century,” not 1200-1300s. It contains “eclipse-prediction tables” and information on “the synodical period of Venus.” The page does not state that it has 78 pages or is made of bark paper.
sources.qualifies: The tables are confirmed, but the stated date differs and the page count and material are absent.

dresden-codex-1200.verification_note: Bricker and Bricker (2011) and the UNAM article confirm Venus and eclipse tables and this codex as one of four survivors; dating ranges from eleventh to twelfth century (Britannica) to a Postclassic first date of 1228, so 1200 is approximate.

picture.alt: Black and white reproduction of a Maya Dresden Codex page with figures and numeral tables, from SLUB Dresden.
picture.credit: SLUB Dresden / Deutsche Fotothek, Public domain, via Europeana

golem-eleazar-worms-1200.summary: Around 1200 the rabbi Eleazar of Worms wrote the first recipe for a golem, a clay man brought to life by words. The Rhineland mystic's instructions appear in his commentary on Sefer Yetzirah, an early Hebrew text on creation through letters. His recipe called for reciting letter combinations with God's name, 221 or 231 pairs in all, over shaped earth. In this tradition such rites were mystical practice and legend, not demonstrated beings; Prague's famous golem is a story first recorded centuries later.

sources.title: Golem - Wikipedia
[PDF] Jack Spira, Divine Speech in Sefer Yetzirah and Jābirean Takwīn
Idel, Moshe, Golem: Jewish Magical and Mystical Traditions on the Artificial Anthropoid (State University of New York Press, 1990), ch. 'Ashkenazi Hasidic Views on the Golem'
sources.author: Idel, Moshe
sources.venue: State University of New York Press
sources.confirms: University-press monograph on medieval golem traditions, with a chapter on the Ashkenazi Hasidim including Eleazar of Worms's letter-permutation recipe in his commentary on Sefer Yetzirah.

sources.title: Scholem, Gershom, 'The Idea of the Golem', in On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism, trans. Ralph Manheim (Schocken, 1965)
sources.author: Scholem, Gershom
sources.confirms: Scholem quotes Eleazar of Worms's instructions: two or three adepts take virgin mountain earth, knead it in running water, form a golem and recite the alphabet combinations derived from the gates of Sefer Yetzirah over it.

hanseatic-league-1200.summary: From around 1200 the Hanseatic League of northern trading towns pooled privileges and protection, running trade from London to Novgorod. Member cities shared trading privileges, defended their ships and ran foreign posts called kontors in Novgorod, Bergen, Bruges and London, carrying grain, fur, salt, timber and cloth in broad cogs. Its first formal diet met in 1356, and it dominated northern European trade for three centuries. Competition from Dutch and English merchants and rising territorial states wore it down, and its last diet met in 1669.

sources.title: Hanseatic League - Wikipedia
Zimmern, Helen, The Hansa Towns (T. Fisher Unwin, 1889)
sources.author: Zimmern, Helen
sources.confirms: The confederation of cities first met under the name Hansa in 1241, the year of the Lubeck-Hamburg alliance.
sources.qualifies: Zimmern dates the first use of the Hansa name to 1241, four decades after the record's 1200.

sources.title: 'Hanseatic League', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Lübeck became a base after its capture in 1158; town associations grew from the early 13th century, and by the 1280s the western merchants’ confederation was joined to the north German towns.
sources.qualifies: London and Bruges as kontors, and the 1356 first diet, are not stated.

hanseatic-league-1200.verification_note: Zimmern (and the Brill Companion chapter titles) place this league's formation in the 1200s, from 1241; 1200 marks only earlier Lubeck-Gotland trade.

lapphyttan-blast-furnace-1200.summary: At Lapphyttan in the Norberg mining district of central Sweden, peasant ironmasters smelt iron in a water-blown shaft furnace tall enough to produce liquid cast iron, which they then refine into wrought osmund bars. A 2011 Journal of Archaeological Science study of lake sediments and radiocarbon dates calls Lapphyttan Europe's oldest known blast furnace and finds mining and settlement there began as early as the 11th or 12th century. Jernkontoret, Sweden's steel producers' association, records 14th-century exports of osmund iron to Lubeck and Danzig at around 2,000 tonnes a year. Chinese founders had cast iron for more than a millennium; blast furnaces reached central Europe only by the mid-14th century and England around 1500.

sources.title: Bindler, R., Segerstrom, U., Pettersson-Jensen, I.-M., Berg, A., Hansson, S., Holmstrom, H., Olsson, K. and Renberg, I., 'Early medieval origins of iron mining and settlement in central Sweden: multiproxy analysis of sediment and peat records from the Norberg mining district', Journal of Archaeological Science 38 (2011), 291-300
sources.author: Bindler, Richard; Segerstrom, Ulf; Pettersson-Jensen, Ing-Marie; Berg, Anna; Hansson, Sophia; Holmstrom, Harald; Olsson, Kristina; Renberg, Ingemar
sources.confirms: Abstract read on the SLU repository page: Lapphyttan described as Europe's oldest known blast furnace; mining and settlement in the Norberg district as early as the 11th or 12th century.

sources.title: Jernkontoret, 'The history of the Swedish steel industry'
sources.author: Jernkontoret
sources.confirms: Osmund iron of about 3 hg per piece; 14th-century exports to Lubeck and Danzig of about 2,000 tonnes a year.

sources.title: 'Blast furnace', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Blast furnaces in central Europe by the mid-14th century and in England about 1500.

lapphyttan-blast-furnace-1200.verification_note: Archaeologists date Lapphyttan's operation broadly to the 12th and 13th centuries; 1200 is a midpoint, not a documented founding year.
lapphyttan-blast-furnace-1200.detail: Britannica dates blast furnaces in central Europe to the mid-14th century and in England to about 1500, two or three centuries after Lapphyttan, so Swedish finds moved Europe's origin of cast iron back by about two hundred years. Groups of peasant farmers rather than lords or monasteries ran the Norberg furnaces, and osmund iron refined from their cast product, sold in pieces of about 3 hectograms, became Sweden's main export through Hanseatic Baltic ports.

picture.alt: Information board and excavated house foundation at the medieval Lapphyttan blast furnace site, Norberg, Sweden.
picture.credit: Calle Eklund/V-wolf, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

motu-hiri-trade-voyages-1200.summary: Motu villages around what is now Port Moresby fired tens of thousands of clay pots each year and sailed them westward in lagatoi, multi-hulled craft lashed from dugout hulls with crab-claw sails, to Gulf of Papua villages 300 to 400 kilometres away. There Motu crews exchanged pots and shell ornaments for sago and canoe logs, waiting weeks for monsoon winds to carry them home. Excavations at Gulf sites found Motu-style pottery in deposits beginning after about 1200 CE, and traced shifting production centres across six centuries. Hiri shows a Melanesian maritime trade system built on seasonal wind knowledge, standardised ceramics and ritual exchange partnerships rather than on markets or money.

sources.title: Skelly, Robert John; David, Bruno, Hiri: Archaeology of Long-Distance Maritime Trade along the South Coast of Papua New Guinea (University of Hawai'i Press, 2017)
sources.author: Skelly, Robert John; David, Bruno
sources.confirms: Excavated Gulf of Papua sites document long-distance ceramic exchange from about 1200 CE
sources.qualifies: Dating of earliest Motu-style wares still being refined

sources.title: Allen, Jim, review of Skelly and David, Hiri, Antiquity 92 (2018)
sources.author: Allen, Jim
sources.confirms: Review confirms chronology and scale of Skelly and David's hiri archaeology
sources.qualifies: Review notes gaps in ceramic sequence

sources.title: Urwin, Chris; Lamb, Lara; Skelly, Robert, 'Rethinking agency in hiri exchange relationships on Papua New Guinea's south coast', Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 69 (2023)
sources.author: Urwin, Chris; Lamb, Lara; Skelly, Robert
sources.confirms: Oral traditions show Gulf partners as active agents in exchange
sources.qualifies: Ethnographic hiri of 1800s may differ from earlier forms

motu-hiri-trade-voyages-1200.verification_note: Start date is approximate; authors speak of hiri developing over several centuries rather than beginning in one year.
motu-hiri-trade-voyages-1200.detail: Lagatoi were assembled from several hulls for each voyage and taken apart afterwards; a single vessel could carry more than 1,000 pots and 20 to 30 tonnes of sago on return. Urwin, Lamb and Skelly argue from oral traditions that Gulf communities shaped exchange terms rather than acting as passive recipients. Earlier ceramic networks along this coast go back 2,000 years; hiri in its documented Motu form dates from roughly 1200 onwards. A 2018 review notes gaps in its ceramic sequence.

picture.alt: Motu lakatoi trading vessel with crab-claw sails near Elevala Island, Port Moresby, photographed by J. W. Lindt in 1885
picture.credit: John William Lindt

sweet-potato-polynesia-1200.summary: Charred sweet potato tuber from Tangatatau rockshelter on Mangaia, Cook Islands, dates to about 1000 to 1100 CE, centuries before any European ship entered Polynesia. Comparison of herbarium specimens collected on eighteenth-century voyages with modern landraces found a distinct Polynesian lineage descended from Ecuadorian and Peruvian varieties, separate from later Spanish and Portuguese introductions through Mexico and Manila. Genomic evidence added a single contact episode between Polynesians and Indigenous South Americans around 1150 to 1230 CE. Together these studies place kumara in Polynesian gardens by roughly 1200, carried by Polynesian canoes rather than drifting across an ocean on its own.

sources.title: Roullier, Caroline; Benoit, Laure; McKey, Doyle B.; Lebot, Vincent, 'Historical collections reveal patterns of diffusion of sweet potato in Oceania obscured by modern plant movements and recombination', PNAS 110 (2013)
sources.author: Roullier, Caroline; Benoit, Laure; McKey, Doyle B.; Lebot, Vincent
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Herbarium genetics show a pre-European Polynesian sweet potato lineage from Ecuador and Peru
sources.qualifies: Cannot tell who sailed in which direction

sources.title: Ioannidis, Alexander G. et al., 'Native American gene flow into Polynesia predating Easter Island settlement', Nature 583 (2020)
sources.author: Ioannidis, Alexander G.; Blanco-Portillo, Javier; Sandoval, Karla; et al.
sources.confirms: Genomic signal of Native American admixture in eastern Polynesians dated c. 1150 to 1230 CE
sources.qualifies: Contact date carries a century of uncertainty

sources.title: Hather, Jon; Kirch, P. V., 'Prehistoric sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) from Mangaia Island, Central Polynesia', Antiquity 65 (1991)
sources.author: Hather, Jon; Kirch, Patrick V.
sources.confirms: Directly dated charred tuber on Mangaia c. 1000 to 1100 CE
sources.qualifies: Single site; identification rests on parenchyma anatomy

sweet-potato-polynesia-1200.verification_note: Roullier (2013) and Ioannidis (2020) agree on pre-European transfer but differ on where contact took place; Hather and Kirch give a date range for Mangaia, so 1200 is a rounded anchor.
sweet-potato-polynesia-1200.detail: Polynesian names for sweet potato (kumara, kuumala) echo Quechua kumar, a linguistic link noted since Rivet. Hather and Kirch's Mangaia tuber remains a key direct date; later finds in Hawai'i and New Zealand are younger. Herbarium genetics cannot tell whether Polynesians sailed to South America and returned, or whether South Americans reached eastern Polynesia; Ioannidis's genomic signal favours contact near Marquesas or Tuamotu islands. Montenegro and others once argued for natural dispersal by seed, a view now seldom held.

tui-tonga-maritime-state-1200.summary: On Tongatapu, chiefs of the Tu'i Tonga line raised stone-faced house platforms, a trilithon at Heketa and a sequence of monumental tombs (langi) at Lapaha from about 1200 to 1400 CE, alongside a rock-cut canal for canoes. Geochemical sourcing found that 66 percent of stone adzes recovered from these central places came from Samoa, Fiji and even Tahiti, some 2,500 kilometres away. Tonga became one polity spanning an entire archipelago, drawing tribute and marriage partners from neighbouring island groups by canoe. Its rulers held exotic stone as political capital, giving archaeologists a rare material signature of long-distance power in Oceania.

tui-tonga-maritime-state-1200.verification_note: Sources place monumental construction mainly in 1300s and 1400s; a 1200 anchor with end year 1500 reflects an approximate start for state formation rather than a single event.
tui-tonga-maritime-state-1200.detail: A 2008 survey dated Lapaha's monumental core to fourteenth and fifteenth centuries; later work at Heketa pushed early ceremonial architecture back toward 1200 to 1300. Tongan oral tradition lists Tu'i Tonga rulers over many generations, and archaeology now gives those traditions a chronology without treating them as literal king lists. Sourcing used trace elements and isotopes on basalt to match quarries in Samoa (Tutuila) and Society Islands. Kingdom structure persisted into Cook's visits in the 1770s.

mongol-empire-era-1206.summary: In 1206 Genghis Khan united the Mongols; the empire that followed carried paper, gunpowder and printing west. Temüjin, having united the nomadic tribes of Mongolia's steppe, was proclaimed Genghis Khan that year. Conquests under him and his successors stretched Mongol rule from Eastern Europe to Japan's sea, history's largest contiguous land empire. It brought about one century of relative order across Eurasia, in which trade routes, postal relays and travellers carried technologies, goods and ideas between China, Islamic lands and Europe. After Möngke Khan died in 1259 his empire split into four khanates.
